en: *Fahua Xuanyi Shiqian*, Scroll One.
Narrated by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhànrán.
Formerly, while on Mount Tiantai, I recorded the responses to various questions as they were posed; I did not have the leisure to seek them out [at that time].

In investigating the development of the textual flow, I have not yet meticulously demarcated the phrases and clauses; returning late to the Vihāra, I have added superficial embellishments based on my own limited perspective. However, what I have recorded is none other than a synthesis of oral reports and my own research into the sūtras and śāstras. While my cognitive faculties are dim and deficient, my tendency toward prolixity or brevity has become habitual; I dare present this to future scholars, hoping they will feel free to add to or delete from it as they see fit.
Regarding the term "Private Record" (Siji): the Venerable Zhiyan recorded what the Great Master had taught at Jiangling for his own use, not sharing it with others; therefore, it is called "private."

Regarding "Dependent Origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*): this describes the occasion for what was recorded and sets forth the origins of the teaching. Within this, first setting forth the virtues of the Master and the intent of the transmission is called the General Introduction.
Next, the profound text (*xuánwén*) is formally introduced, which does not exceed five meanings and the deep purport of the fundamental and the derivative (*běnjì*).
The initial introduction is divided into two parts:
first, the sequence of the Master’s virtues; second, from the words "How fortunate! onwards, the clarification of the intent behind the transmission and narration.
The initial passage consists of two parts:
first, the enumeration of the ten virtues; second, the conclusion that attributes [these qualities] to my teacher, beginning with the words "Only I.
Within the first section on the ten virtues, the term "Great Dharma" (mahādharma) is used generally to refer to the Buddha's teachings as the Great Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "gradual eastward spread": from the time when Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna first arrived during the dream of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, until the reign of Emperor Wen of the Sui when the patriarchs of the Tiantai and Jingxiu schools manifested their responses, all those who practiced meditation, expounded the doctrines, or engaged in translation gradually permeated this land to propagate the Buddha-dharma. Among those recorded in the monastic histories, there is not one who did not attend lectures before attaining their own understanding of the Buddha-vehicle.

The "Buddha Vehicle" (Buddhayāna) refers to this present scripture; it is eternally distinct from other teachings and differs from the three, five, seven, or nine vehicles. Nevertheless, by opening and harmonizing them so that they all return to the single ultimate, it is called the Buddha Vehicle.

As for what is called the "History of the Sangha" (*Sengshi*), it is like the hundred-fascicle collection compiled by Wang Jianqi, the Secretary to the Prince Wenxuan of the Song dynasty, which resembles secular historical records where the Left Scribe records events and the Right Scribe records speech.
The *Book of Rites* states:
"When there is movement, the Left Scribe records it; when there are words, the Right Scribe records them.
All that has been collected here does not exceed these two categories—words and deeds—and following this precedent, it is thus called the *Monastic History* (*Sengshi*).

Furthermore, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) in thirteen fascicles, compiled by Dharma Master Jiao of Jiaxiang, is divided into ten categories; yet none among them ever record anyone like the Great Master Tiantai who was permitted to study on his own initiative. This very practice of being permitted to study on one's own initiative is precisely one of the ten virtues mentioned in the present text.

Furthermore, the nine virtues beginning from "Even if" (*zhònglìng*) are all recorded in the Master’s *Separate Biography* (*Biéchuán*); Zhāng'ān extracted them to serve as a preface to the Master's virtues.
Within the first virtue, the character "jù" (詎) is correctly read as "wú" (無).
Regarding the term "縱" (zòng) appearing within each of the nine virtues listed below, it means to speak from a concessive standpoint.

Although one may concede that there might be a first [virtue], there is ultimately no second, nor even a tenth; therefore, the conclusion below states: "Only I, the wise one, possess all these merits."

"Awakening" refers to his realization and understanding of the One Vehicle within the Samādhi of the Great Enlightenment Lotus Sūtra Dharma-assembly, where he acted as a proxy for the Dharma Master to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* written in golden characters.
“Dhāraṇī” means “total retention” (zongchi) in this language.
Rising from samādhi, he presented his realization to his teacher, who said, “This is the dhāraṇī of the preliminary skillful means for the Lotus Sūtra.”
Regarding the phrase "even if one possesses concentration and wisdom": awakening to insight belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*), while entering meditative absorption belongs to concentration (*samādhi*).
"A grand banquet" refers to the extensive propagation of these two dharmas, concentration and wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "to decline and dismiss" (*xieqian*): one reflects upon one's own inability to benefit others as a form of apology (*xie*), while setting forth the assembly and refusing to accept their offerings is termed "dismissal" (*qian*).
[The Master] lived in seclusion at Huading, Fulong, and Tangxi.

Regarding the phrase "avoiding the world" and so forth: renouncing fame and profit constitutes "avoiding the world," while advancing one's own Way constitutes "guarding the profound. Because Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty repeatedly issued edicts inviting him to reside [at court], it is said that he was "summoned to serve as State Preceptor for two kingdoms."
Regarding the "Taiji Hall," this refers to the name of the principal hall of the Chen dynasty, which was called Taiji.

Regarding the "Three Rites," the Chen Emperor issued an edict stating: "The state has long maintained the two assemblies of the *Renwang jing*. We respectfully request that you deign to open these lectures in the Taiji Hall; all matters concerning the ritual protocols and arrangements shall be subject to your instructions."
When the Dharma assembly was first inaugurated, the Sovereign personally performed three prostrations amidst the multitude.
As the Son of Heaven is the lord of ten thousand chariots, it is said that "the ten-thousand-chariot sovereign bowed his knee."
Regarding the term "ten thousand chariots" (*wan sheng*), Bao of the *Lunyu* quotes the *Wangzhi*:

"In ancient times, there was the well-field system (*jingtian*); a square *li* constituted a well (*jing*), ten wells made one chariot (*sheng*), and thus a state of one hundred *li* possessed exactly one thousand chariots."
The states of the feudal lords possessed a thousand chariots, while the state of the Son of Heaven possessed ten thousand chariots; hence he is called the "Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots.
Regarding the phrase "the monastic and the secular" and so forth: one hundred high seats represent the monastic, and the hundred officials represent the secular.

Regarding the phrase "Profoundly Awakening to the Perfect Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra": it is called "profound" (*xuan*) because it explains the sūtra through five meanings that comprehensively encompass the five flavors.
It is called the "perfect meaning" (*yuan yi*) because it neither combines nor incorporates other scriptures, but rather opens them up or supersedes them entirely.
"Expository eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) is as explained in the first commentary of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Regarding "day and night" and so forth, this is an illustration;
it is like a suspended river flowing forth that does not exhaust itself day or night.

These ten virtues collectively illustrate the characteristics of one who awakens to understanding and extensively propagates the sūtras; thus, the first virtue states, "one personally understands the Buddha-vehicle," while the final virtue states, "it flows forth day and night."

Regarding his conception in the womb, there were spiritual wonders; regarding his birth, there were auspicious signs. From childhood, he was sincere as he followed teachers to seek the Way; both ruler and subjects held him in precious esteem, and both the monastic and lay communities turned their hearts toward him. At the time of his death, he manifested signs, and after his passing, there were miraculous responses, all of which are detailed in the *Separate Biography*.
The subsequent section on the transmission and narration is divided into three parts:

first, an account praising the subtle merit of what has been received; second, from "Furthermore" (*bing fu*) onwards, a formal clarification of the transmission and narration for the benefit of those in the present; third, from "Or perhaps" (*hou yi*) onwards, an account of one's own supplementary assistance to encourage faith.
At the outset, he humbled himself by calling himself by his own name;
this is what is meant by "humble learning. "Xing" (幸) is a term used for self-reflection.
"Jianye" is also called Jiankang; it was the capital known as Ye during the Jin and Song dynasties, and is present-day Jiangning.
Formerly it was called Yangzhou; after the Sui dynasty extinguished the Chen, the name of Yangzhou was transferred to the north of the Yangtze River, while Jiangling became Jingzhou.

Therefore, the subsequent line states, "The journey between Jing and Yang spans nearly ten thousand li. Here, "jāng" (will/should) means "approximately"; it signifies that the distance is roughly, or vaguely, about ten thousand li.
The region south of the Han River is called Jing, extending from the southern reaches of the Han River to the south of Mount Heng.
The region south of the Yangtze River is called Yang, extending from the Jiangjing (the Yangtze at the capital) to the South Sea.
Regarding "Mount Tai" and "Heli," they are fully explained as in the first fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.

Regarding the phrase "not only have they not heard what they have not heard," etc., this expresses lamentation over those who have lost their opportunity to hear. As stated in the *Zhi guan*, the *Chan men*, and the *Jing ming shu*, when there are remaining portions of the teaching that have not been completed, these are termed "not having heard."
The phrase "Moreover" (*yì nǎi*) indicates that the humble author acknowledges his own inability to fully grasp the meaning of what he has heard.

Regarding the expression "unfolding and rolling up, piercing and admiring": this refers to Zhàngān’s general praise for having twice edited and twice read the text, finding its principles firm and its intent lofty. It is like the disciples of Confucius praising the depth of Confucius’s wisdom: as they peered over the walls of his palace, the more they pierced through them, the firmer they found it; the more they looked up at it, the loftier it appeared. It is like drinking from the waters of the Great River—one returns with a full belly, yet cannot fathom its depth.
"Still, I regret that my karmic conditions were shallow. Below this, he clarifies the origin of his private record.

Although he now wishes to record it, he regrets that he heard it only once; since the Great Master passed into extinction, he has been unable to hear it again, leaving him with no one from whom to seek clarification, like a calf longing for its mother's milk.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, he reflects," it is called "both" because he reflects upon himself and contemplates others.

He reflects that his own practice is insufficient and contemplates that others have not yet heard [the teaching]; if he were not to record what he has heard, there would be the suffering for those others in the future of never hearing the Buddha Vehicle. Therefore, it is said, "this is to be pitied."

Regarding the phrase "whether on trees or on stones," it is as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* concerning the youth of the Snowy Mountains, who, having heard half a verse, inscribed it upon a stone wall.

Furthermore, it is as at the beginning of the "Chapter on Rejoicing" in the present sutra, where, according to what one has heard, one explains it to the best of one's ability for parents, kinsmen, and others within villages and fields.
"Yù" (聿) means "to follow.
As for the "sacred scriptures," they refer to those transmitted according to the present sutra and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and others.
The "gate of ambrosia" refers to the true mark of eternal abiding, which is like celestial ambrosia—an elixir of immortality.
Now, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is able to lead one to penetrate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); therefore, it is called a "gate.
The initial general introduction is concluded.
Next follows the formal introduction to the profound text, which consists of three sections in total:

The first is the preface to the *Dachishi biexing jing* (The Scripture on the Master’s Special Practice); next, from "A Private Preface for the King" onwards, is the preface written by the recorder; third, from "This Sublime Dharma" onwards, is the preface by Xuánwén.
At the beginning, the character "Wáng" (王) is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*), meaning "to arise" or "the beginning.
Since it introduces the commencement of the various texts, it is called "Xùwáng" (序王).
The initial introduction is divided into two parts:
first, a general overview of the five meanings to explain the title; second, from the words "The Recordist" (*ji-zhe*) onwards, a detailed explanation based on the general title.
The first section further consists of three parts:
First, the *Saddharma* (Wondrous Dharma) is explained; second, the *Padma* (Lotus) is explained; third, the *Sūtra* is explained.
Regarding the first section, there are two parts:
first, "Wondrous" (*miao*); second, "Dharma" (*fa*).

Regarding the detailed explanation below that first addresses the "Dharma" and subsequently the "Sublime," this was done for the sake of following the logical sequence of the meaning; however, since we have now provided a brief explanation, we shall follow the sequence of the names.
First, in explaining the "Sublime," by citing only the single term "inconceivable," one has already distinguished it from the "conceivable."

In that [system], because they seek to establish contemplation through cessation, they regard mutual dependence as the coarse "conceivable" and the solitary non-dependence as the subtle "inconceivable.

Now it is not so; in the Perfect Middle, both temporal dependence and absolute non-dependence are equally subtle, whereas in other flavors, depending on the specific section, they may be either subtle or coarse.

If the three previous teachings are consistently considered coarse during their respective periods, they are only designated as "wondrous" once they have been opened up by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Because the meaning of the "mutual dependence" (*xiāngdài*) in the *Zhìguān* resembles that of the Separate Teaching (*biéjiào*), it is judged to be coarse.

Now, this "Sublime Name" encompasses both the original and the manifested aspects, whereas that "Sublime Contemplation" in the aforementioned text pertains solely to the Perfect [Teaching]. Although they differ, they are identical; this can be understood through careful investigation.
The subsequent text provides an extensive explanation, so there is no need for further elaboration here.
Next, regarding the explanation of the Dharma: briefly stated, the "realms" (dhātus) fully encompass the three thousandfold world;

a detailed explanation is provided later. As for the "wondrous praise of the Dharma," the Dharma itself is simply wondrous. The terms "expedient" and "real" include [the categories of] bestowal and so forth; since these three meanings differ, they are not separately set forth here as they are discussed within the section on analogies.
Next, the explanation of the lotus flower is divided into six parts:
first, the general establishment;
second, the intended meaning of the analogy;...
Third, from "First, for the sake of... onwards, there is an individual explanation;
fourth, from "Therefore... onwards, there is a conclusion regarding the sequence of the dharma and the parable to clarify their intended meaning;
fifth, from "Dispelling the illusory city... onwards, there is an exploration of the sutra’s essential purport to manifest the relationship between the dharma and the parable.
Sixth, the section beginning with "one period" summarizes the purpose of the preceding analogies to demonstrate their ultimate conclusion.

Regarding the initial passage: since the Wondrous Dharma does not transcend the provisional and the real, the lotus is used as an analogy for the Real, while the flower is used as an analogy for the Provisional.
Regarding the subsequent meaning: "Liang" (excellent) refers to the starting point of its initiation. Why is the metaphor of flowers established for the Dharma?
It is because the Dharma is difficult to understand.
"Jia" (provisional) means to borrow or rely upon; "zhang" (manifest) signifies to reveal or make clear.
It is because there is nothing other than the lotus by which the wondrous Dharma can be manifested.

The term used for what is thus manifested is "how much more" (kuàng). It fully reveals both the fundamental and the provisional aspects of the ten wondrousnesses and the ten coarsenesses, comprehensively encompassing the three categories of cause, fruit, essence, principle, and function; therefore, it is said to be "numerous."

I have no leisure at present to elaborate upon this preface; I shall briefly illustrate the relationship between the "Original" (hon) and the "Trace" (saku) to encompass the many paths. "Nyi" is also used in the sense of "comparison.

Regarding the preceding and succeeding sections, they consist merely of the two gates of Original and Trace, each containing fourteen chapters; since there are three chapters in the former and three in the latter, it is said that "they together comprise six."
In the subsequent detailed explanation, there are two parts:
first, the traces (traces of the Buddha's activity), and second, the fundamental [reality]. This is because it follows the sequential order of the scriptural text.
Second, according to the method of transformation, one must first lower [the banner] and subsequently sweep away [the dust];
third, according to the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, one proceeds from the shallow to the profound.
If one uses the flower to represent the traces and the lotus to represent the source, their sequence cannot be definitively distinguished.

Why is this? When the trace descends from the fundamental, the fundamental is prior and the trace is posterior; when the fundamental is revealed through the trace, the trace is prior and the fundamental is posterior. Although this is so in terms of the capacities of sentient beings, in terms of the Buddha, the fundamental is ultimately placed at the beginning; thus, the lotus is prior and the flower is posterior, which does not represent a sequential order.

However, looking back to the seeds at the beginning of the kalpa, all were born through transformation; since both the lotus and the flower are equally products of transformation and can serve as the origin, the analogy of the lotus flower is employed to accord with both meanings, taking it as a metaphor for the provisional and the real within the traces [of the Buddha's teaching].

The traces are neither real nor non-real; without the provisional there is no way to bestow it, and without the provisional there is no way to manifest the real. Nevertheless, they ultimately take the reality of principle as their foundation, such that the single essence of the provisional and the real is both sequential and simultaneous; this can be understood by comparing the preceding and succeeding descriptions of the lotus flower.
Now, in this discourse, the manifestation of the lotus is used as a metaphor; because the metaphor must be followed, the opening is presented first and the closing later.

Furthermore, presenting the opening first and the closing later also conforms to the analogy, though according to the actual nature of the Dharma, the opening and closing occur simultaneously; this present explanation is based on the final stage of opening and closing.

If the intermediate stages were alternately discarded, then there would be only abandonment and no opening [of the teaching], which is not the intended meaning of the present analogy; this will be explained in detail below.

Regarding the initial statement, "The flower exists for the sake of the lotus," this is spoken provisionally in terms of time, referring to the period following the *Avataṃsaka* (Sudden) teaching; however, the specific principles within the Sudden teaching—the ultimate teachings and the provisional teachings—are set aside for now and not yet discussed.

The Deer Park [teaching] was given as a minor concession, while the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings were already established as skillful means for the opening and closing [of the provisional]. Such explanations pertain, for the time being, to the minor vehicle.

If we consider them according to the teachings, the three vehicles of the preceding four periods are all provisional for the two vehicles; only in the Lotus Sūtra do bodhisattvas enter everywhere. Now, this passage cites [the minor vehicle] specifically because it is difficult to lead those of the minor vehicle, and thus it is spoken by way of reference to them.

"Knowing the foremost tranquility" refers to the Buddha’s own practice; this self-practice is the ultimate reality (*tattva*). "By the power of skillful means" precisely clarifies the employment of provisional teachings (*upāya*).

It should be stated that [the teaching] was for the sake of the five bhikṣus; the omission in the text is because [the Buddha] intended to immediately explain his purpose of employing provisional means (upāya), which is encompassed by the phrase "various" used in the following sentence.
The section beginning with "Although he manifests... clarifies the intention behind the employment of provisional means (*upāya*).
Although provisional means are indeed employed, they are fundamentally for the sake of the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*).

As for "various paths," these refer to the distinct paths of the two teachings for those of human capacity and the separate teaching; because there are five periods and eight teachings, they are called "various."
Next, to clarify "opening": when the real is pointed out as provisional and the provisional conceals the real, this is called the "closing of the gate of skillful means.
Now, when the provisional is pointed out as real and reality is seen within the provisional, this is called the "opening of the gate of skillful means."
"Manifestation" (*shi*) means pointing out; it refers to indicating the place where reality is perceived, hence the term is used.

Third, regarding "abolition" (*fei*): "Abandonment" (*she*) is a specific synonym for abolition. Once [the provisional] has been opened up as universally real, there is no longer any provisional to discuss; in meaning, this corresponds to abolition, wherein the provisional is transformed into the real, and the substance of that which was abolished ceases to exist.
If one remains and delays due to subsequent conditions, that again belongs to the category of giving (*dāna*) and is not the intended meaning here.
If this is so, what is the distinction between "opening" (*kai*) and "abandoning" (*fei*)? Answer:
If the principle (*dharma*) is established only to be discarded immediately upon its opening, and the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*) necessarily requires that its meaning be opened first,
then since the principle and the analogy would be inconsistent, how could they constitute an analogy for the principle? Answer:

From the perspective of principle, this seems to contradict the parable; from the perspective of facts, it seems that what was initially established is later abolished—just as if one first demonstrates the provisional as being the ultimate, once the ultimate is recognized, the provisional is forever discarded.
If one considers this from the perspective of principle, opening and closing occur simultaneously, because at the time of opening, [the state of] closing has already been abandoned.

Next, regarding the passage beginning with "Furthermore, the lotus," the analogy in the original text consists of a general heading in the first sentence, followed by the explicit clarification of the manifestation of traces starting from the phrase "From the origin."

Regarding the phrase "the trace depends upon the fundamental," it shows that the trace does not exist in isolation; rather, the intent behind manifesting the trace was originally intended to reveal the fundamental. Therefore, it is now said that the trace depends upon the fundamental, for the trace is not the ultimate reality.
Regarding the phrase "The text says," the following citation serves as proof; first, it clarifies the fundamental [manifestation].
The term "if such" refers to the kalpa-dust points of the lifespan.
The section beginning with "only the teaching" correctly clarifies the manifestation of traces.
The phrase "speaking thus" refers to the general summary of what was said.
The passage beginning with "I was young," etc., specifically demonstrates the characteristics of that speech.
Since nineteen similes describe the city [of the body] and thirty describe the attainment of the Way, and nothing prior to those is mentioned, it says, "I was young."
Next, regarding the citation of texts within the section on "revealing the traces" (*jì*), the initial passage describes the delusion concerning the traces, hence it says, "All say.
The section beginning with "I have attained Buddhahood" correctly clarifies the revelation of the traces.
As it cannot be fully set forth, it is stated briefly as "immeasurable," and so forth.
Regarding the three instances of the abandonment of traces (*jiej*), they are as explained later and as before.
In the cited passage, the section beginning with "All Buddhas" cites the same principle;
the section beginning with "In order to deliver" correctly clarifies the abandonment of traces.
Since there are no traces once they have been discarded, it is said that "all are real.
Reality is simply the fundamental (ben), while expediency is simply the trace (ji). If one wishes to discern their identity and difference, it is explained in detail as in the seventh fascicle.
Regarding the phrase "Therefore, it is first indicated," etc., in the section on the four fetters (*saṃyojana*), this summarizes the six parables.

There is no lotus that can serve as a metaphor for the provisional and the real, or for the fundamental and the manifest aspects of the wondrous Dharma; nor is there a way to take the lotus as a metaphor except through this wondrous Dharma. Just as in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the metaphor [of the lotus] comes after the Dharma; here, however, we follow that sequence, which is why it says "Therefore," and so forth.
Fifth, explaining according to the purport of the sutra: the purport of this entire work does not go beyond the concepts of the "original" (hon) and the "traced" (jaku).

"Dispelling the illusory city" serves as a metaphor for the preceding section; from the initial dispelling of the illusory city up to the bestowal of predictions constitutes the explanation of the "trace gate" (jakumon).
The section from "Furthermore, he gives rise to the various sages" to "bordering on great enlightenment" explains the Original Gate (Honmon).
Moreover, the Trace Gate (Jikimon) is fully encompassed by the three cycles;
as for the sequence of these three cycles, the Dharma-exposition occupies the first position, but here we shall first explain it according to the two metaphors that correspond to it.

Regarding the mention of the "transformed city" and so forth: the transformed city is a provisional teaching of the Guide; thus the sutra says, "Now you may rest within this great city. Therefore, it belongs to the category of the teaching (*deśanā*).

The thatched hut is what the practitioner clings to; thus the Sūtra says, "He still dwells outside the gate, staying overnight in a thatched hut," and for this reason, it belongs to the realm of emotional attachment (*qing*).

The purpose of the fundamental teaching on sweeping away attachments is to eliminate these stagnant emotions; the purpose of dispelling stagnant emotions is fundamentally to ensure that one does not cling to provisional teachings.
The "transformed city" describes the past, while the "grass hut" serves as a metaphor for the present; since the timing and conditions differ, these are cited alternately.
Regarding "opening up expedient means," it refers to opening up the five vehicles.
The initial passage opens the three vehicles as skillful means (*upāya*).
From the phrase "the assembly’s wholesome [deeds]" onward, it gathers the minor wholesome deeds of humans and devas.

"Dissolving" (*dàng*) is another name for "abolishing"; the characteristics of the similarities and differences between opening, abolishing, and gathering the three vehicles are fully detailed in the subsequent text.
Within both the "Original" (hon) and the "Trace" (jaku), as well as their functional applications, there are ten meanings each.

Furthermore, because the provisional means open up access to the proximate principle, it is called the "wondrous principle"; because it is contrasted with the minor practices of humans and devas, it is called the "Mahāyāna. Although these minor practices are not without their return to the principle, and these provisional means also enter into the One Vehicle, the underlying intent remains consistently pervasive throughout these alternating and complementary expressions.

"Principle" (*li*) is explained solely from the perspective of essence (*ti*), while "vehicle" (*sheng*) is elucidated through the perspective of phenomena (*shi*). Phenomena take essence as their basis, and essence must rely upon phenomena to be manifested.
Since humans and devas fundamentally reside within the realm of phenomena, it is convenient to explain them by opening up phenomena from phenomena;
whereas since those of the three vehicles have already realized the provisional principle, it is easier to clarify them by opening up principle from principle.
Therefore, when the Sūtras address humans and devas, they speak only of the "Buddha-way";
when they address the three vehicles, they speak of the "true mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
If this is so, why does the scriptural text refer to the two vehicles as the "bodhisattva-way" and so forth?

Answer: The name "Path" (mārga) is universal, whereas its specific meaning is restricted. Because it is restricted, the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) were granted the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of the eight aspects [of Buddhahood] after their realization; for humans and devas, however, this is discussed only in terms of the past in a general sense.

Furthermore, if one analyzes according to their respective stages: the two vehicles may attain the stage of semblance, whereas humans and devas remain only at the stage of contemplative practice. Therefore, it is recorded that the two vehicles must undergo further kalpas of making offerings, while humans and devas do not; thus they are not the same. Yet, because they equally ride the Buddha-vehicle, they are not different.

Regarding the phrase "superior, middling, and inferior faculties" and so forth: the previous clearing away of the phantom city was a metaphor for those of inferior faculties regarding their past lives; the previous demolition of the grass hut was a metaphorical teaching for those of middling faculties; and the previous opening of the provisional means was a teaching on the Dharma solely for those of superior faculties. Having completed the three cycles of preaching, each was granted a prediction of enlightenment, as detailed in the commentary.
The three faculties (indriya) mutually transform and receive the designations of "sharp" or "dull," as explained in detail in the ten sections of the fourth fascicle of the Commentary (*śāstra*).
Next, from "Furthermore, he produces... onwards, the Fundamental Chapter (Honmon) is further divided into two parts:
first, the explicit clarification of the revelation of the traces (kaji); second, from "Therefore, increasing the Path... onwards, the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

Regarding the first passage: in the Root Chapter, that which was previously concealed is revealed; thus it is called "unfolding" (*pra-bhā*). The Buddha and his disciples are termed "the assembly of sages.

Śrāvakas such as Pūrṇa were originally bodhisattvas, and bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī were originally ancient Buddhas; these are all provisional arrangements made through indirect means, and are therefore described as "skillful expedients" (*upāya-kauśalya*).
Since his entry into the state of quiescence at the site of enlightenment, he has been obscured by outward traces; now that these have finally been swept away, it is called "Revealing the Origin.
Because this had never been taught before, it is called "Profound and Subtle."

Next, regarding the bestowal of the prediction: the stage of the differentiation of merit reaches "one more birth" (*eka-jāti-pratibaddha*) before approaching *samyak-saṃbodhi*; thus it is called "adjacent" (*upaniṣad*).
This "adjacent" is simply another term for "wondrous."
In this sixth summary, from the beginning at the Vajrāsana until the end at the Śāla grove, it is called "one period.
Because it entices sentient beings to enter into reality, it is termed "conversion and guidance."
Revealing the fundamental [truth] constitutes the perfection of phenomena (事圓), while opening up the provisional [teachings] constitutes the perfection of principle (理圓).

Furthermore, when the work of transformation is complete, it is termed the "perfection of phenomena"; because the principles of the fundamental and the trace are manifested, it is called the "perfection of principle."

The reason other flowers are not used as metaphors is that the six analogies of the lotus fundamentally illustrate both the original and the manifested aspects; thus, all the teachings of the one lifetime of the Buddha ultimately converge upon the true origin, and nothing but the lotus can serve as a metaphor for this. Therefore, it is said: "The intent lies herein."
"Si" (this) means "this," referring here to the "original and the trace.
Regarding the three explanations of the character "jīng" (sūtra): the teachings of the five flavors are all collectively termed "sūtras"; therefore, it says "all are so named."
Since this is fully contained in the eighth [fascicle], it says "as follows later.
Next, regarding the explanation of the general and the specific: from the words "The Recordist" onward, Zhiyan (Zhang’an) explains the meaning of the Great Master’s preface.
However, the preface composed by the Great Master seems to merely explain the title, as its meaning contains further distinctions.

The commentary by Zhāng'ān, on the other hand, fully embodies the essence, the school, and the application; for while explaining the title is general, the essence and so forth are specific. Since the specific is distinct from the general and the general encompasses the specific, the five chapters are all contained within the explanation of the general title.

One should know that the three chapters on "Essence" (*tǐ*) and so forth are nothing other than the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*), and ultimately nothing other than all Three Dharmas. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Explaining the names provides a general discussion of the Three Dharmas," and "The 'Essence' and other categories are opened up in correspondence with the Three Dharmas. Thus, this general title governs the entire treatise; from beginning to end, the work does not transcend these two gates. For this reason, the two gates are established as titles based on the "mind of the text" (*wénxīn*). As the *Zhìguān* says at the beginning of the section on "Arousing the Mind": "The accumulation of essentials is called the mind."
In this present collection of teachings, the distinction between the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku) is the essential point.

Furthermore, since the essence and other aspects within the fundamental are no different from those in the manifested, we distinguish the fundamental and the manifested solely through their names; as for the remaining aspects—essence, doctrine, and function—they are explained directly as they are.

Therefore, Zhan’an, in articulating the Great Master’s intent, captured the core of the sūtra’s text; thus, among the five chapters of the *Xuanyi*, none surpasses "Root and Trace," just as in the explanation of the character "wondrous" (*miao*), where there are ten aspects for both Root and Trace.
The two bodies of the original and the trace are not different in principle.

The cause and effect of the past are termed the "original teaching" (honshū); the cause and effect discussed here and now in the interim are termed the "trace teaching" (jishū). Regarding the two functions of the original and the trace, one does not distinguish them by coarse or subtle, nor by broad or narrow; they are simply judged according to their proximity or distance.
The distinctions between the provisional and the real, and between the near and the distant, pertain merely to the characteristics of the teachings regarding the original and the trace.

Thus, one knows that the core of the sutras does not transcend the principle of the original and the trace; when one contemplates the purport of the original and the trace from above, the textual meanings of the transformations established throughout the three periods of time become crystal clear.
"Cold" refers to a chilling sensation that can be distinguished upon observation.
From "The Sublime Dharma" onwards, the preceding introductory text is cited to demonstrate five meanings.
Thus, one should know that the enumeration of the title applies throughout from beginning to end; as in the previous introduction, it merely enumerates the name.
The three meanings, including "essence" (tǐ), are combined within the term "name" (míng). Since essence belongs to principle (lǐ), how could principle lack a thesis (zōng)?
Since the One Vehicle belongs to the thesis, how could the thesis lack an essence?
This "Dissolving Transformation" (蕩化) is used to rely upon the realm of facts; establishing transformation based on principle is also subsumed under "function" (用).
This can be seen by examining the text.
From the phrase "Private Preface to the King" (*Si xu wang*) onwards, it refers to Zhiyi’s private preface.
Furthermore, it is divided into two parts:
first, the introduction; second, the explanation of the introduction.
The first part is further divided into two.
First, the beginning and end [of the treatise] will be discussed; second, the title of the scripture will be explained.
In the Master’s preface, he states that the title of the scripture encompasses both the beginning and the end.
Following the Master’s principle, the meaning within the title must necessarily include the essence (*tattva*) and other such elements.

Following Zhiyi’s discourse, it must be understood that while the "Exposition of Names" (*Shiming*) differs in its approach, this text provides a further detailed explanation because it relies upon the textual meaning.

Regarding the initial passage: the two cycles of the Dharma and the Parable are not narrated in detail here; rather, they are briefly introduced as a prologue to inspire the present audience. Those who benefited during the two cycles of the Dharma and the Parable were none other than those who had established karmic connections in the past. Because they had regressed from the Great Vehicle and wandered through saṃsāra, they were deluded regarding the principle of quiescence and indulged in the wine of ignorance; because they had lost the mind of great compassion, they were confused about the wondrous cause, perceiving birth and death as vast and remote. The World-Honored One, out of pity, accommodated their limited capacities. Since even those of small capacity were still dim-sighted regarding the beginning, they remained inverted and deluded. By observing their past seeds, he entrusted them with the wealth of their karma; by restoring them to the wondrous practice at its inception, he manifested auspicious omens to stir their hearts. Thus, the phrase "pitying these" within this introduction encompasses the full significance of the matter.
The initial word "Now" (*fu*) serves as the opening of the discourse. Regarding the phrase "the principle is transcendent" (*li jue*) and so forth:

having already revealed that the names of the partial and the perfect have been transcended, this is done to contrast and clarify the partial and the perfect in relation to the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Vaipulya*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* sutras; it concludes the previous discussion on the non-referential conditions of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and now, by means of the metaphor of the perfect pearl, it discourses upon the transcendent principle.
Regarding the phrase "extremely not," etc.:

however, this single ultimate principle is neither near for ordinary beings nor far from the fruit of Buddhahood; it relies upon the distance of five hundred *yojanas* to lead [beings] toward the proximity of the phantom city and to explain the remoteness of the jewel island.

Regarding the phrase "extremely attuned" (*kyō-e*) and so forth: whenever the Perfect Teaching is discussed, the distant is explained as being near, and the partial is discarded. If one darkly accords with the Ultimate, then phenomena and principle are quiescent; when transformation is all-pervasive, it is the quiescence of phenomena, and when reality is revealed, it is the quiescence of principle.
Furthermore, by employing a perfect sphere to manifest principle, one realizes that principle; thus, it is the quiescence of principle.
By relying on a precious object to discuss phenomena, one harmonizes with those phenomena; thus, it is the quiescence of phenomena.
The meaning and intent of these two interpretations are largely the same.
The "jeweled island" is originally intended to cause one to abandon the "transformed city"; once the transformed city is abandoned, it signifies that the transformative ritual is complete.

The "pearl in the garment" is originally a metaphor for having previously heard of the true reality (*dharmatā*); once the true reality is revealed, it signifies that one has accords with the principle of quiescence. This clarifies those who have already entered the reality during the interim.

Regarding the phrase "yet not tranquil": this clarifies that after falling back from the Great [Vehicle], one transmigrates through the five destinies; because one is addicted to and obstructed by subtle ignorance regarding the Middle Way, one loses the great resolve.
Furthermore, they indulge in the active manifestation of coarse desires and, through ignorance, forget the fundamental teachings they have received.

"Being deluded regarding the path to Nirvana" means that after departing from clarity and flowing into saṃsāra, they subsequently take pleasure in the Hīnayāna; this is like a person who, being confused, mistakes the east for the west, thereby losing both the east and the west.

The Nirvana of the Three Virtues is inherently complete within principle; yet, if one regards principle as distant and turns away from the Great to grasp the Small, then both the Great and the Small are lost. To regard the Great as distant is delusion regarding the Great, and to regard the Small as ultimate is delusion regarding the Small.
The "Holy Lord" departs to clarify what is revealed today; having first matured [beings] through the four flavors, he arrives at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

In the introductory section of the Trace, the four flowers and six earth-tremors first symbolize the four stages and six cycles. Upon reaching the section on Dissemination, the transformation of the land and its splitting manifest the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*); because this true reality universally encompasses all, it is called "all."
Because one beholds the auspicious signs and hears the Dharma, it is said "seeing and hearing.

From the phrase "revealing the secret" onward, the title of the sutra is explained in sequence: first, the two characters "Wondrous Dharma" (Myōhō) universally signify both the original and the trace aspects, while the two characters "Lotus Flower" (Renge) universally serve as metaphors for both the original and the trace aspects.
Now, the "long-standing fundamental" (jǐu-běn) is likened to the lotus root, and the "convergence of the perfect" (huì-yuán) is compared to the flower.
Regarding the phrase "revealing the secret and so forth," "revealing" (fā) means to open.

Previously, [the truth] was kept secret and not taught; therefore, all the sections were categorized as coarse. Formerly, the provisional and the real were intertwined yet separated by their distinctions; thus, the correct path of the provisional and the real was not clarified. Although the fundamental fruit had long been accomplished, it was merely covered over by its traces. Now, one simply points to the fundamental and names it "manifestation."
The Dharma is present, yet because recipients conceptualize it as something separate, it must be brought into realization.
Since its stage still resides within the causal condition, it is called the "Path" (*mārga*).

As for "Sound" (*śabda*), it refers to the Buddha's activity primarily based on the time of the Buddha's presence; however, since its meaning extends to the period after his parinirvāṇa, it is called "Sūtra."
Since form (*rūpa*) exists only after cessation, let us set it aside for now.

The Preface by the Great Master states, "There are translations that have counterparts and those that do not," referring to the eighth fascicle; initially, this applies only to form, whereas subsequently it extends to all six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Thus, while the intent of the Great Master’s preface appears at first glance to be restrictive, it is in fact universal;
conversely, while the intent of Zhanran’s (Zhang’an) preface appears at first glance to be universal, it remains somewhat restricted.

Regarding the phrase "the beginning of the perfect exposition" (*en-jun no sho*) and so forth: this is stated provisionally from the perspective of the manifested trace (*jaku*). To be fully expressed, it should be said "the beginning of the exposition of the fundamental and the manifested" (*hon-jaku jun-sho*).

As for the fact that the preceding Master’s preface does not comment on the first chapter, the "Preface" (*jo-hon dai-ichi*), although it appears below the title, it belongs to the sequential order of the chapters themselves and is not part of the meaning within the title; therefore, it is omitted and not discussed.
Therefore, the *Xuánwén* (Explanations of the Profound) does not explain this at its conclusion, but only provides a brief interpretation at the beginning of the *Shūwén* (Commentary).
Zhǎng'ān took advantage of this opportunity and thus discussed it briefly.

Regarding the phrase "the categories follow one another," etc., this is for the time being merely an explanation of why the chapters are arranged as they are; since the reasons for the existence of these chapters are fully contained within the *Wénjù* (Words and Phrases), it would be inappropriate to discuss them here.

Regarding the phrase "the sequence of the assembly" (*zhòngcì*) and so forth: because the twenty-eight chapters arise without confusion and their arising is not singular, it is called "the sequence of the assembly.
Because it is the very first among them, it is called "the head" (*zhīshǒu*).
"First" can be understood as such.
The term "tánjì" (談記) is likely an error; it should be read as "tántuò" (談託), meaning that one entrusts the ultimate principle to the Treasure-store (Ratnakoṭa).
"Perfect" (*yuan*) is a specific synonym for "wondrous," and "ultimate" (*ji*) is the fruit of the wondrous Dharma.
Here, the wondrousness is praised by means of its resultant dharma, as the sutra states, "Only a Buddha can know it"; therefore, this is called "narrating the name."
Regarding the composition of this "xu" (narrative/preface): "xu" means to narrate or describe, thereby articulating the author's intent. Regarding the composition of this "xu":

"xu" here refers to ritual order (*xiangxu*), such as the six auspicious omens which serve as the formal sequence for the main discourse; however, this is not the intended meaning here, and therefore it is not so written.
"Reaching the profound mystery" means attaining the essence of the sūtra.

Universally, it refers to being the essence of all dharmas, all sūtras, and all practices; specifically, it exists only within the cause and effect that is apprehended, and it is only when the true reality (*dharmatā*) is perceived that one is said to have attained the essence.
Now, setting aside the general for the particular, it is said that they "converge on the profound.
Because they converge on the profound, it is called the essence (*tattva*) of the school.

Hearing the Dharma and fastening the jewel constitutes the perfect cause; receiving the prediction and being shown the jewel is termed the perfect fruit. Therefore, the jewel is used to describe the school's essence.

Furthermore, if one discusses the essence of the jewel as being neither bound nor manifested, yet still discusses binding and manifestation with reference to that very jewel, this constitutes the tenet of the "Essence School" (Tijia). Because its transformation is all-pervasive and its principle is manifest, such is the power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; thus it is said, "Both are quiescent," which describes its function.
Precisely because the provisional and the ultimate are employed in tandem, the tuning of faculties to enter into quiescence constitutes the function of the School of the Patriarchs.
Since the "Four Flowers" and "Six Movements" occupy the beginning of this scripture, it is called the "Preface to the Teachings."

Both the general preface and the specific preface describe the teaching; however, because the general preface is broad and diffuse, it is abbreviated in favor of the specific preface. The specific preface possesses five elements, whereas the remaining four are still quite expansive. Among these, the manifestation of auspicious signs to signify the response is the most immediate and essential aspect.

Among the six auspicious omens, the remaining four are still relatively broad; they do not compare to the heavenly flowers in the four stages and the shaking of the earth during the sixfold destruction of delusions. Since the purport of the teaching lies herein, I have cited them briefly.

It is so because the preceding opening of the gate of skillful means was intended to guide the mind; the distinction between the original and the manifested is merely one of distance and proximity. Since the meaning has already been clarified by the Great Master’s exposition, it is said that "it can be known."

Next, from the words "This sublime Dharma" onwards, the first section constitutes the introduction to the profound essence; this introduction captures the meaning of the subsequent text and is not difficult to understand.
Within it, there are also two parts:
first, the introduction, and second, the explanation.
The first section consists of three parts:

first, an account of the origin of the sutra; second, a formal exposition of the present sutra; third, the explanation of the title, beginning with the words "That which is said. As for the first part:
because it is based on fundamental realization, one is able to preach [the Dharma].

Although it is spoken of within the traces (*traces of manifestation*), when one traces the merit back to its source, it resides elsewhere; therefore, it is called the "Original Ground" (*mūlabhūmi*).
The passage beginning with "The text says" cites the traces to verify the original ground; from the perspective of self-realization, there is no dharma that can be spoken of.
The section beginning with “The three periods of time” generally cites evidence of commonality.
Next, the section beginning with “The text says” correctly clarifies the exposition of the sutra.
Furthermore, it first cites the text as internal verification, thereby explaining it for others.

In the section following "The Great Matter" (Mahāvaipulya), the original intent is clarified: the underlying purpose lies in the Buddha Vehicle (Buddhayāna). Therefore, from the beginning to the end, the intent is shown to reside in the Buddha-wisdom; the intervening sections of critique and refutation are not the primary intention of the Buddha, which is why they are described as "auxiliary manifestations."
Next, from "Now" onwards is the actual exposition.
Within the subsequent explanation of the title:

first, the character "wondrous" (*miao*) is explained; next, from "Furthermore, wondrous" onwards, the terms "Dharma," "lotus flower," and "sūtra" are explained. All of these are preceded by the character "wondrous," because there is nothing therein that is not wondrous.
Within this commentary, four meanings are preserved based on a single title.

Regarding "the six metaphors describing function," as the subsequent text states: "In the provisional (traces), the function is to sever doubts regarding the provisional and give rise to faith in the real; in the fundamental, the function is to sever doubts regarding the near and give rise to faith in the distant. Therefore, the following text clarifies that the ten meanings of both the fundamental and the provisional differ.
Ambrosia (*amṛta*) is the principle, and the teaching is the gateway to that principle; therefore, it is called the "Gateway to Ambrosia.
Next, regarding the formal explanation of the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*), first the headings are listed, and then they are explained.
In the explanation, there is first a preliminary judgment and second, the formal explanation.
Within the initial judgment, there are two parts:
first, the enumeration, and second, the judgment.
The judgment also has two parts:
first, a general discussion based on various sutras; second, a specific discussion based on the present sutra.
The first section has three parts:
First, the explanation of the name; second, from "In this way" onwards, the presentation of the essence; third, from "Following the pattern of various sutras" onwards, the citation of examples.
The first two are readily understood.

Regarding the third, in the section citing examples, the phrase "following the pattern of the beginning of various sutras" and so forth refers to citing the five meanings of the general introduction at the beginning of a sutra as the illustrative explanation.
Question:
Since Ānanda is the same [as others], how can there be a difference between persons? Answer:
This is fully detailed in the commentary (*śāstra*), where the four types of Ānanda are presented; the remaining intent can be inferred.
Next, regarding this present sutra, there are five sections within the general and specific [analyses]:

first, the explanation of the name; second, the discernment of differences; third, the identification of the essence (*svabhāva*); fourth, the citation of examples; and fifth, the specific clarification.

Regarding the initial statement that "the 'comprehensive' (tong) means the sense of being common," the seven meanings collectively explain the five chapters, while the individual [meanings] consist of five senses that do not intermingle.

Next, in distinguishing the differences: although there are both comprehensive and specific explanations for a single scripture, it is said that "[this one] is dedicated to a single section"; the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
In the subsequent formal explanation, there is first a general exposition and then a specific one.
Within the initial general exposition, there are four parts:
first, the heading; second, the enumeration; third, the correlation with the five minds; and fourth, the detailed explanation of the seven cycles.
The first two [cases] can be understood.
Regarding the third, there are two parts in relation to the five minds:
first, the actual correspondence; second, the conclusion.
Regarding the three methods of "opening, combining, and so forth" that give rise to the mind of wisdom: these three natures constitute analytical discernment (*viveka*).

As for "contemplating the mind," it means that upon hearing a single phrase, one integrates phenomena into principle; it is not necessary to wait for an external object of contemplation before it is called the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Because there is no extraneous interference, it is called "diligence" (*vīrya*). Phenomena do not exist in isolation;

thus, the seven chapters depend upon the five mental states (*citta*). If these five mental states are established, they stand firm just as grasses, trees, and plants stand when they possess roots, stems, and trunks; therefore, the establishment of the mind is designated as the "root."
Since these five states of mind are called "roots" (indriya), a root necessarily constitutes a "power" (bala).
Regarding the phrase "dispelling obstacles," it is as stated in the *Śraddhādhimukta-parivarta*: "There is no deception, indolence, anger, hatred, or resentment."
Deceit is an obstacle to faith; laziness is an obstacle to diligence; anger is an obstacle to mindfulness; resentment is an obstacle to concentration; and enmity is an obstacle to wisdom.
When these faculties increase and are able to destroy these five obstacles, they are therefore called "powers."

Once the faculties and powers are established, one must necessarily possess the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) to open the three doors of liberation; therefore, it says "up to and including.
By applying the small to the great, this should also be understood accordingly.
The detailed explanation consists of two parts:
first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent; second, the actual explanation.

Regarding the initial passage, the conclusion of the preceding section is self-evident; the phrase "detailed explanation" below introduces the subsequent section, which is also termed the "Chapter on Application."

By means of these seven rounds of general exegesis on the five chapters, one gives rise to the five minds; when proceeding to the specific exegesis of each of the five chapters, every single one likewise brings about the five minds.

Since the five chapters have been briefly explained through these seven rounds, one should know that a detailed explanation of the five chapters will likewise possess all seven [rounds]. Therefore, one attains the three liberations of the Perfect Gate and enters the First Abode to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The reason for the initial conclusion is as follows:
secondly, in the main explanation, the text itself is divided into seven sections.
First, regarding the presentation of the titles, this refers to the initial presentation of the five chapters.
Within the five chapters, this first section provides the title; therein, the internal content is divided into four parts:
first, the presentation of the headings; second, the explanation.
Regarding the phrase "originally holy" (*yuánshèng*) and so forth in the initial presentation, the term "establishment" (*lì*) refers to the name of the *Saddharma* (Wondrous Dharma).
"Original" (*yuan*) means fundamental. "Establishing" (*jian*) means to set up.

The Great Sage established these names to reveal profound principles for the advancement of those at the beginning of their practice. The locus of the single reality is called "profound principle," while those at the seven stages of expedient means are all termed "beginners. Regarding "seeing and hearing," both the present and the future are included; when the Buddha is present, it is solely through sound that benefit is conferred. Since this benefit extends across two lifetimes, it is said that "both seeing and hearing are attained."

By following the names associated with the immediate objects of sound and form, one reaches the ultimate principle of signlessness; therefore, this name of the "wondrous Dharma" is used to designate the Dharma of the true nature (*dharmatā*).

Regarding the establishment of wondrous capacities for those who should enter the reality: if explained in a general sense, there is no teaching door throughout the single lifetime of the Buddha that does not open up the profound principle of the true nature; however, here we follow the specific sense, which is precisely the intent of this sutra.
In the subsequent analysis, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the preceding teachings by contrasting them with the present sutra; second, further elucidating the present sutra by means of the five flavors.
The first section consists of five parts. The phrase "However, dharmas have coarseness and subtlety" is the general heading.

Next, the section beginning with "If they are sequential" serves as a distinction: from the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra down to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, although the names differ, these are all subsumed under the sequential three truths; it is only in this present sutra that they are reconciled with reality and termed "perfectly interfused."
3. From "This wondrous truth" onwards, there is a praise and explanation of the single reality-principle of the present sutra.
4. From "The text says" onwards, there is the citation of scriptural evidence.

5. From "It is not even" onwards, there is the citation of a sutra passage to provide an illustration: it is not even known by those at the stages of practice in the Separate Teaching who have attained non-retrogression, let alone by the classes of humans and devas.
"Multitude" (qún) means a great number.
"Sprout" (méng) refers to the state of a seed before it has split open.
Since humans and devas are entirely shrouded by ignorance, they are called the "multitude of sprouts."
Next, there are two further sections specifically concerning the five flavors:

first, a general statement regarding the intention of not immediately expounding the ultimate reality; second, from the words "The reason why" onwards, a detailed progression through the five flavors to clarify the intention behind what was taught and what was not.
The initial section also has two parts:
first, a brief clarification of why [the Buddha] does not speak; second, citing the text to explain the reason for not speaking.

Regarding the first part, it directly restates the preceding passage, such as: "Only I know this mark, and the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise. Why is it that he does not immediately speak?
The citation and its detailed explanation are as in the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paryāya*).
Next, from the words "For this reason" (*so yi*) onwards, the text specifically addresses the five flavors (*pañca-rasa*), which is further divided into two parts:
first, the four flavors; second, the *tathāgata-garbha* (the *amṛta* or *sarpir-maṇḍa*).
The first section also has two parts: first, the enumeration of the four flavors; second, the clarification of the meaning of the four flavors.

Within the initial text, all four flavors possess the designations "fused" and "unfused," though there are slight differences among them. In the milk [flavor], the "distinct" is designated as unfused; in the curd teaching, the single flavor is entirely unfused; and within the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the term "fused" carries two meanings.
If one uses the Perfect Teaching (the *yuan*) to critique the Three Teachings and the Treasury Teaching (the *zang*), then one takes the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*) as "fusion.

Alternatively, if one uses the Three Teachings to critique the Treasury Teaching, then one takes their mutual penetration (*tongrong*) as "fusion. Although both the Great and the Small are critiqued, the primary intent lies in critiquing the Small; therefore, it is said that this causes those of small capacity to feel shame for the Small and to aspire to the Great.

Regarding the statement in the *Shusuo* (Matured Ghee) that "it causes the small root to be entrusted to the fused [state], which is not fused": this means that in the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), the Small Vehicle is entrusted to the fusion of pervasive interpenetration to attain the small fruit; thus, the small fruit itself is designated as "not fused."

To cause the "great roots" to move from the non-fused toward the fused refers to taking the "common" and "distinct" [teachings] as the non-fused; that is, it means causing the common and distinct bodhisattvas to turn toward the fusion of the perfectly round (perfect teaching).
Question:
If it is feared that those to whom the Buddha Vehicle is taught might fall into suffering, could it not be the case that the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka* are not the Buddha Vehicle? Answer:
If we discuss this according to the teachings, the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras also contain the Buddha-vehicle; why then would it be unique to the Avataṃsaka?

The present statement regarding "falling into suffering" is based solely on the fact that [certain beings] were incapable of receiving the One Buddha-vehicle; thus, by hearing the three distinct vehicles and others, they were still spared from committing slander. Consequently, through the power of secrecy, the Lesser Vehicle was temporarily concealed while the teaching was delivered.

Although it is said that the great capacity is still separated from the distinct [teaching], those of small faculties are obscured and do not hear it at all; because the small is thus concealed, it cannot be called "established together. Therefore, only the name of "sudden greatness" is established, rather than the designation of "the One Vehicle's unique excellence," which is contrary to the Buddha’s original intent; this is precisely why.
The sudden and great teachings of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra are already not its primary intent; how much less so the Deer Park [teachings], which establish only the non-fused?

Therefore, even at the beginning of the Tripiṭaka teachings and within their respective sections, the coarse is still not exhaustive; thus, the sublime title is entirely absent. This can be understood by comparing it with the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings.

Next, from "Although there are various [teachings]" up to "is not the Buddha’s original intent," the text clarifies the underlying purpose of employing the four flavors (*catur-rasa*). It reveals that while the *Lotus Sūtra* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) draws upon those four flavors, their original intent was not fully expressed therein; therefore, they are all brought back to converge in the *Lotus Sūtra*.

The terminology used for "provisional establishment" (prajñapti) applies to both the coarse and the subtle, because prior to this point, provisional establishments were still employed through skillful means (*upāya*).

Regarding the three categories beginning with "following others," these three—following others and so forth—possess both general and specific applications. If one were to explain them individually across the seven stages and the four teachings, this would be a general exposition based on those various teachings; however, here they are explained specifically according to the distinct characteristics of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* onwards, all [teachings] are said to be "following others" (*tāntrika*). Therefore, although there was already a degree of integration within the preceding teachings, because they were still characterized by a dual approach (*ubhayatobhāga*), they all belonged to the category of following others; they were not yet capable of being opened and revealed, and thus are called "not intent on speed," meaning they were intent on the speed of accomplishing worldly matters.

Only now does this sutra open up all that was previously incongruous, leaving only a single point of harmony, so that the various preceding sections may share in the same wondrous Dharma and the intent of its appearance in the world be fully realized; therefore, the subsequent text says, "it is finally elucidated."
Regarding the phrase "Therefore it is said," etc., this concludes by returning to the meaning of the initial passage concerning what was not spoken; "diligence" (*wu*) also implies urgency.
Next, from "Now in this sutra" onwards, the flavor of *amṛta* (the supreme nectar) is elucidated in three parts:

first, the direct elucidation of the present sutra; second, from "Causing all" onwards, the elucidation of the Buddha’s original intent in preaching; and third, from "Therefore established" onwards, the conclusion regarding the establishment of the title.
Regarding the first passage on "abandoning" (*śe*), "abandoning" is simply "setting aside"; thus we know that while the names differ, the essence is the same. Regarding the subsequent passage:

when circumstances leave no other recourse, one sound may be understood differently; yet once [the minds] have been fully matured, there is no difference in the flavor of the Way. As for the remaining thoughts of extinction, if the five thousand [monks] were to rise and depart, they would all be left behind to await a future assembly, hearing [the teaching] only upon reaching that other land.

Regarding the phrase "Thus it is fully expounded" and so forth: the Sūtra states that [the Buddha] appeared in the world "for the sake of the one great cause and condition. Since this great task has now been accomplished, his purpose for appearing in the world is complete.

Regarding the "three fetters" (*trisaṃyojana*): since this sutra is named "Subtle," the preceding four are still considered "Coarse. Within the three fetters, all four flavors are subsumed; for what reason is the name "Subtle" not established? Because it encompasses both [the subtle and the coarse], it is judged as belonging to the category of the "Coarse. This is like the case where both a "refined person" and a "coarse person" commit an offense; from the perspective of the offense itself, both are called "coarse persons."
This sutra differs from those [previous ones], and thus it says "no longer," for it alone now possesses its own sublime name.

Regarding the term "analogy" (*dṛṣṭānta*) in the parable: because a parable is established for the sake of the Dharma, the parable serves as an analogy for the Dharma; therefore, following the three preceding chapters, all use the flower as a metaphor.

First, the title is established as in the preceding model; second, from "How so" (*kathaṃ*) onwards, it analyzes as in the preceding model; third, from "In this way" (*evam*) onwards, it concludes as in the preceding model. Regarding the first section:

while the initial establishment of the "Middle" (*madhyama*) refers only to the name "Subtle" (*sūkṣma*) while traversing the five periods, it is only by opening up the profound and advancing from the beginning that one reaches the ultimate. Now, the analogy is also presented in brief; it simply states "coarse and subtle" (*audārika-sūkṣma*) to encompass the many preceding points in their entirety.

Next, regarding the analysis by means of analogies, whereas previously the five flavors were fully detailed, here we proceed solely from the perspective of the persons [to be taught], distinguishing them from the various non-Buddhists and the three previous teachings, because within these various sections, the "wondrous" (the ultimate truth) does not differ.
It can be understood that "wild flowers bear no fruit.

Furthermore, one should add the case of "fruit without flowers" as an analogy for the heterodox views of non-Buddhists who reckon that fruits arise spontaneously (*svabhāva*). As the *Wu lu dili zhi* (Record of Geography of the Wu Dynasty) states:
"In Guangzhou there is a tree named *du*; it bears fruit without flowering, and the fruit emerges directly from the bark."
They are the size of pomegranates and red in color; they can be cooked and eaten.
If left uneaten for several days, they all transform into insects.
Like winged ants, they are able to fly and alight upon human dwellings.
Although the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon that fruits arise spontaneously, such fruits lack reality.

For instance, "one flower with many fruits" is seen in sesame and the like; "many flowers with one fruit" in peaches, plums, and the like; "one flower with one fruit" in persimmons and the like; and "fruit before the flower" in melons, rice, and the like.
Therefore, Nanyue’s *Four Modes of Peaceful Practice* states:
"Other flowers may have such things as madness, but the lotus flower is not so.
It further says:
"The other flowers that form fruit are manifest and easy to see, like the various vehicles of skillful means;
the lotus flower is hidden and secret, like the Single Buddha Vehicle.
Next, the section from "lotus flower" downward illustrates the *amṛta* (clarified butter), which is divided into two parts:
First, many wonders are presented in general; next, they are matched individually to three specific meanings.
The initial passage may be used as an analogy for the ten wonders of the original and the trace, as well as the three chapters on essence, doctrine, and function.

"Wonders" (qí) are simply "wondrous" (miào); among the ten wonders and the three chapters, there is nothing that is not wondrous. If it were not for these many wonders—the flowers and fruits—how could one possibly emulate them?
Now, taking the lotus and the other two [the tree and the jewel] collectively to encompass both the original and the manifested (honji-suijaku), the text designates them as "many wonders.

Next, three meanings are listed; regarding the first meaning, "the flower and fruit are fully complete," and so forth: for the sake of the lotus there is the flower, and the flower conceals the fruit. For the sake of the Real (shitsu) there is the Provisional (gon); the Real exists within the Provisional, and since their essence is not different, it is said that "the Provisional is identical with the Real."
When the conditions are ripe, one must open [the door]; opening that which can cover is called "opening. When the mind longs for the proximate fruit, it is termed "covering" (*nivṛti*).
To remove that proximity is termed "opening" (*vivṛti*). What is it that is opened?
That very [state] is what covers.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the flower falls and the lotus forms," the falling of the flower is a metaphor for that which is not provisional (non-expedient), and the falling of the lotus is a metaphor for that which is not real. Once opened, they are immediately discarded; there is no difference in their timing. Since the practitioner who opens the teaching and the principle are of one and the same principle, once the reality is established, they together merge with the three virtues (*triguṇa*). Thus, we know that the three virtues do not correspond to the provisional and the real.
In the exposition of the essential body (*śarīra*), there is first a listing and then an explanation.
Within the explanation, there is first the Master’s interpretation and then the private interpretation of Zhǎng’ān.
The initial section consists of four parts:
First, from the character "essence" (tǐ) onwards, the initial explanation is provided.

Second, from "therefore, the Chapter on Life Span" (Huishòuliàngpǐn) onwards, the second section cites parallels. Third, from "now, speaking of the true mark" (shíxiàng) onwards, the third section distinguishes what is incorrect. Fourth, from "this is indeed" (sī nǎi) onwards, the fourth section concludes with the correct interpretation.
The initial explanation of the characters is further divided into three parts:

first, the explanation of the character definitions; second, from "each [is] intimate" (*geqin*) onwards, citing examples as illustrations; third, from "transcending the world" (*chushi*) onwards, correctly presenting the essence of the scripture to align it with the meaning of the characters.
The meaning of the first passage is clear.

As for the second passage, although it employs the principles of the Confucian school, its intent differs from theirs; for they clarify that because the Way has been lost, people are restricted to being intimate only with their own kin and raising only their own children, which is why ritual (*li*) arose.
Now, borrowing those ritual laws as a metaphor for their identical essence, all sutras converge upon the true reality, just as each person cherishes their own kin;
this true reality gives rise to all phenomena, just as each person nurtures their own children.
The seventh chapter of the *Book of Rites* (*Liji*) states: "Confucius said:

'When the Great Way was practiced, the world was held in common; the worthy and the capable were selected, trustworthiness was promoted, and harmony was cultivated. Therefore, people did not regard only their own parents as parents, nor did they regard only their own children as children.'"
The commentary states:
"The Way of filial piety and compassion is vast.

Now that the Great Way has become obscured, the world has come to treat each other as private families; everyone cherishes only their own kin and regards only their own children as sons. Ritual and righteousness serve as the guiding principles to rectify the relationship between ruler and subject and to strengthen the bond between father and son; thus, the principle of righteousness is the same [in both cases].
Next, citing the similarities between the two [positions] has two parts:
first, citing the similarity regarding the lifespan; second, citing the similarity regarding the two treatises.
The first section further has two parts:
First, the lifespan is cited; next, the passage on skillful means is presented to demonstrate their identity.
In the initial passage, the phrase "not as in the three realms" means it is not the same as what is perceived by those within the three realms.
Therefore, those within the triple world perceive only differentiated marks, whereas the followers of the Two Vehicles perceive suchness, which is emptiness itself;
this is what Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can know.

As for why only the *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* (Life Span Chapter) is cited and not other sections, it is because those other sections already share the same identity between the provisional traces and the ultimate reality.

Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "Now, this Sūtra’s *jitemon* (trace-gate) shares both similarities and differences with other sūtras; 'differences' refers to its inclusive nature, while 'similarities' mean it is no different [from others]. Thus, there is no need to cite [other texts].
