Next, regarding the three periods of time, that which belongs to the future life is what constitutes being human. Because the future is anticipated through the present, the present is termed "past" (or "prior").

Because the ultimate truth (paramārtha) permeates both the beginning and the end, it may also be applied generally within the stage of ordinary beings.

Now I ask:
Is there a primary truth (paramārtha) that serves as the antidote for human beings, and does this primary truth have three aspects?

Therefore, the present text says they arise sequentially from one another: because one contemplates the world, goodness arises; because goodness arises, evil is destroyed; because evil is destroyed, one perceives the principle (li); and within that principle, there is no world and so forth.
This constitutes the arising of the good and the extinction of the evil; if they were alternately present or absent, one would ultimately fail to perceive the principle.

At that time, Śāṭhira heard that there was a great master of debate in that forest; he immediately went to his location, and having arrived, he exchanged greetings and sat to one side.
Then Śāṭhira said to the Venerable One:
"Who shall establish the thesis first?"
Answer: "I am the elder; you should establish your thesis first. Śāṭhira said:
"All doctrines entail retribution.
At that time, Vairaṣṭra sat in silence.
The disciples of Vairaṣṭra cried out:
If your teacher were Śreṣṭhila, he would know this for himself:
having risen from the grove and departed, he proceeded further and further along his way.
Then his teacher thought to himself:
"O Śramaṇa son of the Śākyas, why do you speak these words? Your teacher alone shall know if he is a Sātīra.
He then immediately recalled his own words: "All discourse has its retribution."
That śramaṇa remained silent; thus my argument was unanswered, and the śramaṇa had already prevailed.
He then said to his disciples, "I shall go back to him."
The disciple said,
"Since you have already achieved victory among the assembly, for what reason do you go further?
The Master replied:
"I would rather be defeated by the wise than be victorious over the foolish.
Immediately, he went to him and spoke these words:
"You are the victor; I am the one who has been defeated."
"You are my teacher; I am your disciple.
This passage from the *Vāseṣṭha-sūtra* should properly be read as "silently refuting," though the wording and names differ slightly from the present text.
Regarding the next question, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:

"The four *siddhāntas* encompass the eighty-four thousand dharma-treasuries and the twelve divisions of the scriptures. While the inclusion of the twelve divisions has already been explained above, what is the nature of the inclusion of the eighty-four thousand?

In the response, the sūtra is cited in full to detail the numerical characteristics; since it states "from the initial resolve up to Śāriputra," we know that the four *siddhāntas* encompass the teachings of a single period, which is why it says "eighty-four thousand."
Within this, first the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* is cited, followed by the citation of alternative explanations.
The initial section has two parts:

first, citing the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* to address general difficulties; second, from the words "If one were to... onwards, extensively gathering various teachings to specifically correspond to the four *siddhāntas*.

In the text of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, [the four practices] were applied to the Four Noble Truths; here, they are applied to the Fourfold Purpose (*caturvidha-saṃgraha*). This is because the meaning of the Fourfold Purpose is identical to that of the Four Noble Truths, as explained in detail within the section on the application to the Truths.
There are further eighty-four thousand other distinct characteristics, as recorded in the first fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.

Regarding "Pāramitās," the *Bhadrakalpika Sūtra* enumerates three hundred and fifty pāramitās; subsequently, by correlating these with the six perfections and the four divisions of afflictions, they constitute the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, as also recorded in the first fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.

Furthermore, in the *Mahāvaiḍūrya-sūtra*, all six perfections are referred to as "pāramitās" (度無極); thus, in the translations of the Jin and Song dynasties, *pāramitā* was consistently rendered as "du wuji" (度無極).
Regarding the seven cases of "permissible" and "impermissible" use: "permissible" (*de*) refers to self-realization, while "use" (*yong*) refers to benefiting others.
This is divided into two parts:
first, the heading; second, the explanation.
The explanation consists of two parts:
first, citing the ultimate fruit; second, citing those on the path of cause. Within the section on those on the path of cause, there are two further divisions:
First, the four propositions are set forth; second, they are explained.

In the explanation, there are differences between ordinary beings and the four teachings. Within the first two teachings—the Tripitaka and the Shared—each is separately explained by distinguishing between the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the first three sections on the Two Vehicles, the Śrāvakas are discussed first, followed by the Pratyekabuddhas.
Within the section on the Śrāvakas, there are two parts:

first, it clarifies that they have attained [realization] but cannot employ it; second, from "Even if" (*jialing*) onwards, it clarifies that although they can employ it, they are not equal to those who can employ it properly.
The first passage is easily understood.
The second passage clearly elucidates the characteristic of being unable to employ the four *siddhāntas*.

Only when one can accord with the capacities [of beings] is it called "being able to employ" them. Even if a *śrāvaka* were to desire to benefit others, because they miss the mark regarding capacities, they are unable to employ them; hence it says, "even if."
Within this, the first section presents the full vows and the penetrating clarity to distinguish the capacities of the practitioners.

Next, from "As with Pūrṇa" onwards, it is treated according to the four *siddhāntas*; in each case, one first enters and exits [the state], and finally concludes that [the practitioner] is incapable of utilizing it.
The initial text states, "Just as Pūrṇa converted non-Buddhists for ninety days," as recorded in the sixth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.
Regarding Śāriputra’s failure to match the capacities [of his audience], it is as recorded in the seventh fascicle of the *Zhiguan*.
Regarding the *kaṭhina*, it is as recorded in the ninth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
As for the phrase "just as Śāriputra did not deliver Puṇyavardhana," the treatise states:
"This bhikṣu was a fish in a previous life, seven hundred *yojanas* in length. Although he had fallen among the fish, the seeds of his former merit remained because he had once heard the Dharma."

At that time, there was a merchant leader who, leading a company of merchants, had entered the sea to gather treasures. Suddenly, he saw the current surge and the ship heading toward White Mountain; furthermore, he beheld three suns appearing simultaneously, whereupon he informed the navigator.
The master mariner said:
"This is a calamity! It is not that three days have passed; two are the eyes of a fish, and one is the sun in the sky. The white mountain is the fish's teeth;
you will surely enter the belly of a fish."
The people on the ship each invoked their respective deities; among them was an upāsaka who recited, "Namo Buddhāya.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s name, the fish thought to itself:
"This is a disciple of the Buddha, and I too was once a disciple of the Buddha."
The fish immediately endured death and kept its mouth closed; consequently, the flowing water receded.
Because the fish had relinquished its life, the wind blew its carcass onto the shore.

Its spirit was reborn at a time when it encountered the Buddha, yet Śāriputra and the five hundred others were not yet saved. The Buddha then delivered the fish, and it attained the fruit of realization.

The Buddha ordered him to travel along the seashore, where he saw a mountain of bones seven thousand yojanas high; its northern side was not reached by the sun. Upon returning, he informed the Buddha, who said:
"These are the bones of your own body."
Question: The fish’s body is seven hundred yojanas long, yet the mountain of bones it sees is seven thousand yojanas high; why is its body small while the mountain of bones is so large?
Answer: Perhaps there is a scribal error; it should likely be "seventy.
Regarding the phrase "Great Physician" and so forth: Śāriputra is the Great Physician, while the five hundred [disciples] are the Lesser Physicians.

Regarding the phrase "The Pratyekabuddhas are likewise," since they do not understand the capacities [of others] according to principle, it is clear that they cannot employ the four [methods of conversion]. Although they may practice in groups, this is merely out of compassion; as Śāriputra said, "I do not know their capacities, but I preach the Dharma for them only out of pity. This can be understood by analogy with the Śrāvakas.

Next, it is explained that the Bodhisattvas of the Three Piṭakas have not yet attained the Truth of Cessation; this is termed "not having attained one," yet they are fully capable of employing the four [truths].
The section beginning with "Why is this so? provides the explanation.
Because they do not sever their afflictions, they are called "doctors for the sick.

Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching who have not yet attained skillfulness up to the sixth stage are equal to Arhats; although they also preach the Dharma, they cannot adapt it to the capacities of others, and thus they are said to be "not yet skillful."

Since the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*) in the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) involve the progressive cultivation of the Middle Way, its semblance Middle Way (*pratibimba-madhyamā*) is more efficacious than the preceding stages; from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, the True and Responsive [bodies] manifest spontaneously.
Eighth, regarding the provisional and the real (*upāya-tattva*): first the heading, then the explanation.
The explanation consists of two parts:
first, the direct explanation; second, the analytical inquiry. Within the direct explanation, there are two further sections:

The first section, "Reiteration," refers back to the previous discussion on the correspondence with the Truths (*satya*), which had not yet distinguished between the provisional and the real; hence it says, "generally.
The second section, the "Actual Explanation," has two parts:
first, the four teachings; second, the five flavors.
The initial section consists of four parts; within the first three [sections] regarding the Tripiṭaka, there are again four sub-sections.

First is the citation of treatises for a general judgment: the statement, "The *Śāstra* says that most sūtras speak of the three *siddhāntas*," etc., is made in contrast between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. That is to say, it refers to the sūtras of the Tripiṭaka as "most sūtras" and the *Prajñāpāramitā* as the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*), each having its own intended meaning.
Next, below the section on the "Three Piṭakas," the essence of the teaching and contemplation is shown.
It is not that the principle of emptiness is absent, but rather that it is not identical to emptiness; therefore, it is described as "slight.
Third, from the section "Regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Three Piṭakas" onwards, the third and fourth [stages] are provisionally permitted for discussion according to their respective teachings.

Regarding the statement, "To explain the four by means of the three," it is not only that the Middle Way of the First Noble Truth (paramārtha-satya) is absent, but even the True Truth of the First Noble Truth is absent; rather, the name "First Noble Truth" is established merely from the perspective of suppressing afflictions through the contemplation of the conditioned truth. Therefore, it is said, "to explain the four by means of the three."
Furthermore, "illuminating the four" means being able to explain the four to others; thus it is called "illuminating the four," whereas in one's own practice, one has only attained three.
From the words "Although this is so" onwards, there is a formal judgment that these belong to the provisional.
Next, within the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna), there are also four parts:
first, establishing the name by contrasting it with what precedes;
second, from the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) onwards, citing treatises to demonstrate skillfulness, specifically clarifying the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) in terms of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
3. From "Regarding the Buddha" below, one should explain the judgment of attainment.
4. From "Yet, in terms of" below, there is the actual judgment that it belongs to the provisional.
Next, within the Separate Teaching (biejiao), there are three parts:

First, [the passage] prior to "form" contrasts with what precedes; second, from "yet still" (*ér yóu*) onwards, it looks toward what follows; third, from "the path of teaching" (*jiàodào*) onwards, it formally judges this to belong to the provisional (*quán*).

Next, within the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*), there are two parts: first, again contrasting with what precedes; second, from "therefore, the four *sī*" onwards, it formally judges this to be the Sublime (*miào*). These can be seen according to the five flavors (*wèimì*).
Next, regarding the five layers of questions and answers within the "Discrimination" section:
in the first question, it says,
"Although the Bodhisattva attains four, these also refer to the four according to the Three Treatises, as previously explained."
In the answer, it is stated that since the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) lacks the Middle Way, it logically follows that it lacks the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha).

Regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka who do not sever their afflictions: if one views them from the perspective of the Shared Teaching, they are identical to those who have attained the four [results].

It is said that from the perspective of realization (sākṣātkriyā), there are four [bodies], while from the perspective of teaching (deśanā), they are provisional; yet it is not stated that from the perspective of teaching there are three. This is because both the path of teaching and the path of realization are said to have four, but they are not called "three" because their provisional and ultimate aspects differ.

If one takes the stage prior to the first bhūmi as the path of teaching (śāsana-mārga), then because there is the phrase "if one takes," it should be understood that from the first bhūmi onwards there still exists the significance of the path of teaching, as detailed in the third commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
Within the ninefold exposition, there are two parts:
first, the heading; second, the explanation.
Within the explanation, there are two parts:
First, the formal opening; second, the detailed analysis.
Within the first section (the formal opening), there are two parts:
first, clarifying the intent behind the provisional opening; second, formally discussing the opening in relation to the previous four periods to harmonize it with the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The initial section also has three parts:

first, a general clarification of the fundamental reality of all dharmas; second, from "Great Compassion" onwards, the employment of provisional means (*upāya*); and third, from "Now [I] reveal" onwards, the manifestation of the ultimate reality.

Regarding the initial passage: since the Dharma is fundamentally subtle, its apparent coarseness arises from the dispositions of sentient beings; thus, one should know that by simply opening [the teaching], their emotional and intellectual conditions will naturally return to the source.

Within the section on the application of skillful means (*upāya*), there are three parts: first, the actual application of means; second, the citation of scriptural evidence beginning with "The Immeasurable Meanings" (*Anantārthasamuccaya*); and third, the actual opening [of the teaching] beginning with "Now I open..."
The opening section further has two parts:

first, a general exposition on the Dharma to clarify the original intent of the transformative teaching; second, from the passage beginning with "extinguishing" (*chumie*) downward, an exposition on the characteristics of the opening by means of the difficulty posed by the Two Vehicles, because the coarse is itself the subtle, and the city of transformation is itself the treasure-destination.
Next, from "If it is milk" onwards, there is a formal clarification regarding the four periods, which is further divided into two parts:
first, the actual opening [of the precepts]; second, from "Vaipulya" onwards, the clarification of the limits of this opening.

Within the milk and the two types of ghee (*sarpis*), although the four *siddhāntas* (teachings) of the distinct instruction contain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they all pertain to the path of teaching; therefore, it is said: "Only the four provisional [teachings], the twelve provisional [teachings] of raw ghee, and the eight provisional [teachings] of matured ghee can all enter the wondrous."

In the *Clarifying Authority through the Metaphor of Raw and Refined Ghee*, the passage simply states, "The twelve hundred arhats and those who have reached definitive understanding of the śrāvaka-dharma. Regarding this, since the previous citation from the milk-teaching already included bodhisattvas—and because the status of a bodhisattva is the same [in both cases]—I have not cited it again here to avoid redundant text.
Since it is stated that "Bodhisattvas also remove the net of doubt," we know by verification that Bodhisattvas must likewise realize the three [vehicles].

Regarding the passage from "Vaipulya Prajñā" to "is here," within the opening of the *Fenqi* (Analysis of Limits), one should also mention the *Avataṃsaka*; its absence in the text is due to abbreviation.

To verify that the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) of those three divisions is no different from the perfection of the *Lotus Sūtra*, while asserting that the Sudden Teaching (Dun) resides solely in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, is surely a case of generating groundless excrescences.

Moreover, since the Dharma is fundamentally wondrous yet obstructed by the sentiments of sentient beings, the *Lotus Sūtra*—having already opened [the way]—is instead degraded as "gradual"; the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), which are the wondrous reality of the objective realm, are rendered coarse; the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are demoted to the level of bodhisattvas; the ten parables of Bhaiṣajyarāja praising the teaching are reduced to empty words; the comparison of the three ages regarding the Dharma-preacher is deemed generally unreal; and the assembly of the emanated Buddhas and the emergence of the jeweled stupa into the sky are rendered a mere display of formal courtesy.

Having realized this gradual teaching, the characteristics of its similarities and differences cannot be fully discussed; the doctrinal system of our own school alone is sufficient for thorough investigation. Why, then, do you alone treat it as exceptional and reject this wondrous sutra?

Next, regarding the section on "Questioning and Resolving the Provisional *siddhāntas*," from "Question" up to "Not so": the intent of the question is as follows: If one resolves the coarse to enter the subtle, does this mean that all four coarse *siddhāntas* equally enter the subtle ultimate *siddhānta*, or does it mean resolving the worldly to enter the worldly, and so on, up to resolving the ultimate to enter the ultimate?
Regarding the phrase "it is not so": does this mean that it is otherwise, as intended by what follows?
There is also a version that reads "is it indeed so? (為當爾不), which I suspect was an erroneous emendation.
The meaning of the response is that since both meanings are equally applicable, it is said to be "sovereign.

Regarding the phrase "even if," it refers to the intent of the initial question: even if one were to enter entirely into the wondrous primary meaning (paramārtha), since that wondrous primary meaning is not separated from the third [meaning], how would it differ from the second meaning?
Therefore, it is said that "one and three are sovereign.

In this present text, if we provisionally adopt one interpretation, it accords with the second sense by correlating [the text] with the opening of five chapters, as the names and meanings thus correspond;
however, if one were to enter solely into the primary meaning (paramārtha), one would only obtain the correlation with the essence (tattva), while the remaining meanings would be deficient.
Regarding the phrase "If one decides," the second meaning is applied below to provide a specific correspondence for each item.
Within the first section on the world, there are two parts:
first, the formal assembly; second, from "It is also... onwards, the demonstration of the assembly and entry into the characteristics.
The world is nothing other than all phenomena; because these various coarse [phenomena] are definitively made to enter this wondrous [reality], it is given the name "Wondrous.
Next, the demonstration of the convergence and entry into the Middle has two parts:
first, the comprehensive intent explained by way of phenomena; second, the comprehensive intent explained by way of analogy.

In the initial discourse on the Dharma, the seven stages of expedient means are shown to equally lead to the fulfillment of the Buddha-vehicle; in the discourse by way of parable, the names of the two vehicles are likewise referred to as "bodhisattvas," as in: "The path you practice is the bodhisattva path. Since the path practiced has already become the bodhisattva path, how could those who practice it still be called followers of the two vehicles?

Next, in determining the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the four *siddhāntas* are applied according to the five chapters; therefore, the ultimate truth is placed second, as both that which the Buddha knows and perceives and the precious destination he has reached pertain to the principle (*li*).

In the subsequent section concerning the "Exemplification for Humans," it is stated that the "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*) takes the vehicle as the cause and the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) as the fruit.

In the subsequent section concerning "Counteractive Measures," it is cited that "this precious jewel is used to trade for what is required. This means that within the teachings of expedient means (*upāya*), the dharmas have limitations; they are neither ultimate nor sublime, and are therefore arduous.

If one seeks with diligent effort, the true principle is inexhaustible, doubts are eliminated, and faith becomes complete—just as a priceless jewel can trade for endless goods. In thoroughly eliminating the suffering of poverty, nothing is more effective than the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
The meaning of "this excellent medicine" and so forth can be understood through reflection.
Therefore, the exchange [of the coarse for the subtle] and the curing of illness are both alternative names for the specific application of remedies (*pratipakṣa*).

Herein, the classification of the teachings is used to distinguish similarities and differences; since the primary intent is to manifest their identity, the two gates of the fundamental and the provisional (*honji* and *jakuji*) had not been explained prior to this point. Consequently, through this opening and closing [of the gates], there is nothing that is not heard.
Regarding the ten masters of the sūtras, there are again two parts:
first, the question; second, the answer.
Within the answer, there are two sections:
First, a general enumeration; second, a detailed explanation.
Within the explanation, first the exposition and then the conclusion.
Within the exposition, there are two parts: first, the traces (*traces of manifestation*), and second, the fundamental reality (*the source*).
Regarding the two aspects within the traces:
first, the listing of the sūtras; second, the explanation.
The same applies to the main text.
Both the traces (the phenomenal) and the fundamental (the noumenal) take nature as the source of their goodness, for the nature of goodness resides within them.
Both take advancing power and practice as their antidotes, thereby presenting the practices that serve as the means of cultivation.
The "raising of the faculties" refers to the person capable of awakening, while the "raising of perception" refers to the mind capable of seeing; this is the slight difference between them.
Thus, both equally possess the four *siddhāntas*.
The conclusion following the section on "the two places" can be understood accordingly.
Next, regarding the second detailed explanation: the first section briefly sets forth five chapters, which have already been listed above.
Now, within these five, the first chapter provides an extensive explanation of the title in two parts:
first, the opening of the chapter; second, the explanation itself.
The explanation of the [four] sections within the commentary is as follows: first, the explanation of the initial gate is divided into three parts:

first, the establishment of the title within this very sutra; second, from "Establishing this" onwards, clarifying the intent behind establishing the title; third, from the "Question" onwards, providing a detailed analysis.

Regarding the first point: although there are both general and specific aspects to the present scripture when compared with other texts, the name and meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* differ from those of other scriptures; whereas the single character "sūtra" (經) is the same in name as other texts but differs in meaning. Here, we speak of it as "general" because we follow its common name.
Next, regarding the establishment of the meaning of the title: for what reason is the name of this sutra established?

Since the name encompasses the entire treatise, and the purport of the treatise does not exceed three [points], and because the names differ in being both general and specific, the three points of purport likewise follow the names in being general and specific; therefore, these three points of purport are explained:
the discernment between the coarse and the subtle, the distinctions among teaching, practice, and principle, and the different paths of the general and the specific.

Regarding the first, the explanation of the title of the treatise,
First, there is a general explanation of both the universal and the particular; next, there is a specific explanation of the universal and the particular.
"Universal" refers to that which is common to all scriptures, teachings, practices, and principles; "particular" refers specifically to the teaching of perfect expression.
The initial general explanation has two parts: first, the brief; second, the detailed. Regarding the brief:

within all the names found throughout the holy teachings of a single lifetime, there are none that do not possess these three—teaching, practice, and principle; none that do not accord with the universal through the particular; and none that do not respond to the particular through the universal. Therefore, these three comprehensively encompass the Buddha-dharma: teaching corresponds to the response to the capacity [of the listener], practice corresponds to cause and effect, and principle corresponds to name and reality (or phenomenon and principle). Without these three pairs, the categories of the universal and the particular would be established in vain.
Next, within the detailed explanation, there are three parts:
first, regarding the teaching, there are two sections:
the explanation and the conclusion.
The explanation has two parts:
first, clarifying the specific [teachings]; second, from "The Golden Mouth" onwards, clarifying the general [teachings]; and third, from "Therefore, the General" onwards, the conclusion.
Next, regarding the application to practice, there are also two parts:

This consists of an explanation, a conclusion, and within the explanation, first a specific analysis, followed by an analogy drawn from the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (the *Dàlùn*) based on the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*.
Within the initial specific analysis, there are two parts:
first, the formal proposition, and second, the citation of scriptural evidence.

These are all general principles applied to specific instances; for now, they are explained according to their particularities. For example, when it says "Dharma Jewel," it is general because it encompasses various types, yet it is specific [in its application].
Next, in the citation of scriptural evidence, one first relies on the Hinayana; each statement is specific, yet because both are correct, they are general.

Regarding the phrase "each explaining the cause of the body," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the thirty-second fascicle within the explanation of speech according to one's own intention (*svacchandavāda*), states:
"For example, five hundred bhikṣus asked Śāriputra:
'The Buddha has spoken of the cause of the body; what is it?'"
Śāriputra replied:
"You all have likewise attained right liberation; you should know this yourselves.
For what reason, then, do you ask such a question?"
A bhikṣu said: "When we had not yet attained right liberation, we thought that ignorance was the cause of the body; when we cultivated this contemplation, we attained the fruit of arhatship."

Some spoke of craving, some of volitional formations, and so on, up to food, drink, and the five objects of desire. After these five hundred had each explained their own understanding, they went together to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves, circumambulated him to the right, and sat down, each recounting their own interpretation.
Śāriputra asked,
"Who speaks correctly?
The Buddha replied:
There is nothing that is not the correct teaching.
Next, by relying on the fact that within the Great [Vehicle] each enters separately while remaining non-dual, they are thus universal.

Regarding the "thirty-two bodhisattvas entering the gate of non-duality," since there is already the gate through which they enter and all gates lead toward the principle, by analogy with the five hundred [bodhisattvas], these thirty-two are likewise nothing other than the correct teaching; this cites the practices capable of leading toward the goal in both the Great and Small Vehicles.
Next, in this analogy, "unattainability" is precisely the principle (*li*).

By citing the inferior to illustrate the superior, it is shown that even the contemplation of the breath is itself the principle; how much more so, then, the practices capable of leading toward the two vehicles, both Great and Small?
"Know that" concludes the preceding section, which itself has two parts:
first, the conclusion; second, the citation of scriptural evidence.
Next, within the section on principle, there are three parts:
First, the establishment; second, the citation of evidence; third, the conclusion.
Regarding the first section, because it is not two, it is "universal" (tong); because it is not one, it is "particular" (bie).
The two sections within the citation of evidence can be understood by analogy with the establishment.

First, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is cited; next, the statement from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* that "liberation is likewise, possessing many names" is cited. When the Great Master was at Lingshi Temple, he lectured on the "Hundred Phrases of Liberation" for an entire summer retreat, providing a hundred-fold explanation for each phrase. Thus, liberation possesses ten thousand names.
Regarding the statement, "As Śakra, Lord of the Devas, has a thousand names": he is also called Kauśika, Vāsava, Vṛṣabha, Indra, Sahasrākṣa, Śacīpati, Vajraśikhara, Ratnadhvaja, and so forth.
The section below, "Different Names," concludes that because the names differ, they are distinct; yet because the ritual is one, they are universal.
Regarding the phrase "now called" and so forth within the section on the distinct: the "wondrous Dharma" is distinct because it differs from other sutras;
the "sutra" itself is universal because the term "sutra" is common to all.

Thus we know that this present sutra, from its general and specific opening words "Thus [have I heard]" to its conclusion "and withdrew," is entirely the Buddha’s teaching; it is all the wondrous Dharma. From beginning to end, every part is both specific and general.

Within these general and specific aspects of the teaching, the practices and principles are explained both generally and specifically; thus, one should know that the fundamental and the manifested are nothing other than cause and effect, as well as name and reality. Since it would be impossible to cite every instance, I shall briefly indicate the general direction by roughly citing analogies to demonstrate the general and specific aspects of practice, as well as the provisional and the ultimate truth within the expedient means, which constitute the general and specific aspects of principle.

Regarding the parable: the fact that the sons' causes for practice differ constitutes the distinction between their practices (*caryā-bheda*); the equal bestowal of great chariots leading directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) constitutes the commonality of their practice (*caryā-sāmānya*). The great chariot is the vehicle of the commonality, while the site of enlightenment is the true reality (*dharmatā*) to which they accord. Even the names such as "Great Wisdom" (*mahāprajñā*) constitute the distinction between names; yet, since each distinct name is established based on that same principle, this is the commonality of the principle (*tattva-sāmānya*).
This is the general and specific [distinctions] of the principles currently being treated, which will be explained more extensively below in the commentary.
Fourth, the section beginning with "In terms of this" concludes [the discussion].
Next, in the section on analysis, there is first a question, followed by an answer.

Regarding the reason why, among the questions, one asks only about the teaching (*śāsana*): the teaching, practice (*pratipatti*), and principle (*tattva*) are mutually interdependent and permeate one another. Since the teaching occupies the initial position, one asks only concerning the teaching; the other two types [of categories] are naturally revealed by relying upon the teaching.
The initial two interpretations—the extensive and the abbreviated—apply broadly across all teachings; therefore, they generally take a single Buddha as the common subject.

Now, however, these are distinguished into four different Buddhas, each with their own distinct gateways and variations in teaching; thus it is said: "The teachers differ, and the teachings they establish are likewise diverse."
Regarding the objection posed in the section beginning with "How so?": it challenges the present four specific [categories] by means of the previous general [principle].

As for the meaning of the subsequent response, it encompasses both the sense of being "within the respective category" (*dang-fen*) and "spanning the sections" (*kua-jie*); one should know that these two senses are no different from the two excellences of "relativity" (*dai*) and "transcendence" (*jue*).
Furthermore, the two preceding interpretations also each possess two meanings.

What are they? If one relies on the employment of skillful means (*upāya*), it is the meaning of "respective stages"; if one accords with the Buddha’s intention, it is the meaning of "transcending stages. Although each possesses these two meanings, because their specific intent was not discussed and they were explained in a general manner, and furthermore because the two paths had not been clearly distinguished, their meaning remained broad and indistinct rather than being vividly revealed. For this reason, it is necessary to answer by distinguishing between these two meanings.
When [the teaching] is categorized according to its general application throughout the entire dispensation, it becomes a matter of mutual dependence in the present context;
yet when spanning across the various sections, it pertains exclusively to the present sutra. However, the Buddha’s intention does not apply solely to the present.
To explain these two meanings, first the headings are presented, next they are listed, and finally they are explained.

In the explanation, one should first treat the "internal divisions" (*dang-fen*) and then the "crossing the sections" (*kua-jie*), each of which is analyzed according to the three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle.

First, regarding the internal divisions: following the intent of the preceding questions, this is done to clarify the crossing of sections; for it is difficult to establish that the four teachings, when considered within their own respective divisions, all fully possess these three meanings.

Within this, the primary correct explanation comes first, followed by a synthesis; as these cannot be fully detailed here, they are established alongside the subsequent meanings as being either difficult or easy.
The initial passage is extensive according to the Tripiṭaka, while the remaining three follow the same pattern.
Within the first of the three [sections], there are three parts:

first, the formal explanation of the characteristics; second, the citation of scriptural evidence beginning with "The Sūtra says..."; and third, the clarification of the meaning within that specific category beginning with "This, then..."

The initial passage is clear. Regarding the citation of evidence which states, "He immediately cast off his necklaces and so forth": on the forty-one stages of the *saṃbhogakāya*, precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and *dhāraṇīs* constitute the necklaces; the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*) is the soft upper garment; the major and minor marks and the ocean of signs are the ornaments; the sixteen-foot physical marks are the coarse attire; the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena are the tattered rags; and the manifestation of afflictions, conditioned existence, and outflows is the dust covering the body. In reality, there is no birth-and-death or affliction, yet appearing to have birth-and-death and affliction is the semblance of having something to fear.
As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, "Chapter on Fearlessness":
"As the Sūtra says, 'Come, Bhikṣu; since you follow my Dharma, I am pleased,' this seems to imply the presence of craving."
As it was said to Devadatta:
"You are a foolish person, eating the spittle and saliva of others.
This appears to be an expression of anger.
He says of himself: "I am a lion among men.
This appears to be pride.
"Uphold my Dharma well, as if carrying a bowl of oil.
Furthermore, it was as he said to Devadatta:
"I would not even entrust the Dharma to Śāriputra and others; how much less would I give it to you?"
"This appears to involve views.
In the text, only the single phrase "soiled clothes" is briefly cited.

As for "speech and diligent practice" and so forth, these refer to the Lesser Vehicle; the seven categories of the Path (saptavidha-mārga) are the vessels for removing the filth of views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa).

"Speech" refers to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); "diligent effort" refers to the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*); "Ho, man! and so forth refer to the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*); "Settle your mind well" refers to the five faculties (*indriya*); "For what reason? and so forth refer to the five powers (*bala*); "I shall give you another name" refers to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); "Though you rejoice at this encounter" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); and "I shall increase your price" refers to the stage of *uṣmagata*, which cannot yet produce the truth, whereas the bases of psychic power can; therefore, it is said that "the price is increased."
The current text is very brief.

Regarding the phrase "oil for anointing the feet," it refers to attaining the power of psychic travel (*ṛddhipāda*) as described in the following verse: just as one whose feet are anointed with oil can walk upon water, so too can one attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, oil can eliminate wind, just as meditative concentration eliminates distraction; this is explained in detail in the commentary on the "Chapter on Resolute Belief" (*Adhimukty-adhikāra*).
This serves as an analogy specifically for the teachings, practices, and principles of the Tripiṭaka, which can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the statement in the subsequent section on the three teachings, "The same applies to the Shared, Distinct, and Complete [teachings]," this can be understood by synthesizing it with the explanation provided below in the "Excellence of the Fruit" section of the Root Chapter concerning the four different types of bodily manifestations.
Next, within the section on "spanning the joints," there are four parts:

first, the refutation of the respective categories; second, the establishment of the characteristics of spanning the joints, beginning with "If one opens..."; third, the summary of the intent, beginning with "In this way..."; and fourth, the harmonious integration, beginning with "Acting in this way... and so forth.
The initial passage is further divided into two parts:
first, the direct refutation; second, from "Merely hidden" (*zhǐ yǐn*) onwards, the clarification of the meaning within its own category (*dang-fen*).

As for establishing the meaning within its own category: having completed the exposition on the provisional (*quan*), because the provisional and the real (*shi*) are contrasted, there are four primary [teachings], each of which is distinct.

Therefore, it is clarified that "the appropriate division" (dang-fen) has no separate reality; it is merely the concealment of the ultimate truth and the provisional manifestation of means, which is tentatively termed the "appropriate division.
From the beginning up to the phrase "Golden Radiance," this manifests the body of the appropriate division.
The phrase "does not speak" below refers to the teaching of the dharmas belonging to their respective categories (*pratyeka-dharma*).
It is an abbreviation for the category of bodily phenomena (*kāya-dharma*);

the other two categories are likewise omitted. Regarding the statement, "It does not speak of the flavors of sweetness, permanence, and bliss, but speaks of saltiness, acidity, impermanence, pungency, and bitterness," the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

"Suffering has the taste of vinegar; impermanence has the taste of salt; non-self has the taste of bitterness; pleasure has the taste of sweetness; self has the taste of pungency; and permanence has the taste of blandness.
With afflictions as the fuel and wisdom as the fire, by these causes and conditions, the food of Nirvana is prepared."

Because those [flavors] break down the three types of cultivation, there are only three tastes; as these are contrasted by their superiority and inferiority, they form six tastes. Therefore, the pure and the impure are omitted and not discussed.
In the present text, following the inferior [category], it says, "it does not speak of sweet and pleasant," and so forth.

"Discarding the King’s Regalia": this repetition of words conceals the subtle and manifests the coarse; it is also identical in intent to the previous concealment of merit and manifestation of the sixteen-foot [form].

Just as when a destitute son sees his father’s noble, majestic, and dignified bearing, one should know that the immeasurable merits adorning him with necklaces and regalia as a king are, in truth, of one and the same nature regarding the principles of body and speech, and there is no separate path.
To now discard these garments and ornaments is precisely the provisional meaning of "dividing and bestowing.
The term "feces vessel" refers to the factors of the Path (mārga-dharma) involving birth and extinction.
The passage beginning with "If one opens up the skillful means" correctly clarifies the characteristics of transcending the stages; this sentence provides the general opening.
Regarding the phrase "directed toward the body, directed toward the Dharma, directed toward practice," etc., this refers to the principles of the preceding preparatory practices of body and speech.

Among the three summarized intentions, the first states: "While it is universally the teaching of a single sound, there are distinctions between the Small and Great Vehicles. This refers to the "single sound" that transcends the boundaries [of the vehicles] in the *Lotus Sūtra*, which differs from the "single sound" of the Small Vehicle’s own specific stage, as detailed in the first commentary of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
Therefore, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the Buddha’s single voice refers only to that within the Three Piṭakas.
By analogy with the general and the specific, there should likewise be a "single voice" appropriate to each respective category (*dang-fen*).

Within the aforementioned meaning of the "respective categories," the four types of teaching masters are divided, each having their own specific doctrines and the principles they practice; thus, the meaning is easy to understand.
Principle has no variety; why, then, do the four teachings each have their own objects of elucidation?
Since the objects of elucidation differ, the principle ought not to differ; therefore, it is said that [the principle] is difficult to harmonize.

In the sense of "spanning the stages" (*kuajie*), the four teachings are not distinguished as having separate elucidations of principle; therefore, it is said that [the principle] is easy to understand.
In various sutras, cause and effect are explained as being distinct; now, transcending those distinctions, we discuss only a single principle, which is why it is difficult to comprehend.

If two meanings mutually support one another, both the principle and its manifestation are easy to understand; if the two meanings are separated, both are difficult to clarify. Therefore, these two meanings require one another: when analyzed according to their respective divisions, they constitute the aspect of "mutual dependence" (*xiāngdài*) in this sutra; when spanning across the sections, they constitute the aspect of "opening up the provisional" (*kāi quán*) in this sutra.

Furthermore, if one considers the provisional meanings found within the Vaipulya, Prajñāpāramitā, Avataṃsaka, and other such scriptures, these still constitute the employment of expedient means (*upāya*).

However, when one arrives at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, from the perspective of their provisional meaning, the distinction between the provisional and the real is established. Once this distinction is made, the provisional is then set aside; once it is set aside, it is revealed. This process of revealing and setting aside is simultaneous and cannot occur at different times.
Regarding the sequence of the two sublime dharmas of meditative concentration, there are four parts:

first, the heading; second, the clarification of the sequence starting from "If according to the meaning"; third, the explicit explanation of the present intent starting from "According to the current title"; and fourth, the reconciliation of the two approaches starting from "Although."
The first part is as stated in the text.
Regarding the subsequent passage, both the meanings and the names each have their own underlying purpose.
Within the section on meaning, there is first the establishment of the position, followed by the citation of scriptural evidence.
Within the section on names, it is first established and then followed by the citation of actual instances.
Regarding these instances, there are two parts:
first, proving that [the name] follows from the name itself; second, from the passage beginning with "Dulun" (篤論), it further conforms to the meaning.
Regarding the term "dǔ" (dedication/sincerity), the *Erya* states:
"It means firmness. The *Laozi* says:
"Guarding stillness is called 'sincerity' (*du*)," where "sincerity" means uprightness and correctness.
To clarify the present meaning, one should know that the titles must follow their conventional usage; thus, "Sublime" comes first and "Dharma" follows, as was already indicated in the headings.

Now, because we wish to explain the meaning, we must follow that meaning. In the section beginning with "The reason why," within the formal explanation, there is first the Dharma and then the Sublime.

Regarding the fourfold mutual integration: it is precisely because there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows that the explanation follows the convenience of the meaning; thus, one should know that both the preceding and the following do not deviate from principle.
The old commentary has two parts:
first, the presentation of various masters; second, the critique by our own school.

Regarding the first part, the reason why the first three masters were not refuted by the Great Master is that the subsequent text states, "The others [were dismissed] because they merely followed the wind."
If one wishes to have a slight understanding of gain and loss, one may follow the approach of Guangzhai’s intention to dismantle [false views], wherein there is nothing that is not discarded.
As the *Daochang guan* states:
"The three are not real."
Not knowing which of the three teachings was not truly real,
and since they were unaware that there were Bodhisattvas distinct from those three [vehicles], their devotion to the One Vehicle and the Unsurpassed remained unmanifested despite its subtlety.

If one cites the present sutra to prove that [the vehicle] is "sublime," this may be somewhat reasonable in principle; however, as for what is being proven, there is nothing sublime to be discussed, and everything else remains unintelligible.

Regarding the phrase "it is sublime because it is unsurpassed," this cites the sutra passage: "This vehicle is subtle and wondrous, the foremost in purity. It should be stated in full as: "Among all worlds, it is without superior."
Some versions lack the third phrase;
only when combined with the preceding two phrases can it be proven that [the teaching] is wondrous because it is unsurpassed.
Furthermore, regarding the statement, "To entrust words to discourse beyond the image," the intended meaning is as follows:

The wondrous principle is formless, yet discourse relies upon images; by entrusting discourse to that which has form, one uses images as a medium for expression. While the medium of images is subtle and that which has form is coarse, when the principle expressed through images is realized, both the subtle and the coarse vanish. Because the subtle and the coarse have vanished, it is called "wondrous."
Furthermore, it is not known where the image—whether its manifestation be utterly refined or utterly coarse—is headed.
The citation of scriptural passages to substantiate this meaning is also as before.
"Ji of Kuaiji" refers to the foundation (or site) of Fahua Temple.

Regarding the statement "the manifestations are the same," it is unclear what teaching was previously held to be different among the three, and by reconciling with which teaching they were made the same.
Furthermore, it is unknown what is being pointed to as the "three causes" of the past.
Therefore, it also renders the "Exquisite" (Miao) school untenable.
The three masters of the Northern Land hold the same underlying intent.
The views of these three masters do not diverge from those of Guangzhai; thus, it is said that they were merely "gauging the wind."
It is like breaking an array with the wind at one's back: once the vanguard is broken, the rest surrender at its mere sight.
As for the next, Master Guangzhai, even Master Zhigong, who was moved by heavenly flowers, still called him "one who bites fleas."
Emperor Wu wished to pray for rain and questioned Master Zhi.
Master Zhi said,
"Clouds can bring about rain."

He then invited Master Yun to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. When they reached the passage on the "Universal Rain Falling Equally in the Four Directions," as soon as the rain fell, it was sufficient.

Furthermore, before Master Yun was born, someone found a commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in the water, with the inscription: "Sent to Master Yun. The details are as recorded in his separate biography.

If such a response through spiritual resonance is still not in accord with principle, how much less so for others? Examining the fact that he personally received the teachings at Vulture Peak, there is no error in his realization;

yet, the three masters were somewhat similar to Guangzhai, while falling short of Guangzhai’s Bodhisattva who employed three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Thus we know that Guangzhai had three points that could be reconciled, but lacked even one point to which to return. Because there was nothing to which to return, his refutation failed to establish the "wondrous," and because he pointed to the past as being merely general and diffuse, his refutation of the "coarse" was not truly coarse. This is precisely why he encountered twenty-four difficulties; there is indeed a reason for this.
Within this, first the general framework is established, followed by a detailed explanation.

In the explanation, first the three types of coarseness in the causes and effects of the past are explained, and next the three types of subtlety in the causes and effects of the present are explained.
Regarding the initial passage, there is first the cause and then the result.
Within the initial cause, there is first the heading, then the explanation, and finally the conclusion.
The first is as the text states.

In the explanation, while the substance (*tǐ*) fully enumerates the stages of the three vehicles, the function (*yòng*) mentions only the Bodhisattvas; this is because citing the superior includes the inferior. Since the Bodhisattva of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* does not sever the causes of delusion and thus resembles the ordinary stage of the two vehicles, it is termed "identity of cause" (*yīntóng*).
All of these take the initial illumination of the Truths (*satya*) and so forth as their essence.

Regarding the statement "the ninth unimpeded [knowledge]" within this stage: because the period of subduing afflictions (*kleśa*) during the three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is long, one continues until the ninth grade of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) has been subdued but not yet severed. Since the stage has not yet transcended the realms of existence, let alone the *pariṇāmika-vipākaja* (transformative) realm, it is therefore termed "lower."
The application of brevity can be understood.
One should know that the applications in the stages of the Two Vehicles are inferior and brief; this can be inferred by comparison with the present case.
Regarding the three meanings of the former fruit: first, the heading and enumeration; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.

Regarding the explanation of the essence (*tattva*): even upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood, there remains only the *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* [nirvāṇas]; therefore, its essence is narrow when compared to that of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). The fruit of Buddhahood likewise occupies the same station as the "transformed city" (*pariṇāmika-nagara*), and the fruit of Buddhahood likewise halts at the elimination of only the four abodes of attachment (*catur-vāsabhūmi*).
The phrase "Furthermore" below reiterates the function [of the lifespan].

Regarding "eighty" and so forth, the lifespan established during the time he was practicing the bodhisattva path as a former fruit—exceeding the sands of the Ganges—is surpassed by the present lifespan, which has not yet been exhausted and is twice that aforementioned number; this is designated as the "latter."
Because the Buddha did not have such a lifespan during the eighty-year period, it is termed "short.
Next, regarding the explanation of the three meanings for each of the present cause and effect, there are two parts:
first, the explanation; second, the conclusion.
The explanation has two parts:
first, the cause; second, the result. Within the section on the cause, there are three parts:
This consists of the enumeration, the explanation, and the conclusion.

Within the explanation, it says: "Practicing the bodhisattva path outside the realm. If one practices solely for oneself, one must necessarily be outside the realm; if one also transforms sentient beings, one takes birth at will.
Regarding the results [of the practice], there is likewise first a presentation, secondly an explanation, and thirdly a conclusion.

As for "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*), when at the stage of the cause, their function consists in subduing and severing [afflictions]; when at the stage of the fruit, their function consists in benefiting sentient beings. According to the intention of Guangzhai, the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Nirdeśaparivarta*) represents the extension of life through supernormal powers to benefit sentient beings.
The section beginning with "That is" concludes [the preceding argument].
Next, the section beginning with "Now and ancient" provides a refutation, which consists of three parts:

first, citing a difficult case as an analogy for an easy one; second, the formal refutation beginning with "The essence of the cause"; and third, establishing the force of the refutation beginning with "That which is produced by another."

Regarding "the south" in the opening passage: the Southern Dynasty refers to Jiangdong; it was formerly referred to collectively as the Southern Dynasty, but later divided into two circuits, hence the specific designation "Jiangdong."
The phrase "Sheng, Zhao, Shi" is used merely for the sake of linguistic convenience.

The "Four Sons of Guanzhong" were Daosheng, Sengzhao, Daorong, and Daoyi. Later generations adopted and utilized the teachings of these four masters; thus, people of the time said, "Daosheng and Sengzhao give expression to the true nature. If one considers this from a contemporary perspective, their views mostly adhere to the principle of universal integration (tong), yet they are not necessarily entirely correct; hence it is said that they "mostly adhere" to it.
"Fu" (attached) means "in proximity. Since Guangzhai was also in proximity to Sengzhao and Kumārajīva, it says "Ningyuan" (How distant!).

People of the time believed that Guangzhai had grasped the essential meaning, so [the author] suppressed this by saying "not distant," first refuting the objection regarding the attainment of the essential meaning; the remaining points will clarify themselves easily.
Next, within the section on the correct refutation, there are two parts:
first, the cause; second, the result.
Within the cause, there are three aspects—essence, state, and function—each of which is challenged by four "one-ness" arguments.

In the initial refutation of the essence of the cause, the author first generally rebukes Guangzhai. Because his previous statements were vague and he had granted [the opponent's position] too broadly, it says, "It may be so.
The section beginning with "Why is this? constitutes the formal refutation, which has three parts:
first, citing the former [position] that there are four kinds of oneness; second, citing the present [position] that there are no four kinds of oneness; third, the conclusion of the difficulty.
The first section has two parts:
first, the enumeration; second, the conclusion.
Regarding the initial passage, *prajñā* (wisdom) raises up the vehicle (*yāna*); since the vehicle is itself the teaching, it is called "transporting."
Since it is stated that all things are universally pervasive and equal to the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), one should know that its essence is vast.

The *Prajñāpāramitā* contains the "one" of teaching; the *Candrapradīpa* (Siyi) contains the "one" of practice; the *Avataṃsaka* contains the "one" of persons; and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* contains the "one" of principle.
"Because of this in the past" concludes [the previous section].
"If one says" and below critiques the absence of the four and the one in the present sutra; this further consists of two parts:
first, the enumeration, and second, the explanation. The enumeration follows the intent of the Guangzhai commentary, and subsequent sections should be understood by analogy.
"Know that" [marks] the section on refuting the force [of the opponent's argument], wherein one uses their own logic to refute them.
This section on refuting the stages consists of four parts:
first, the introductory intent; second, the thesis; third, the explanation; and fourth, the conclusion.
The first two [sections] are already known.
The commentary also has two parts:
first, the past; second, the present.
In the previous section, there was first an explanation and then a conclusion.
In the initial passage of the explanation, it says: "The 'unsurpassed' refers to the Dharma; by citing the Dharma, one identifies the person.
Regarding the statement, "Prajñā is the unsurpassed vidyā-mantra," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks Śakra Devendra: "For what reason is Prajñā considered the unsurpassed vidyā-mantra?"
Answer:

Various non-Buddhist sages possess diverse incantations that benefit the people; those who recite these incantations can, according to their wishes, command all ghosts and spirits. These seers possess incantations through which they attain great renown, and because the people submit to them and hold these incantations in high esteem, Prajñā is therefore called a mantra.
Śakra addressed the Buddha:

"Because this Prajñā mantra constantly bestows upon sentient beings the joy of virtue and the Way, whereas other incantations and arts can only increase evil; this divine Prajñā mantra can even extinguish attachment to the various dhyānas and nirvāṇa, let alone [attachment to] greed and the like."
Therefore, it is called the "Great Bright Mantra.
Regarding "unsurpassed brightness": since some greatness may still have something superior to it, it is next termed "unsurpassed.
Regarding "unequaled with the unequaled": that which is equal to this state of being unequaled is called "unequaled with the unequaled."
Because they all destroy ignorance, they are collectively termed "clarity" (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, among the non-Buddhists there are mantras that can know the minds of others, mantras that can effect flight and transformation, and mantras that can prolong one's lifespan;
yet among all such mantras, Prajñāpāramitā transcends them immeasurably and boundlessly, and is therefore called "unequaled."
Furthermore, because all Buddhas are peerless among all sentient beings, Prajñā is called "peerless" (*asama*).
Moreover, "unequaled with the unequaled" (*asamasama*) refers to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
There is nothing capable of equaling this peerless state; therefore, it is called "unequaled with the unequaled" (*asamasama*).

Thus, the bodhisattvas praised in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* are all those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), whose rank is adjacent to Sublime Enlightenment (*tathāgata-jñāna*); hence it is said, "approaching the sovereign wisdom of the Buddha, who is unequaled with the unequaled. Since the supreme meaning of this mantra is identical to Sublime Enlightenment, it is called "unequaled with the unequaled."
This is because the meaning of the mantra is "unequaled" (*asama-sama*).
Furthermore, regarding the citation from the *Mahā-śāstra*, it should state "causal practice" (*hetu-caryā*); the use of the term "stage" (*bhūmi*) is likely an error.
Receiving the Dharma-nature body and practicing the bodhisattva path is explained as before.

Regarding the citation from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* concerning "approaching the Unequaled" (*asama-sama*): the Buddha is called "Unequaled" (*asama*), and because he is the most supreme among those who are unequaled, he is called "Equal to the Unequaled" (*sama-sama*).
Because they approach the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*), and because what they approach is raised up [as the subject], it is called "the Buddha’s sovereign wisdom.

Regarding "the Māras of the ten directions," this refers to the text of the "Inconceivable Chapter" (*Acintyaparivarta*): Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages (*bhūmi*) can become Māras, yet not all Māras are such Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages; therefore, the text simply says "many. Since practitioners of reality cannot be troubled by those in the deep stages, it says, "not something a donkey can endure."
This is why it is now said, "All are," and so forth. Next, regarding the "Text of Vimalakīrti":

because the first dwelling (*prathama-bhūmi*) and the eight aspects are not yet the ultimate stage, they are designated by the term "although. Therefore, one must still practice the Bodhisattva path, cultivating oneself and transforming others in order to advance to subsequent stages; this is because, through the first dwelling, one has perceived the principle (*tattva*).
Therefore, by citing the principle (li) to manifest the virtue, the secret treasury precisely accords with the principle as it is perceived.
The section beginning with "In this way" concludes [the preceding].

Next, regarding the passage beginning with "If one says," which clarifies why this present sutra also uses the term "stage" (wei) instead of "practice" (xing)—it should be understood that the stage is used to manifest the practice; the same applies to the preceding text.
"Should be known" concludes [the preceding section].
Next, the application is explained in three parts:
namely, the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
The explanation has two parts:
first, the past; second, the present.
Regarding the past, there are again two sections:
The commentary on the *śloka* and the *nigamana* begins with the teaching.

Next, in clarifying the practice of the Elder [Śāriputra], it first states "ignorance" (*avidyā*) to indicate the attainment by pointing out the loss; "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) correctly clarifies the practice of knowing; "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) simultaneously cites the objects of observation to reveal the observing subject; and from "knowledge and ignorance" (*vidyā-avidyā*) onwards, the characteristics of the contemplation are set forth.

The passage beginning with "If one knows" explains the characteristics of contemplation (*guanxiang*), while that beginning with "This is called" concludes the characteristics of contemplation; since both constitute the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), the word "and" (*yong*) should also have been included, though it is omitted for brevity in the text.

Next, regarding the passage in the "Explanation of the One Person" that says "one day," and so forth, these are all terms used for refutation and supersession; they are cited to demonstrate the superiority of the person by means of what they supersede.
The initial statement, "Practicing Prajñā for one day is like the sun illuminating the world," and so on, refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "Chapter on Cultivating Response," which states:
"A Bodhisattva practicing Prajñā for a single day surpasses those of the Two Vehicles."
The followers of the two vehicles are like fireflies; they do not form the thought:
"By my power, I can illuminate Jambudvīpa and cause it to be universally and brightly lit.
The followers of the two vehicles are likewise; they do not form such a thought.
I practice the six perfections until reaching bodhi.

The Bodhisattva illuminates the world, penetratingly shining upon the dharma-realm as if illuminating the three thousandfold world system; therefore, it is said that he is like the sun illuminating the world.
Therefore, it surpasses the light of the omniscience of those in the two vehicles.
Because the Bodhisattva of Crude Deliverance has not yet seen emptiness, he is like a firefly.

As for the phrase "If one enters the Campaka [flower]" and so forth: if one enters the chamber of Vimalakīrti’s land of eternal quiescent light, one perceives only the fragrance of the myriad virtues of the Buddhas’ Dharma-realm; one does not even smell the fragrance of the teachings of the stages prior to the grounds—how much less would one delight in the merits of the minor practices of crude deliverance?

Therefore, the Dharma-body Bodhisattva establishes the body of all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñā-jñāna) upon the seat of the true aspect of reality. Without relying on the majestic power of the King of Lamps (Dīpaṃkara), the various habitual tendencies of view-delusions and thought-delusions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have already been exhausted. Consequently, the five objects of the sensory realm in the two lands of the provisional and the segmented cannot defile the Dharma-body of true retribution. Thus, one should know that these are all of the class of "non-retrogression through mindfulness" within the Dharma-body; hence, they are called "A-vue" (超越, *chao-yue*).

Regarding the statement in the *Liyi zhong* (One Meaning of Principle), "Because form is boundless," and so forth: since the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are principle itself, these very aggregates are the *prajñāpāramitā* of the true mark; therefore, they are all boundless.
Because it is based on principle, the Dharma is made boundless.
"One should know" below concludes [the section].

Next, "If one says" below is the refutation: the present teaching lacks the four and the one, and thus is coarse; the text omits the person, but this is because practice subsumes the person, for practice necessarily entails a person.

Regarding the term "concealed aspect" (*paryāya-lakṣaṇa*): it refers to concealing the aspect of the eternally abiding reality and employing provisional means; furthermore, the abbreviated use of characters is as can be understood from the preceding discussion.
Regarding the four difficulties concerning the breadth and narrowness of the essence of the subsequent fruit, there is likewise a presentation, an explanation, and a conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are two parts:
first, the past; second, the present.
The first section also has two parts:
first, the objection; second, the conclusion.

Within the initial objection, all four "unities" are fully present. The text here cites the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Vimalakīrti*, but these only concern the unity of principle and the unity of teaching. The remaining two [unities] can be inferred by comparing them with the various passages above and below; thus, they are omitted here.
Next, from the passage beginning "If it is claimed that the present fruit... onwards, the four points regarding the failure to establish the fruit of the present sutra are refuted.

First, the point regarding the failure to fulfill and the failure to comprehend the teaching is addressed. In the *Commentary* by Guangzhai, it is stated: "Because it clarifies the One Vehicle, it is fulfilled; because it does not clarify the Buddha-nature, it is neither fulfilled nor comprehended."
From "For what reason it is further said" onwards, the practice of the one [vehicle] is not established.
From "If the substance is extensive" onwards, the person of the one [vehicle] is not established.
These are all the interpretations found in the *Guangzhai* commentary.
Regarding the phrase "seven hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas," the lower fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhaśiras addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!
How long is the lifespan of the Buddha?'"
"When will you enter parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha told Dṛḍhamati:

"To the east, thirty-two thousand buddha-fields away, there is a land named Vyūha. The Buddha there is named Ālokavyūheśvararāja; he is endowed with the ten titles and is currently preaching the Dharma. As is the lifespan of that Buddha, so too is my own."
He asked again:
"What is the lifespan of that Buddha?
The Buddha replied:
"You should go yourself and ask; he will surely answer.
Endowed with the Buddha's spiritual power, Dṛḍhaśiras went to that land in a single thought-moment, prostrated before and circumambulated the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is his lifespan?
When will he enter parinirvāṇa?
That Buddha replied:
"As was the lifespan of Śākyamuni, so too is mine.
If you wish to know it, my lifespan is seven hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and that of Śākyamuni is likewise.
Having finished speaking thus, Dṛḍhaśiras returned to address the Buddha once more.
Ānanda said, "As I understand what the Buddha has taught, that Buddha is another name for Śākyamuni.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is by relying on the Buddha’s power that you are able to know this matter.
Even the lands in the upper direction named One Lamp Brightness and so forth are all emanations of Śākyamuni.
From the words "If one says... onwards, the reasoning is not established.
Regarding the statement that one should be equipped with the five eyes to see the Buddha-nature: it is based on the fact that if one does not see the Buddha-nature, there is no Buddha-eye.
The section beginning with "One should know" concludes this.
Next, within the stage of fruition, there are also three parts:
This consists of the thesis, the explanation, and the conclusion.

Within the explanation, one should first cite what existed in the past and subsequently refute its absence today; however, the text here omits this for brevity and directly cites its absence today. Based on the preceding various explanations, one may verify that it was refuted in the past.
Next, within the section on the function of the fruit, there are also three parts:
the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Within the explanation as well, nothing is presented that does not follow from the previous section; one should understand it by analogy with what precedes.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the formal refutation of the absence of four or one; second, the extensive refutation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
In the first section, there are two parts:
The preceding section on refutation and the subsequent section on synthesis can be understood accordingly.
*Fahua Xuanyi Shiqian*, Scroll Three; *Fahua Xuanyi Shiqian*, Scroll Four.

In the *Pò shéntōng* (Refutation of Supernatural Powers) composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhànrán, it is asked: "Why is it that while [the Buddha] can prolong his lifespan, he cannot prolong his eyesight?
To deny this would be irrational."
Why not extend the tongue to seize its lack of instruction?
One should also further say: Why not extend wisdom to know the eternally abiding and seize its lack of practice?
Why not extend the body to cause it to accord with the Dharma-body and seize its lack of personhood?
The absence of textual [repetition] is due to abbreviation.
The single phrase "the eye does not see its own nature" is an abbreviated citation of the logical principle; if fully expanded, all four propositions should likewise be cited.
The section beginning with "the former one" below is the summary.
Regarding the formation of the difficult-to-overcome force of the three fetters, there are again two parts:
first, the explanation; second, the conclusion.
The enumeration also has two parts:
First, I shall enumerate the points, and second, I shall explain the present intent.

Regarding the first section: although the meanings refuted within the twenty-four objections are all contained in the Guangzhai commentary, I have here cited them directly as objections without providing exhaustive detail.
Regarding the statement "twenty-four": this is based on a relative comparison between the present and the past; since they are discussed together, there are twenty-four.

If the present and the past were discussed separately, one would raise three difficulties regarding the causes and effects of the past, totaling six difficulties; likewise, one would raise six difficulties regarding the causes and effects of the present, totaling twelve difficulties. Since each of these consists of four points, they constitute forty-eight.

Furthermore, in the current text, the three meanings regarding the fruit merely challenge the present stage and its function, omitting any mention of the past; thus, two locations and four sets of arguments are missing, so that the manifest text actually consists of forty sets.
"Contradiction" is as explained in the fifth commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*.

Now, by using those four "ones" to challenge that [the provisional] is subtle and establish it as coarse, and by using those former three to challenge that [the provisional] is coarse and establish it as subtle, there is no excess or deficiency.
The present intention regarding the four correct doctrines has two parts:
first, employing the meaning of Guangzhai to reveal the present marvelousness; second, the formal explanation.
The initial section consists of three parts:
First, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are two parts:
first, the explanation itself; second, the judgment from "First, regarding... onwards.
The initial text consists of four sections;
the first, which explains [the subject] by means of the ten realms, has two parts:
first, the explanation, and second, the conclusion.
The initial explanation consists of two parts:
first, the cause; second, the result. Within the section on the cause, there are two further parts:
First, the explanation; second, the integration.
Within the initial explanation, there are three parts: essence, stage, and function.

Because a single dharma subsumes the nine within a single thought-moment, it is called "vast"; because within a single thought-moment there are no nine that are not the Buddha-dharma, it is called "lofty.
These ten dharmas are none other than the three truths, and they all possess the function of destroying the three delusions and manifesting the three bodies.

Regarding the meaning within the subsequent "Integration": the preceding broad meaning resembles the horizontal, while the subsequent lofty meaning resembles the vertical; within their application, each seems to possess all three aspects individually. Therefore, it is necessary to unify these two preceding meanings to form a single intent; this is simply the essence, position, and function of the Three Truths within the One Mind.

Regarding the phrase "the essence is pervasive" within the three meanings of the subsequent fruit: this refers to the fundamental Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is the Dharma-body already perfected in its original ground.

It is not merely that [the fruit] is superior in terms of height, breadth, and so forth; it indicates that the causes and effects of the two gates—the fundamental and the manifested—are eternally distinct.
The section beginning with "This is" is the conclusion, which may be understood accordingly.
