Third, regarding this present sutra: first, I shall briefly state its purport; second, I shall briefly provide a correspondence between its sections.

Regarding the clarification of the stages (*bhūmi*) in the present sūtra at its beginning, middle, and end: although these do not reach the level of detail found in those two other sūtras concerning the stages, they appear more subtle. Furthermore, the meaning of the present sūtra encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as their opening and discernment, aspects not clarified in other sūtras.

What are these? For instance, the four kinds of flowers raining from the heavens in the "Introduction" chapter; the opening, showing, awakening, and entering in the "Expedient Means" chapter; wandering in the four directions in the "Parable" chapter; and the city of five hundred *yojanas* in the "Transformed City" chapter—these all belong to the stage of reality within the Trace Gate.
The grass hut, the transformed city, and the three types of grasses and two types of trees all belong to the stage of expedient means within the Trace Gate.

The "discrimination of merits" begins from non-arising, which is the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), and extends to the single lifetime of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); this is also the fundamental, true position.

Just as when Anxi was abandoned and only Zhuzhai remained, where plants and trees alike depend upon the same earth and receive the same rain, this represents the convergence of all provisional positions into the single reality; therefore, it is called the "rough judgment of the provisional and the real."
Regarding the phrase "the text does not exhaust the measure," tradition states that in the West,
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* covers one *yojana*.
Next, among the two [points] corresponding to the middle:
First, the sutra is cited; second, it is correlated with the text.
Regarding the fourfold extensive explanation: within the text, the three types of grass, the two types of trees, and the single fruit are distinguished as six stages.
The first section, "The Small Grass," has three parts:
first, a brief citation of scripture to establish the position; second, an analysis of its causes and effects; third, the formal explanation beginning with the section on "The Human Stage.
Within this explanation, there are two parts:
This refers to humans and devas. Regarding humans, there are three parts:

first, the causes are distinguished; second, from "inferior grade" (*hīna-prakāra*) onwards, the results are briefly explained; third, from "all are" (*sarve*) onwards, the human rulers are further elucidated.
The first part is as stated in the text.

Regarding the four wheels of the human stage in the subsequent section, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Gold, silver, copper, and iron wheels [rule] over one, two, three, and four continents respectively"; that is, an Iron Wheel-turning King rules over one continent, up to a Gold Wheel-turning King who rules over all four continents.
Now, a Wheel-Turning King first practices seven dharmas: first, bestowing gifts upon the poor and destitute;

second, honoring the people and providing filial support; third, performing sacrifices to the four seas at the four seasons and the eight festivals; fourth, cultivating patience at all times; fifth, sixth, and seventh, eliminating the three poisons; thereafter, he bathes, observes the fast, and makes vows, after which the divine treasures naturally appear accordingly.
The ruler of men is the foremost among blessings; because he is the pinnacle of merit, his retribution is that of a sovereign.

Next, I shall clarify the celestial realms, distinguishing between the various heavens within the threefold world (*tridhātu*). Within this, I will first briefly describe the causes for rebirth as a deva in the three realms, followed by a formal explanation.
Regarding the explanation, the first four kings have forty abodes; this is a brief account of the abodes of the Four Great Kings based on the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*.
As for the "Mālādharas" (Garland-Holders), the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Dṛḍha, Mālādhara, Sadāmada, and Mahārāja reside respectively on the four terraces, and they also dwell on the other seven mountains. Their physical dimensions and lifespans are fully detailed in the "World Chapter" (*Lokadhātu-nirdeśa*) of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Regarding the "Four Heavenly Kings," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"In the east is Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which in the language of Qin means 'Lord Who Sustains the State'; in the south is Virūḍhaka, which in the language of Qin means 'Lord of Increase'; in the west is Virūpākṣa, which in the language of Qin means 'Lord of Variety'; and in the north is Vaiśravaṇa, which in the language of Qin means 'Lord of Much Hearing'."
These four serve as kings over the four continents; each of the four terraces has ten abodes, and these forty heavens are all named according to their causal conduct.

Regarding the "Three Refuges," according to the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra*, which extensively compares and evaluates the merit of the Three Refuges, it says: "To cause those in the four continents and the six heavens of the desire realm to attain the four fruits [of the śramaṇa] does not produce as much merit as the Three Refuges."

Furthermore, as it is said in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, there was a son of the Trāyastriṃśa devas who manifested the five signs of decline and was about to be reborn among pigs; the sound of his lamentation was heard by the Lord of Devas.
When the Lord of Devas heard this, he summoned him and said:
"You must take the Three Refuges.
Immediately, following these instructions, he was spared from being reborn as a pig.
The Buddha spoke in verse: "All who take refuge in the Buddha shall not fall into the three evil realms; having exhausted their outflows among humans and devas, they shall surely reach Nirvana.
Having thus taken the three refuges, he was born into the family of a householder and subsequently left the home life to become an Arhat (one who has attained the state of no-more-learning).

Regarding the statement in the text that he "clapped his hands ten times," it is likely that while previously observing the natural precepts (śīla), he received the three refuges for such a duration and then immediately passed away; thus, he obtained this retribution. Because his mind was unmixed with defilement, he earned the name "White" (Śukla); that the devas surpass the wheel-turning kings is simply the natural order of things.
Regarding the phrase "sixteenfold," it refers to returning from the superior [realms].

As for "mountains and rivers flowing forth," the sutras state that everything flows as rivers, even including rivers of wine and so forth; these forty heavens must all be understood in detail according to their causal practices, whereby the names of the results are explained accordingly.
"Steep cliffs" refers to the fact that the Yellow River and the Ji River are difficult to cross.
"Fruitful life" means that pure precepts are like fruit. Furthermore, planting fruit trees yields the greatest merit for a stūpa;

white is the fundamental color, and those who see flowers all feel joy. By extinguishing fire with water, one practices the path of compassion; by harmonizing anger and strife, one deals with desire. Because preaching the Dharma gives rise to wholesome states, and because seeing a field of purity moves the mind of faith, it causes others to rejoice as if in joyful play. Comparing these causes, the names may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the passage, "The sun travels through the path beyond the heavens and is called the Sun-Planet," and so forth: outsiders further speculate that the stars in the north do not set; furthermore, in the *Lishi Apitan* (Abhidharmakośa), there is an account of non-Buddhist practitioners who speculate that the great earth moves constantly and without ceasing. The Buddha refuted this by saying: "If one were to throw an object forward, the object would instead move backward."

Furthermore, there was a calculation [of certain theorists] claiming that the earth is constantly falling downward; the Buddha said, "If one were to throw an object upward, it should not reach the ground.
There was another calculation claiming that the stars do not move but the earth itself rotates; the Buddha said, "If one were to shoot an arrow, it should not reach the target."

The deities of the six heavens of the desire realm ought to be endowed with the ten wholesome actions; as for the present statement that they possess "non-killing" up to the seven precepts, it is merely because they fully receive and partially maintain them, and since what they uphold is predominant, they are so designated.
"Worldly precepts" refers to the precepts of avoiding reproach.

Regarding other matters, such as the lifespans and physical dimensions of the various devas, they are fully detailed in the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*; here, for the sake of a brief understanding of the successive stages, I shall not engage in extensive discussion.
Within the middle section on the status of the intermediate [being], there are two parts:
first, determining the person to distinguish cause and effect; second, the formal explanation.
Within the explanation, there are three sections:
First, the refutation of ancient views; second, a brief presentation of the two treatises; third, an extensive explanation of the Gate of Existence (*yǒumén*).
Regarding the "Twenty-seven Sages and Worthies," the *Madhyama Āgama*, "Sūtra on the Thirty Fields of Merit" records: "A householder asked the Buddha:
'How many fields of merit are there?'"
The Buddha said:
"There are eighteen types of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and nine types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

As for the eighteen in training, they are: those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), those liberated by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), body-witnesses (*kāyasākṣin*), those who go from family to family (*kulaṃkula*), those with only one interval remaining (*ekavīcika*), those proceeding toward the first fruit, those who have attained the first fruit, those proceeding toward the second fruit, those who have attained the second fruit, those proceeding toward the third fruit, those who have attained the third fruit, and the five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*): namely, those who attain nirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain it upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), those who attain it with effort (*sābhisamskāraparinirvāyin*), those who attain it without effort (*anabhisamskāraparinirvāyin*), and those who flow upward (*ūrdhvasrotas*)."
"The nine factors of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are: reflection, diligence, regression, non-regression, immovability, abiding, protection, wisdom, and their totality.
The text in the *Abhidharmakośa* is the same; one should further consult the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
The formal explanation consists of two parts:
first, the heading; second, the exposition.
Within the exposition, this refers specifically to the Two Vehicles.
Among the śrāvakas, there are first the noble ones (ārya) and second the sages (ārya).
Within the first group, the sages, there are two parts:
first the enumeration, and second the explanation.
The commentary consists of three parts:
first, the explanation of the name; second, the functions; and third, the formal explanation.
Regarding the functions, the seven stages of the noble ones (*saptakula-putra*) have already been briefly discussed within the section on the excellence of wisdom.

Regarding the current statement "love and views regarding the Four Truths," this refers simply to the basis upon which the two delusions of love and views rely; although both love and views are present, they are all subsumed under "views" (*dṛṣṭi*), as explained in detail among the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*).
The main exposition itself consists of seven parts.

The first five involve the application of the five "cessations" (nirodha) to remedy the five obstacles, as detailed in the seventh fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* under the section on "Countermeasures.

Regarding the statement that "the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is the initial gateway," the subsequent text explains that for the Pratyekabuddhas, the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) serves as the initial gateway, whereas for the Śrāvakas, the Truth of Suffering comes first. Furthermore, because they first contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the Truth of Suffering is primary for them; however, for the Pratyekabuddhas, ignorance (*avidyā*) occupies the head of the chain of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), as they first eliminate craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*).
Regarding "the objects are general and the contemplations are general," this means that the four contemplations universally observe the four objects.
Regarding "the objects are particular and the contemplations are general," this means that each individual object is observed by means of all four contemplations.
Regarding "observing the general while observing the particular": this means that by means of each individual observation, one observes the four objects collectively.
This is known through the three or two categories [of wisdom].
This has already been explained within the section on the wisdom of the various texts such as "Heat" (uṣmagata).
Now, having briefly understood the sequence of stages and their relative depth, this section remains concise; for a detailed understanding, one should consult various treatises.
Furthermore, the seven noble beings (āryapudgala) are treated in three parts:
the enumeration of their positions, the explanation of their names, and the formal exposition.

The details are extensively set forth in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*; the present text is extremely concise, yet sufficient to determine the levels of depth. Regarding the explanation of the names, it says:

"With the clear arising of the patience toward suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), one abandons the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and enters the state of a noble one (*ārya*). Upon reaching the patience toward suffering, one necessarily enters the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) immediately thereafter; here, speaking from the perspective of the subsequent stage, they are collectively referred to as "noble ones."
The three fetters (*saṃyojana*), the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), and the seven births are recorded as in the sixth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Regarding the three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), they are: the swift, the non-swift, and the long-dwelling. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, these constitute nine types in total, meaning each of the three is further divided into three—namely, the intermediate, the birth, and the upward-streaming (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

There are those who attain parinirvāṇa after being born in the form realm through either application (*sābhisaṃskāra*) or without application (*anabhisaṃskāra*); these are both subsumed under "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*).

Regarding the three intermediate types, they refer to those who attain it quickly, not quickly, or after a long duration. These three meanings may be understood by reflecting on the analogy of a flying spark.
Furthermore, regarding the *antarābhava-śāstra*, it discusses "swift," "not swift," and so forth.

As for the three types of birth: first, birth is established in terms of swiftness; second, birth with movement (*sābhisaṃskāra*) is established in terms of not being swift; and third, birth without movement (*anabhisaṃskāra*) is established in terms of requiring a long duration.
The simultaneous rebirth in the form realm has already been discussed in relation to the "swift" (*kṣipra*) and other types.

Regarding the three types of "up-streamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*): first, the "complete leaper" (*pluta*) is established based on being swift; second, the "half-leaper" (*ardhapluta*) is established based on not being swift; and third, the "one who passes away everywhere" (*sarvasthānacyuta*) is established based on requiring a long duration.

From the first stage of form (*rūpa*) to the final stage of form, these three types of persons exist from beginning to end; thus, the three sets of nine differ according to their karma (*karman*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and faculties (*indriya*). Regarding the difference in karma:

those who perform karma conducive to the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*) achieve the intermediate parinirvāṇa (*antarāparinirvāyin*); those who perform karma conducive to the next birth (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*) achieve the parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*); and those who perform karma conducive to subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karman*) achieve the parinirvāṇa of the upstreamer (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

Regarding the three grades of delusion: those with inferior-grade delusion attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin); those with medium-grade delusion attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin); and those with superior-grade delusion attain parinirvāṇa by going upstream (ūrdhvasrotas).

Regarding the distinction of faculties: those with superior faculties attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; those with medium faculties attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; and those with inferior faculties attain parinirvāṇa by going upstream.

Regarding the severance of the fetters of the upper and lower realms: the five upper fetters refer to restlessness, pride, ignorance, attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), and attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).

The five lower fetters refer to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and ill-will (*vyāpāda*). Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "By two, one does not transcend the desire realm"—namely, sensual desire and ill-will; "by three, one returns to the lower"—namely, the view of a self-identity, adherence to precepts and rituals, and doubt.
The meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is as recorded in the ninth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

In the twenty-second fascicle of the *Vyākhyā* (Shèlùn), among the explanation of the four pairs and eight classes of noble ones (*catur-yugāny-aṣṭa-pudgalāḥ*), seventeen [categories] are subsumed; however, it simply states that there are eleven types of *anāgāmin*, five of which are precisely the *anāgāmins* [proper].
Regarding the inclusion of the five types of *anāgāmin* within the six types of candidates for *arhatship*: it is likely that one is the "attainer in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*);

three are the "attainers in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyin*), namely those who attain quickly, not quickly, or after a long stay; and one is the "attainer upon rebirth" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*).

Regarding the six types of candidates for arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*), namely: those who practice with effort (*sābhisamskāra-parinirvāyin*), those who do so without effort (*anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin*), those who leap entirely (*ūrdhvasrotas-sarvacyuta*), those who leap partially (*ardhacyuta*), those who pass away everywhere (*sarvasthānacyuta*), and those who attain it in the formless realm (*ārūpya-gāmin*); when these are added to the candidate for the first fruit, the first fruit itself, the candidate for the second fruit, the second fruit itself, the candidate for the third fruit, and the third fruit itself, they constitute seventeen [types].
Regarding the phrase "the twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty types of Abhidharma," the *Saṃyuktābhidharma* states: "As for the Anāgāmin, there are five, seven, or eight [types].

The five refer to the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), and the one who flows upward (*ūrdhvasrotas*)."
The seventh refers to the three further divisions of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), illustrated by the analogy of flying sparks.

The eighth refers to the five aforementioned types plus those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and those of indeterminate timing (*aniyata*). Furthermore, based on the five types of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are fifteen when distinguished by faculties (*indriya*), because each of these five is divided into superior, middling, and inferior grades.
In terms of the stages (*bhūmi*), there are twenty, as each of the four dhyānas has five types.

Thus, in terms of their natures (*gotra*), there are thirty; that is to say, the regressive (*hāna*), the reflective (*cetanā*), the protective (*anurakṣaṇā*), the abiding (*sthiti*), the advancing (*viśeṣa*), and the immovable (*akopya*), because each lineage (*gotra*) consists of these five.
There are eighty abodes, from the Brahmakāyika up to the Nirmita, because there are five for each of the sixteen levels.
Each of these types of kalpas consists of two thousand five hundred and ninety-two.
How so? Based on sixteen locations, there are sixteen persons; based on six lineages (*gotra*), this is multiplied by six to reach ninety-six.

Based on three faculties (*indriya*), this is tripled to become two hundred and eighty-eight. Furthermore, by multiplying this ninefold by means of the nine types of persons who have abandoned desire (*vairāgya*), it results in two thousand five hundred and ninety-two persons.

If one person is thus, then the five types of *anāgāmin* are five times that number; this results in twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty varieties. Because the treatises on these are difficult to perceive, they are now presented here in brief.
Regarding the "nine who have abandoned desire," this refers to nine types of persons based on having abandoned the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm.

Regarding the five types of Arhats, a brief explanation according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: one of "deteriorating nature" (*parihāṇadharman*) is so called because their mind gives rise to weariness regarding the dharma of reflection.
One who is said to be "of the nature of reflection" (cetanādharman) is so called because they intend to harm themselves with a blade.
One who is said to be "of the nature of protection" (anurakṣaṇādharman) is so called because they cherish their own liberation and guard it well.
That which is called "abiding in the Dharma" refers to neither regressing nor advancing.
That which is called "advancing in the Dharma" refers to being able to advance until reaching the immovable state.
That which is called "the immovable" refers to abiding in its original state without movement.
Question: Does one of the nature of falling back (parihāṇadharman) necessarily fall back?
And so on, up to: does one of the nature of advancing (prativedhanadharman) necessarily advance?
Answer:

Some say that it is not necessarily a falling back, nor even necessarily a progressing; for this reason, there are five types of arhats, and thus it is said that falling back is not necessarily falling back, and so on, up to progressing being not necessarily progressing.
Question:
If this is so, why are they called "retrogression" up to "progression"? Answer:

Those who regress possess the nature of regression, and so on, up to those who advance, who possess the nature of advancement; because there are five such natures, there are five types of Arhats. Together with the one person of the Dharma-practitioner type, known as the Immovable (Akopya), there are thus six types of Arhats.
If one regresses from the fruits, even the two fruits of Sakṛdāgāmin and Anāgāmin are lost, until one returns to abiding in the first fruit;

this is the natural law (*dharmatā*). Within this very life, one will certainly attain it without doubt. It is like a superior person who falls flat on the ground: looking around in all directions and seeing no one else, and feeling myself falling, I am unable to rise immediately; yet, even at the very moment of death, one may attain the state of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Thus it is.

One who attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) has already cultivated both the innate and the acquired foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) during the causal stage; thus, upon reaching the fruit, they are designated solely as one liberated through both parts (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta). This is because, since they have not cultivated the mindfulness of objects (ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna), they can never be one liberated through non-delusion (akopya-vimukta).
"Knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna) refers to having seen suffering and thereby abandoned it, and so on up to the path being likewise [abandoned].
"Knowledge of non-arising" (anutpādajñāna) refers to no longer needing to abandon anything further.
Regarding "the right view of one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*), the attainment of worldly knowledge is also termed "equal knowledge" (*samatājñāna*).

The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "That which has completed what was to be done is called 'knowledge of exhaustion' (*kṣayajñāna*); that which arises from the cause of one beyond training is called 'knowledge of non-arising' (*anutpādajñāna*)."

Furthermore, that which has been previously attained is termed "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*), while that which has not been previously attained is termed "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*).

It is also said: "That which is subsumed under the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is termed knowledge of exhaustion; that which is subsumed under the path of excellence (*viśeṣamārga*) is termed knowledge of non-arising."

Furthermore, it says: "There are five types of Arhats regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), while there is only one type regarding the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*, namely the immovable one).
This refers to the faculties (*indriya*) and does not concern the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding "the right view of those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*): all Arhats and others possess this view; they know for themselves that they have attained the fruit of Arhatship and so forth, and thus it is called "right view."

"Repetitive Emptiness Samādhi" refers to the samādhi of the emptiness of emptiness, the samādhi of the signlessness of signlessness, and the samādhi of the wishlessness of wishlessness. Because one practices emptiness again within the noble dharmas that are themselves empty—thereby striking at those preceding noble dharmas—it is called "repetitive."
Regarding the term "Śramaṇa": *śramaṇa* is translated here as "deprivation" (or "exhaustion"), while *na* is translated here as "path.

As for the statement that for Pratyekabuddhas "the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is the initial gateway," persons of the Three Vehicles all take the Four Noble Truths as their object of contemplation; however, there is a distinction between the general and the specific. Because they follow the convenience of their respective meanings, the initial gateways differ: the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is the initial gateway when following the meaning of the Four Noble Truths; the Truth of Origination is the initial gateway when following the meaning of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; and the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) is the initial gateway when following the meaning of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). These are all according to the principles of the Tripiṭaka.

In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the three vehicles take the truth of cessation within the realm of desire as their initial gateway; in the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), the bodhisattvas take the truth of the path outside the realm of desire as their initial gateway; and in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the bodhisattvas take the truth of cessation outside the realm of desire as their initial gateway.
The origins of the Tripitaka and the Six Perfections, as well as the Mahāyāna practitioner’s critique of the Hinayāna, are fully detailed in the third commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
Regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka, there are two parts:
first, the establishment of the gates; second, the elucidation of the stages, which is divided into three sections:
There are three stages: first, the stage of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; second, the stage of the hundred kalpas; and third, the stage of the fruit of Buddhahood.

Within these, the distinction between the stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and sages (*ārya*) is as described in the text, with full details provided in the *Zhi guan fu xing chuan* (Commentary on the *Mohe zhiguan*).
Next, the common stage for the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying the similarities and differences among the three vehicles; second, the main exposition of the stages, which itself is divided into two sections.
First, the common stage is as previously described; second, regarding the meaning, the text itself is further divided into two parts.
The first two [of the three] sections of the middle [part]:
first, clarifying the intent of establishing the stages; second, the formal explanation of the initial text beginning with "Dry Wisdom" (śuṣka-vipaśyanā), which is further divided into two:
first, pointing to the text; second, establishing the intent.
Next, regarding the formal explanation, the textual presentation is somewhat extensive; when reading that text within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, one must understand this underlying intent.
This section has two parts:
first, the explanation; second, the concluding judgment.
The commentary is divided into ten sections. Regarding the first, the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*), there are four parts:

first, the general establishment of the common intent; second, from "But the Bodhisattva" onwards, the establishment of the distinct intent; third, the explanation of the characteristics of the Four Great Vows; and fourth, from "This is called" onwards, the discernment of their differences.
In the explanation of the Four Great Vows, the first vow is extensive while the subsequent three vows are concise.
The first vow, in turn, has two parts:
first, the explanation; second, the citation of evidence.
Within the stage of the "Ground of the Nature" (dharmatā-bhūmi), there are three parts:

first, establishing the common intention; second, from "And the bodhisattva... onwards, explaining the characteristics of practice to establish the distinct intention; third, from "As in the Tripiṭaka... onwards, judging the stages and distinguishing their differences.
Next, the section on the eight persons who see the ground is divided into three parts:

first, establishing a common intention; second, the formal explanation beginning with "And the bodhisattva..."; and third, clarifying the reason for establishing patience, beginning with "For what reason... and so forth.
Next, the section beginning with "Furthermore" explains the Stage of Thinness (tanubhūmi) in three parts:
first, establishing a common perspective; second, criticizing the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas); and third, the formal explanation starting with "The Bodhisattva."
Regarding the "playful exercise of supernatural powers," it is fully explained as in the fifth commentary of the *Śikṣānanda* (or *Zhiguan*).
Next, from "Anāgāmin" onwards, the stage of freedom from desire (*vairāgya-bhūmi*) is clarified in four parts:

first, establishing the common intention; second, refuting the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); third, the formal explanation starting from "The Bodhisattva is able..."; and fourth, clarifying the reason for establishing this stage and distinguishing its unique characteristics, starting from "The reason why... and so forth.
The first three points are as stated in the text.
Regarding the differentiation of differences, there are two parts:

first, clarifying that the wisdom employed for contemplating the truths differs; second, from "Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*" onwards, citing the treatise to prove the establishment of the name "Bodhisattva."
Next, from "The Stage of the Arhat" onwards, the stage of having completed what was to be done (*kṛtāvi-bhūmi*) is clarified in two parts:
first, the distinction [from the previous stage] is established;

second, scriptural evidence is cited. Next, from "The Pratyekabuddha" onwards, the stage of the Pratyekabuddha is clarified; since it is identical to that of the Arhat, it says, "It is also like this."
Next, the Bodhisattva-bhūmi is explained in four parts:
first, a brief establishment;
second, a brief analysis.

3. From "This then" onwards is the brief explanation: although the ten stages (daśabhūmi) still receive the name of "bodhisattva," they are further called the "stage of a Buddha" because the name of the bodhisattva stage exists at the periphery of the Buddha stage; thus one knows that from beginning to end there is always the position of a bodhisattva, which is why it is said, "specifically for the sake of the bodhisattva.
4. From "Up to this point" onwards distinguishes between what is exhausted and what is not.
Next, from "The Bodhisattva Who Transcends" (*atikrāntabodhisattva*) onwards, the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) is explained in two parts:
first, a brief establishment; second, from "the five characteristics" (*pañcalakṣaṇa*) onwards, the distinctions are clarified.

Within this, there are three distinctions. Regarding the distinction of *nirvāṇa*, it says "leaving behind relics" (*śarīra*). If, in the lower section on the "Original Gate" (*mūlaparivarta*), it is said that even the Universal Buddhas enter the same state of ash-like cessation (*kṣaya-nirodha*), this is because the two meanings within the provisional teaching are not fixed, and because what is seen by bodhisattvas of sharp and dull faculties differs.

Next, the distinction between names and the universality of their meanings, as well as the establishment of the term "patience" (*kṣānti*) for Bodhisattvas, are fully detailed in the sixth fascicle of the *Śikṣānanda-śāstra* (or *Zhiguan*).
The present text is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation; second, the critical analysis.
The initial text consists of four parts:
first, the intent of the passage; second, the enumeration of the distinct stages; third, the correlation of these stages; and fourth, the conclusion beginning with "This then.
The first two parts are as explained in the text.

Regarding the first three pairs of stages, the preceding nine grounds are as stated in the text. Upon reaching the Buddha-ground, the text first refers back to the previous passage, noting that the ten grounds of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) are merely called "Bodhisattva grounds" within the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).

Next, from "This Buddha" onwards, the similarities and differences with the Tripiṭaka [teachings] are distinguished. Regarding the statement that "the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka illuminates sentient beings three times a day," this is taught in various sections of the *Āgamas* as well as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. It says that the Buddha enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*) three times a day to seek those beings who can be saved; this is because, according to the gate of provisional teaching, he cannot be seen at all times.
It is also as described in the *Māyā-sūtra*: Ānanda was standing close behind him, and [the Buddha] then asked, "Ānanda, where are you now?
He further asked, "For what reason are there so many crows in the Jeta Grove?"
If even those who are slightly advanced do not yet know this themselves, how could they possibly possess spontaneous and constant illumination?
Regarding the initial question in the subsequent "Analysis" (Liaojian) section, it is easily understood.

In the response, it is clarified that the characteristics of the teachings for these general stages (*tongwei*) differ greatly, which leads teachers and masters to each rely upon their own particular path.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, seeing; second, reflection.
Within the first, there are three sections:

First, the similarities and differences are presented; second, the objection begins with "However, according to the Shared Teaching" (*butong jiao*); third, the concession begins with "If one were to sever...
Next, within the section on the delusions of thought (*sifan*), there are two parts:
first, the differences are presented; second, a general judgment is made incorporating the preceding points.

The brief statement "one must not adhere to a fixed interpretation" means that, in general, a definitive judgment cannot be made; this is because, when teaching for the benefit of others, the duration is long and the capacities of sentient beings are diverse, which necessitates such an approach.
The subsequent question-and-answer section has three parts:
first, a brief judgment; second, an explanation beginning with "What are they..."; and third, the formal judgment beginning with "This is...".

Regarding the subsequent question, the phrase "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the burning of the wick in three places," etc., refers to the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*), the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), and the First Dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 48, elucidates the forty-two letter-gates (*dvāra*), which correspond to the stages from the first *vihāra* upward.

Fascicle 49 elucidates the Bodhisattva’s stages from the first Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), providing a detailed explanation of the cultivation and purification of the practices of these stages. Following this text, it states: "Furthermore, there are two kinds of stages:
first, the exclusive Bodhisattva stages; second, the shared stages, namely from the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi*) up to the Buddha Stage."
Thus, it is known that the three teachings are clearly elucidated.

Therefore, one should know that the intent of the inquiry here differs slightly from that in the *Zhiguan*; for this [text] poses the question in terms of the three teachings, whereas the ground and the wick are set aside and not discussed. If one grasps this meaning, the text of the *Zhiguan* will naturally appear distinct by itself.

Next, regarding the question, "One who benefits others should not have ten stages," the intent of the question is as follows: Since one who benefits others has already severed the afflictions of wrong views at the first stage (*bhūmi*), they should sever the afflictions of mental cultivation (*saṃskāra-kleśa*) from the second through the fourth stages, attaining Buddhahood at the sixth or seventh stage; if this is so, would there then be no ten stages?

The intent of the answer is that the teachings are complete; one does not prohibit benefiting others. For instance, if someone transcends the fruits and attains arhatship, could it then be said that the other three fruits no longer exist?

The meaning of the subsequent question is: if there are those of sharp or dull faculties within the Separate and Perfect Teachings, should they not abide in the stages prior to the Grounds (the "stages before the Grounds") where the wick is being consumed?
The meaning of the answer is: although there are differences between the sharp and the dull, the stage of severance is necessarily fixed.
Next, regarding the distinct stages as being like a great tree, there are three parts:
the heading, the enumeration of the sections, and the formal explanation.
The first two are as stated in the text.
The commentary consists of three parts; the first part further comprises six sections:

first, the naming [of the teaching]; second, the basis for its stages and dharmas; third, a general enumeration from "immeasurable" onwards; fourth, a judgment from "distinctive teaching" onwards; fifth, a judgment on the peripheral and the primary from "however" onwards; and sixth, a concluding demonstration of the differences from "since there already exist" onwards.
The first two [sections] are understandable.
The third consists of three parts:

first, the enumeration of the four numbers; second, the listing of the four dharmas beginning with "There are immeasurable..."; and third, the explanation of the four dharmas beginning with "How is it that... and so forth.
The first two points are as stated in the text.

To explain the meaning: the reason why the severance and suppression [of afflictions] in the four teachings are all termed "immeasurable" is that the characteristics of both severing and suppressing are not uniform; therefore, they are collectively designated by this name.
This is because all [the preceding] refers to Bodhisattvas.

Initially, as the Tripiṭaka masters say, "subduing the afflictions of views and thought" specifically refers to Bodhisattvas; here, it is clarified that the vast majority are engaged in "going forth into the provisional" (出假), and thus the Two Vehicles are set aside.
Within the Shared Teaching (通教), "going forth into the provisional" is also pointed out; "assistance" (助) refers to assisting the Distinct Teaching (別教).
Regarding the statement in the Separate Teaching (biejiao) that there are "inner and outer Four Truths," one should know that those of the Separate Teaching possess four sets of the Four Truths.

As for the phrase "there is the meaning of severing ignorance," although according to the beginning and end [of the path] one severs it upon ascending the stages (bhūmi), since the realization of the Way is identical to that of the Perfect Teaching, one should know that this refers only to the sense of severance within the Path of Teaching (jiaodao).

Therefore, in our current practice, since the stage prior to the discernment of the ground (bhūmi) belongs to the Separate Teaching (bye-gyo), one suppresses the expectation of the Perfect Principle (won-ri) during the stage of dedication; thus, it receives the name of "phenomenal" (sa).

Because the stage of destroying ignorance (mum-myeong) for a person of the Perfect Teaching is long, the fourfold judgment of "immeasurability" (mu-yang) is designated as beginning from the first dwelling (chu-joo).
Regarding the fifth point, "the five lateral and the one correct," it can be understood by judging them according to the beginning and end of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
Regarding the sixth point, "concluding by indicating similarities and differences," there are two parts:
first, a brief indication; second, from "If [one considers] the *Avataṃsaka*" onwards, indicating the differences in the teachings, which is divided into three sections.

First, the teachings are listed; second, from "Furthermore, it eliminates" onwards, the differences in the characteristics of the teachings are clarified; third, from "The reason for this being so" onwards, the differences in their underlying intent are clarified.
The first section [on the characteristics] further has two parts: first, the Sūtra, and second, the Śāstra.

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains only the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; likewise, in the seventh [fascicle] of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, within the explanation of the "Superior Characteristics of Cause and Effect" (the fourth topic), it also clarifies only the ten stages beginning with the Joyful (*pramuditā*). As for the six stages such as the "lineage" (*gotra*) explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, they are cited in the fifth fascicle of the *Śikṣānanda’s Commentary on the Mohe Zhiguan*; and in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*, the initial text clarifies only the ten stages.

Next, regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*), there are likewise no distinct levels; the *Mahā-śāstra* briefly presents both the general and specific aspects, citing examples only for the sake of illustration. Thus, one should know that the explanations of the stages in various treatises are coarse and summary.
Next, the differences between the severance and suppression of delusions according to the characteristics of the teachings are clarified as per the text.
Third, regarding the meaning [of the teachings], there are two parts:
first, the general purport of the holy teachings is clarified; second, from the words "Now, if... onwards, the specific intent of our own school’s application of the holy teachings is clarified.
Furthermore, there are four [sections]:

the first provides a general outline of the main intent, the purpose of which is to establish the correct intention for practitioners at the initial stage of the path; if there were no stages of progress, how could one listen to the worthy and reflect upon them as models for emulation?
How can one transcend the sin of overweening pride?
If one follows the diverse paths according to individual capacities and accords with what they delight in, it is for this reason that the aforementioned [teachings] appear inconsistent and unequal.
If, however, one intends to establish the contemplation of the teachings for those at the initial stage of the path, one provisionally employs these three sutras.
Next, from "All the Sages" onwards, there is the exhortation to practice.
Third, from "Now, the judgment" onwards, the intent of the three sutras is correctly demonstrated.

Therefore, our school differs from worldly people's explanations of the sutras and treatises; we do not merely rely on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) to establish hierarchical positions.

Now, regarding the distinct stages within this single school: if one does not rely on the *Śrīkāya-sūtra*, the stages would lack a beginning or an end; if one does not rely on the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, there would be no basis for the sequence of severing delusions or the scope of meditative contemplation across the various stages; and if one does not rely on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the shallow or deep characteristics of the Bodhisattva’s vows and practices, as well as their distance or proximity, could not be known. When these three sutras are mutually integrated, the intent of the Buddha’s teaching remains unerring.
The four explanations of the three passages are divided into three parts.

First, regarding the statement in the *Śrī-mālā* and *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* concerning the "Prajñā of the preceding four periods," ancient masters judged that there are five periods of Prajñā in total:
first, the *Mahā*; second, the *Vajra*; third, the *Devarāja*; fourth, the *Prasphuta-praśaṃsā*; and fifth, the *Benevolent Kings*.
This, too, cannot be accepted in its entirety; nevertheless, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* must certainly precede the *Ratnarāja*.
How is this known? The *Ratnarāja* states:
"Twenty-nine years after the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, he previously expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* for my sake"; thus, it is clear that the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* was explained later.

According to the catalogs of various scriptures, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Guangzan jing) refers to that which was completed on the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the fifth year of Hongshi, consisting of twenty-seven fascicles.

Later, Zhu Fahu translated the first fascicle during the first year of the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty as the *Guangzan*; furthermore, Zhu Shiheng translated it in twenty fascicles, naming it the *Fangguang Banruo*. Kumārajīva later retranslated it in ten fascicles, naming it the "Small Version" (*Xiaopin*), while Zhi Chen also translated it in ten fascicles, naming it the "Course of Practice" (*Daoying*).
Furthermore, there was someone who translated it in five fascicles, titled *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
There was also someone who translated an abridgment of the *Prasphullapraśastā*, titled *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, there was someone who translated an abridged version of the *Prasphulla-prajñāpāramitā* (Guangzan) and titled it "The Great Perfection of Wisdom" (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā*).

There was also someone who translated it under the title "The Large Chapter" (*Mahāsaṃnipāta*). One should know that the *Prasphulla-prajñāpāramitā* is simply the first volume of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*; because it was translated later, one must not regard it as having a different temporal significance.
For this reason, the sequential arrangement [of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*] with the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* and the *Heavenly Kings Sūtra* cannot be adopted in its entirety.
Although the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra* encompasses all things, its specific names and ranks are not clearly manifested; therefore, only these two sūtras are employed.

Regarding the statement, “The *Śīla-saṃgraha* [treatise] speaks of ninefold precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms,” since the treatise itself states that all six perfections (pāramitās) each consist of nine aspects, the present text mentions only three. This is either because the three encompass the six, or because it briefly cites the three essential elements. However, such matters as the functions of the various stages, the characteristics of vows and practices, the categories of delusions severed, the breadth or narrowness of benefiting sentient beings, the purity or defilement of the lands relied upon, the frequency of manifested traces, the distinction between the true and the responsive bodies, and the corresponding dharma-gates cannot be listed in full. Therefore, this current text clarifies only a single path; thus, there is no leisure to extensively explain the characteristics of the dharmas. Furthermore, following the style of the text, I shall not be overly prolix. I fear that consulting the sutras and śāstras at great length would only clutter the original text. One should know that based on the characteristics of this text, the provisional and the real can be sufficiently discerned.
Next, the general explanation of the stages (*bhūmi*) is also based on three sūtras: first the presentation, then the explanation.
The explanation has two parts:

first, the enumeration and explanation according to the *Śrīkūṭa* (or *Ratnakūṭa/Śrīgarbha*), and second, the clarification of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) according to the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Question:

In this present text, these four meanings are correlated with the three contemplations; how does this differ from the explanations in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding the general and specific aspects within the cause and the general and specific aspects upon the fruit?
Answer: The words differ, but the meaning is the same. Why is this?

Emptiness and the provisional serve as the cause, while the Middle Way serves as the fruit. Entering emptiness from the provisional is the general characteristic within the cause; entering the provisional from emptiness is the specific characteristic within the cause. For an individual practitioner cultivating the Middle Way, initially taking only the general characteristic as the fruit constitutes the general aspect of the fruit; if they enter the first stage (*bhūmi*) and simultaneously illuminate the two truths, this constitutes the specific aspect of the fruit. One should know that these four meanings are not different from the three [aspects].

Regarding the separate explanation of the seven stages: as clarified in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, there are six kinds of natures (*gotra*), and when combined with the stage of faith prior to the [ten] abidings, they constitute seven.

The "six stages of the *Śrīmālā*" refer to: the nature of the seeds of practice during the ten abidings; the nature of the seeds of nature during the ten practices; the nature of the seeds of the path during the ten transferences; the noble nature of the seeds during the ten grounds; the nature of equal enlightenment; and the nature of wondrous enlightenment. One should seek these within the original texts of the Four Teachings.
The stages of the three types of grass and two types of trees are concluded.
Next, the stage of ultimate reality is clarified; this refers to the successive stages produced from the single ground (*ekabhūmi*).

Therefore, while the three teachings and the realms of humans and devas were established previously, they now reside solely within the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*). If one does not reach the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation and manifestation, how could one know that [all beings] are produced from the single ground?
This refers to what is meant by "within the single Buddha-vehicle, one distinguishes and teaches three.

Therefore, we know that the three types of grass and two types of trees each thought they stood independently, yet only upon receiving the rain of a single flavor do they realize they were born from the same ground;
it is like that impoverished son who only recognized his father at the time of his death. For this reason, one must clarify the stage of the one true reality.
In order to enable one to recognize the father, it is necessary to clarify the preceding provisional stages.
Within this, there is first the presentation and then the explanation.
In the explanation, the text naturally divides itself into ten points.

Regarding the initial listing of the ten meanings: although they equally explain the Perfect Teaching (yuanmen), there are slight differences among them. The first four meanings and the tenth meaning correctly explain the stages of the Perfect Teaching, while the remaining five meanings are elucidated incidentally based upon these.

Why is this? Since this section exclusively elucidates the stage of the single reality (*eka-tattva*), it is inappropriate for it to include passages concerning the coarse and the subtle; therefore, such passages should instead be placed after the "Excellence of the Text" (*miāo xing*) and at the beginning of the "Excellence of the Stages" (*wei miāo*) chapter.
It should be said that first the various stages are clarified, followed by the clarification of their coarseness or subtlety, their arising or ceasing, and their revelation.
The reason for returning to this point now is the desire to further weigh and resolve them against the provisional stages, and to reveal those coarse stages.
Therefore, having completed the preliminary explanation, we shall again judge the coarse and the subtle, as well as the revelation and so forth.
Question:

Now, this initial section employs three phrases to analyze the Tripitaka, Shared, and Complete [teachings]. When reaching the concluding text below, it states that [this teaching] is the same as the Tripitaka and Shared; why, then, in the initial analysis, was it not contrasted with the Tripitaka?
Answer: First, because this general [classification] is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna and is capable of leading one into what follows;
second, because the name "Arhat" is identical in both places, the first [classification] corresponds to the general [Mahāyāna], while the latter encompasses both [Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna] Piṭakas.

Regarding the sequence of these ten chapters: although the principle (li) is nameless, it relies upon names for its manifestation. Only when there is meaning beneath a name is that which is expressed revealed; only when there is a name upon the meaning is the distinction of the expression known. Therefore, the chapter on "Name and Meaning" stands at the very beginning.

Having already understood the names and meanings of the Perfect Teaching (yuanmen), one next distinguishes the number of stages (wei-shu) it elucidates; only then will one recognize the different ways in which the Perfect stages (yuan-wei) may be expanded or condensed.

Although one knows the number of stages, if one does not understand that the purpose of these stages is fundamentally to differentiate between what is severed and what is suppressed (duan-fu), what would be the point of establishing them in vain?
Therefore, next, the abandonment and suppression [of afflictions] are clarified.

Having understood abandonment and suppression, one should clarify that their functions differ; for if one understands the function of abandonment and suppression in the Perfect Teaching (yuanmen) yet does not compare it with the preceding stages as being all coarse, how could one know that this stage is the most excellent among all the stages?

Since you already know what is coarse and what is subtle, why not simply teach the single stage of ultimate reality? What need is there for the various preceding coarse stages? One should understand that both the coarse and the subtle arise in response to conditions.

As conditions arise alternately, phenomena must necessarily be alternately discarded. In the teachings prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, they arose and were discarded in turn; although these teachings were discarded in relation to specific individuals, their underlying principles still remained. How much more so when both the Great and Small Vehicles arise together, yet the benefits received by beings are unequal?

Whether manifest or esoteric, their origins differ at each stage; whether horizontal or vertical, the flavors of the Dharma vary in degree. Once the time for maturation has come and transformation is complete, all shall converge upon the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Since their faculties and conditions are now identical, there can be no divergent traces; as all coarseness reaches this point, the wondrous principle is uniform. Therefore, there must be the manifestation of opening and revealing.

Although the process begins with the establishment of names and meanings and culminates in the revelation of the provisional (*upāya*), the various stages of the provisional and the real must necessarily rely upon rational evidence. To proceed from beginning to end without recklessness—possessing both a commencement and a conclusion—is the mark of the Sage alone.

Since this is the fundamental intent of the Buddha, one cannot help but comprehensively elucidate its essential structure; therefore, by summarizing the entirety of his teaching through ten gates, one may finally realize the meaning of the wondrous stages of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Within this, first the meaning of the names is explained, which consists of two parts:
first, pointing to the subsequent text; second, clarifying the present intent, which further consists of two parts:
first, stating and listing the three meanings; second, explaining them.
Within the explanation, there are three parts; now, for the first part of the explanation, there are two:
first, the restatement, and second, the interpretation.
In the restatement, first, the two names are shown to be identical to those in the Hīnayāna teachings, followed by the conclusion.

Next, the section beginning with "What is... provides the explanation. Within this explanation, the initial name of the sutra is first addressed; while it previously only mentioned the title "Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings), it now fully explains it through the three meanings associated with the fruit of Arhatship. In each passage, the partial is used to manifest the perfect.

Regarding the statement "the three kinds of mental aggregates," the two vehicles are included within one of these three; since they are discussed here collectively, it is called "three kinds," not implying that the two vehicles fully possess all three.

Regarding the term "aggregate of mind" (*manaskāya*): it is called the aggregate of mind because the aggregates arise from the mind; furthermore, it is called the aggregate of mind because the act of mental attention (*manasikāra*) gives rise to the aggregates; and finally, it is called the aggregate of mind because the mind itself is the aggregate.
The first two explanations derive their names from the cause, while the latter explanation derives its name from the fruit.
Furthermore, although it is called the "aggregate of mind," it may also possess all five [aggregates]. Why is this so?
The Buddha himself is still fully endowed with the five constant qualities, such as form; how much more so, then, for those who rely on him?
It is simply that within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings, it is not stated that there are further places of birth beyond the realms.
Yet, even in those teachings, it is said that the mind ceases—how much more so, then, regarding form?
Regarding the phrase "Vimalakīrti says, 'He shall provide for you,'" this borrows from the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* to deliver a reprimand.
That sutra rebukes [the view] that equates [the śrāvaka] with the state of compassion; one should know that the meaning of the śrāvaka as an "Arhat" (one worthy of offerings) is partial.
Next, the explanation of the subsequent names can be understood.

Next is the explanation of the "distinct names with perfect meaning": although the fifty-two names do not differ from their individual meanings, from the beginning to the end, they represent the perfection of contemplation and the perfection of realization. As stated at the end of the sixth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*: "Borrowing the lower to achieve the high"—this is precisely what that refers to.
Next, regarding "both name and meaning being perfect": from beginning to end, there is nothing that is not the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom.
As for the phrases such as "entering the room," they all refer to the "Tathāgata"; therefore, one knows that the name is perfect.
Since it is said that all dharmas are the seat of emptiness and the chamber of great compassion adorned by the Tathāgata, one knows that the meaning is perfect.

Next, the number of stages is clarified; although in the section on the perfection of both name and meaning the term "the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" was used for both, one must understand the number of stages within the vast scope of the various teachings in order to lead the practitioner's mind toward its aspiration.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the headings and enumeration; second, the explanation.
The explanation itself has three sections:

First, regarding the explanation of the four within the enumeration: first, the ancient masters are cited; second, starting from "Now it is said," the old views are refuted; third, starting from "Furthermore," the refutation is restated; fourth, starting from "The treatise says," the present author's own position is correctly elucidated.

Regarding the initial teacher’s intention: he cites passages concerning the "non-abiding" (amūla) side by side; however, some of his views arise from personal conjecture and do not accord with the general path, while others cite scriptural texts without understanding the distinct intentions of the Sages. For these reasons, his views must be refuted.

Regarding the statement, "Sudden awakening at the initial stage is itself the ultimate," the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra encompasses both the Perfect (Yuan) and the Separate (Bie) teachings within its stages. Yet, people fail to comprehend the intended meaning of the stages of these two teachings, and furthermore, they do not grasp the beginning and end of the Perfect teaching’s stages. By directly identifying the initial stage as the state of wondrous enlightenment (*abhisaṃbodhi*), they value only the sudden gate for its swiftness in attaining Buddhahood. Consequently, the subsequent stages of the Perfect Teaching become rendered superfluous, and it further incurs the fault of making the Buddha's exposition redundant and cumbersome; therefore, to judge [the teaching] based on this old [interpretation] is truly inadmissible.
Next, the refutation of the middle [position] has three parts.

First, regarding the general refutation, the statement "all are partial" means that, from the perspective of principle (*li*), the realized Dharma is nameless; yet, from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), the various stages are not non-existent. Therefore, we know that these masters are all speaking from the standpoint of principle alone.
Next, from the word "However" (*rán*) onwards, the specific intent of the critique is set forth.

Since the three preceding masters all asserted sudden enlightenment (*dùn wù*), [the author] refutes them collectively with the charge of "sudden enlightenment. By citing the scripture while missing its essential meaning, their reasoning naturally falters; thus, we know that "enlightenment" refers to the first stage (*chū zhù*), whereas "not yet enlightened" refers to the stages prior to that.
Since you have already admitted both awakening and non-awakening, why should it not be possible for both positions to possess degrees of depth, thereby constituting the fifty-two stages?
Third, regarding the section beginning with "Ultimate," the scriptural passages cited all contain two meanings; how can you claim that only the state of "no stage" is being discussed?
Next, the second section reiterates the middle [position] in two parts:
first, the restatement; second, the refutation.
Regarding the initial passage: the intention of this master is to simultaneously refute the three preceding masters, and thus he establishes a definitive statement.
Next, following the section "Now, by way of example," the argument is presented through scriptural testimony (*āgama*), which is further divided into three parts:

first, the formal presentation of both provisional and ultimate proofs; second, the citation of a simile from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; and third, the citation of the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* as proof.
The first part is as stated in the text.
Regarding the citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are two sections:
first, the citation of the treatise itself; second, an illustration of the treatise’s intent, namely the analogy of the shallow and deep waters of rivers and seas.
Citing the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra*, it says:

"The Mahāyāna exists because of causes," and so forth. Although the causes and effects of the true reality (*dharmatā*) are both manifest and clear, if there are causes and effects, there must be degrees of depth. As analyzed in the four propositions of "sudden within the perfect" and "gradual within the perfect" in the *Mohe zhiguan* and in the following text, the "gradual" aspect of the Perfect Teaching can be clearly understood.
Next, the explicit clarification of the present intent is divided into three parts:

first, a general statement of the purpose of the stages; second, the enumeration of the stages under the heading "Returning to the [analysis]"; and third, the explanation under the heading "Now, regarding... etc.

Regarding the initial statement, "in accordance with the sūtras" and so forth: these are the fundamental principles of the Buddha’s spoken teachings, which correspond like a tally; therefore, they are called "tallies" (kīya).
The Buddha still accords with the capacities of beings to explain the various stages; in propagating the teachings during the final age, one should comply with the holy words.
If it were otherwise, for what reason would the Tathāgata have extensively explained these stages for the sake of such ordinary and inferior beings?

Thus we know that these are all intended to cause sentient beings to hear of the stages [of realization], so that they may give rise to joy, produce wholesome roots, destroy evil, and awaken to the truth; this is precisely the meaning of the intention to benefit others through the clarification of the stages.
Therefore, what is cited below according to various teachings is exactly this point.
The subsequent list is visible [in the text].
Regarding the three explanations, there are two parts:
first, an account of what is established in the present text; second, an extensive explanation of the various stages.
Regarding the initial text, there is first the preliminary exposition and secondly the explanation.
Within the explanation, there is first the Master’s [commentary] and secondly my own private explanation.
The preceding text is divided into three parts:
First is the formal explanation; second, from "In this way" onwards, is the concluding praise; third, from "If one wishes" onwards, is the determination of the stage.
The first [section] itself has five parts. Regarding the text of the first chapter, there are further two:
first, the description of the object, which refers to hearing the Perfect [Teaching] and giving rise to faith.
Within a single mote of dust there is a great thousand-fold world-system scripture, as recorded in the third fascicle of the *Zhi guan*.
Next, from "desiring to open" (*yù kāi*) onwards, the text explains the arousal of practice based on faith, which is further divided into two parts:
first, the explicit exposition of the ten vehicles of practice; second, from "raising [the example]" (*jǔ*) onwards, the conclusion that demonstrates the stages.
The first section also has three parts:

first, a general clarification of the intent of the practice; second, a general demonstration of the characteristics of the practice from the words "the practitioner of the perfect path" onwards; and third, a specific demonstration of the characteristics of the practice from the words "to speak briefly" onwards.

First the numbers are raised, and next the circular practices are listed as ten; these constitute the "Ten Dharmas that Complete the Vehicle," as explained in detail from the beginning of the fifth fascicle to the end of the seventh fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mohe Zhiguan).

Now, as this *Zhengyi lun* (Treatise on the Correct Meaning) pertains to the gateway of the teaching, the textual characteristics of the contemplation of phenomena are somewhat abbreviated; therefore, I have merely listed them briefly to serve as a comparative decision with the preceding three teachings, thereby revealing the perfect meaning of the Sūtra.

Next, from "The practitioner" (*yogācāra*) downward, the second stage is elucidated. This section is divided into four parts: first, the correct explanation of the characteristics of the second stage;

second, from "Internal and external" (*adhyātma-bahirdhā*) downward, the explanation of the ten contemplations within the second stage; third, from "Vajra" (*vajra*) downward, the citation of scriptural evidence; and fourth, from "Hearing that there is" (*śrutvā asti*) downward, the conclusion regarding the position.
The first two points are as stated in the text.
There are three sections for citing scriptural evidence:

first, citing the *Vajracchedikā* to prove that which serves as the support; second, citing the subsequent chapter to show how it supports the preceding chapter; and third, citing Maitreya’s treatise to prove the great power of that which provides the support.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra*, "As for the real [nature], it is the revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*)," and so forth: the meaning of the verse correctly clarifies that reciting and chanting the *Prajñāpāramitā* serves as an aid to the true reality (*dharmatā*). Therefore, such recitation is called the revealing cause; thus it says, "as for the real. Beyond this, all else is merely called the producing cause (*janaka-hetu*), and the producing cause refers to contaminated causes (*sāsrava-hetu*); hence it says, "as for other merits. Regarding the phrase "not tending toward Bodhi, whereas the two tend toward Bodhi": giving the seven treasures in quantities like Mount Sumeru constitutes merit.
Both upholding and reciting these two lead toward Bodhi; therefore, these two are called the "causes of realization" (*parijñā-hetu*).

Although in the treatise the two lines "Merit does not lead to Bodhi" appear first and the two lines "Regarding reality, they are called causes of realization" appear later, following the present arrangement for the sake of thematic convenience does not contradict the underlying principle.
Furthermore, according to the five kinds of Dharma-preachers, each of the two categories in the treatise is divided into two; by adding the name "Dharma-preacher," they become five.
Now, citing the text of the treatise, we shall for the time being maintain the perspective of personal practice; therefore, there is no preaching of the Dharma, nor is one designated a "preacher."
The *Anle xing shu* (Commentary on the Practices of Peaceful Conduct) provides an extensive explanation of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers.
Next, from the section beginning with "the practitioner" (*xingzhe*) below, it clarifies the third stage, which is divided into three parts:

first, an explanation of the characteristics of the third stage; second, from "Peaceful Conduct" (*anle xing*) below, the citation of scriptural evidence; and third, from "preaching the Dharma" (*shuo fa*) below, the summary of its status.
The first part is as stated in the text. Regarding the citation of three passages next, the *Anle xing pin* (Chapter on Peaceful Conduct) is readily apparent.

Next, regarding the passage from the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* that says, "the purity of preaching the Dharma," and so forth: it is called "pure" solely because one preaches the Perfect and Eternal [Dharma] with an internal mind free from attachment. This is as cited from the *Anle xing pin*, which states, "Answer only with the Mahāyāna Dharma," and so on. Thus, we know that through the power of preaching the Dharma, one internally perfumes one's own wisdom, causing it to become doubly pure; that the merit of transformation returns to oneself—this is the intended meaning.
Since this applies equally to both the great and the small, I have cited the Abhidharma as a parallel example.

As for the statement that "one attains liberation by hearing the Dharma," it occurs at the initial stage of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); the textual meanings are distinct, yet they follow one another in succession.
Next, the section beginning with "The above" clarifies the fourth chapter, which is divided into four parts:

first, the explanation of the characteristics of the stages; second, the citation of scriptural evidence beginning with "The Great Chapter"; third, the explanation of the intent of the stages beginning with "This then"; and fourth, the conclusion of the stages beginning with "Merit through deeds."
Next, from "The practitioner" (*yogin*) onwards, the fifth stage is elucidated. This section has two parts:
first, the characteristics of the stage are clarified; second, from "Endowed with" (*samanvāgata*) onwards, the stage is concluded.
The first part has two sections:
First, there is a general clarification; next, from the passage beginning with "If one practices giving," the characteristics of the six perfections are specifically demonstrated.

Thus, we know that within the text concerning the correct practice of the six perfections, the phrase "the ten realms of both the environment and its inhabitants are all relinquished" is stated for the purpose of briefly clarifying the perfect realm.

To clarify the characteristics of practice extensively, one should follow the *Sui-zi-i* and the *Zhi-guan*; only when the primary and auxiliary practices are combined and phenomena and principle are non-dual can it be called "right practice."

If one grasps its essential meaning, then employing the matters of the Tripiṭaka and the characteristics of the Six Perfections, all are fused by means of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) so that they become non-dual and nothing is not the Dharma-realm; this is precisely its characteristic.

Regarding "the gift of fearlessness and so forth," the treatise states there are three kinds of giving: namely, material gifts (*āmiṣadāna*), the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), and the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
Giving away both the primary body and its environment is called the gift of material things; since the gift of Dharma is omitted for brevity, the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used.

The subsequent summary can be understood accordingly. Regarding the third section on determining the stages, the phrase "the stage of the *smṛtyupasthāna* of the Tripiṭaka, etc. indicates that when comparing the Great and Small Vehicles, both are considered external ordinary persons (*bāhyapṛthagjana*); this does not depend on internal contemplation or the superiority or inferiority of the objects. This applies to all subsequent comparisons of stages. Within each chapter, the ten [factors] should be fully present and increasingly manifest; where they are not explicitly mentioned in the text, they are omitted for brevity.
Therefore, at the beginning of the Ten Faiths, it is restated that one "causes the five [stages] to be five times more profoundly clear.

In my private commentary, because the preceding section resolved the stages of determination (*niyata-bhūmi*), I have correlated the five grades (*pañca-vastu*) with the five cessations (*pañca-nivāraṇa*).
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a general correspondence; second, a specific correspondence.

Regarding the statement, “Syllables are the vital breath of the Dharmakāya,” it is, for example, like the contaminated physical body in the desire realm, which persists as long as the breath persists and ceases when the breath ceases.
The Dharma-body is likewise: it abides as long as there is the Dharma-body of the teaching that can express it; if the Mahāyāna teaching disappears, how could the Dharma-body remain?

Therefore, within the stage of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), one contemplates the Dharma-body; if one ceases recitation and upholding [the teachings], the life-force of wisdom will be destroyed by discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*). Thus, the Dharma-body is ruined.

Regarding the statement in the *Six Paramitas of Right Practice* that "principle is identical with phenomena" (*ji-shi-er-li*) and so forth: principle is precisely the Buddha, while phenomena obstruct the Way. By realizing principle within phenomena, one ensures that phenomena do not obstruct; for obstruction is itself a hindrance. When principle is identical with phenomena, there is no longer any hindrance to be discussed.
Regarding the "Stage of the Ten Faiths," it is further divided into five parts: first, citing the Five Ranks as the cause for the Ten Faiths;

second, correctly explaining how the ten dharmas correspond to the Ten Faiths both horizontally and vertically; third, citing scriptural evidence from the section on "Samantabhadra" onwards; fourth, the functional efficacy from the section "Entering this" onwards; and fifth, pointing to the detailed exposition from the section "This stage" onwards.

Regarding the initial passage: herein, we first reiterate the beginning of the preceding five chapters, wherein one hears the Perfect Arousing of Faith and is able to practice the ten dharmas, thereby accomplishing perfect conduct and entering the Chapter on Rejoicing;
