Only then can it be called the "non-differentiation of the three," which is established through the gate of the non-duality of self and other.

The ninth, the Gate of the Non-duality of Expedient Means and Reality: Equal Great Wisdom constantly mirrors the Dharma-realm. This is because, through the rational nature, there are nine expedients and one reality; yet within reality there are again nine realms, and the same applies to the expedients. Expedient means and reality are mutually merged within a single thought-moment across the hundred realms; they are beyond discrimination, spontaneously and eternally so. Upon reaching the fruit, one accords with the fundamental single principle, which is neither expedient nor real, yet both expedient and real. This is as previously described regarding the sovereign mastery of the mind-wheel, whereby the mind and speech respond to the capacities for both expedient means and reality. Thus, the three karmas in a single thought-moment do not conflict with expedient means and reality; how could the application of non-action involve any separation or distinction?

In terms of speech, they are designated according to the provisional and the real; in terms of the body, they are named according to the true and the responsive. Since the principles of the three karmas are identical and the provisional and the real are in profound union, this is established through the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas.
Regarding the tenth gate, "The Non-duality of Receiving Moistening": The nature of phenomena is fundamentally endowed with both the provisional and the real.
Since beginningless time, habitual perfuming has been either real or provisional; yet, while the provisional and the real arise through perfuming, the principle remains eternally equal.

When meeting with the appropriate conditions, these form habits that are supported by practice and vows. If there were no original cause, perfuming would be in vain. While meeting with perfuming may result in differences, these do not arise [from the principle itself].

Natures differ; yet although natures themselves have no difference, they must necessarily rely upon illusion to be manifested. Through illusory capacity, illusory resonance, illusory response, and illusory engagement, both the one who responds and those being transformed are neither provisional nor ultimate.
Nevertheless, because sentient beings possess that which is neither provisional nor ultimate, they form the capacity for the provisional and the ultimate;

likewise, the Buddha possesses as a fruition that which is neither provisional nor ultimate, thereby manifesting as the provisional and ultimate response. Thus, the capacities of beings and the responses of the Buddha accord with one another.

Since body and land are without partiality, being equally the eternally quiescent light and nothing other than the Dharma-realm, we know that the three thousand realms are simultaneously present within the mind-ground;
they are no different from the three thousand realms of the Buddha’s mind-ground. The four subtle elements are identical in essence, and their provisional and ultimate aspects are equal in benefit.
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the ultimate.

Therefore, through each of the ten gates, one universally enters into both form and mind; this applies even to the moisture of the *dharmadhātu*, which is likewise so. Thus, the ten wonders (*daśa-prakāra-vaipulya*) are of a single principle from beginning to end. Just as the objective realm inherently possesses the three [aspects], understanding is produced based on that principle and is therefore called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). Wisdom and understanding guide practice, and the union of practice and understanding accords with the principle. These three factors correspond to one another; they are not different yet appear different. While provisional designations of shallow and deep are established and positions are set to avoid confusion, these three factors are simply the realization of those three aspects of the principle.

The final five chapters concern the manifestation of function through the threefold reality (*tridharmas*). Since these threefold realities are themselves a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*), and the three thousand realms are empty, provisional, and middle, they possess functional utility by virtue of being established as such. If one realizes this single thought-moment, the fundamental and manifest aspects of the Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time are not remote. Therefore, the ten gates are restated so that the practices of contemplation may be understood. As the title indicates, the specific details are subsumed within the general; thus, the correspondence between the text and its symbolic meaning can be known.
*Fahua Xuanyi Shiqian*, Scroll 14 and Scroll 15,
composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhànrán.
In explaining these ten wonders of the Fundamental Gate, there are two parts: first, the fundamental and the trace; second, the ten wonders themselves.
The reason for clarifying the fundamental and the trace first is that the terms "fundamental" and "trace" are general designations, and thus they must be explained comprehensively.

To clarify the general through the specific, so that the present aspects of origin (*hon*) and manifestation (*saku*) may be clearly observed, I shall first discuss origin and manifestation generally within this section, and subsequently discuss them specifically.
The general discussion has two parts:
first, the enumeration, also called the "arising";
second, the explanation.
Regarding the initial mention of "phenomena and principle," these are simply the ultimate and the conventional.
As for "principle and teaching," the ultimate and the conventional constitute the principle; the explanation of this ultimate and conventional is termed the teaching.
The explanations regarding practice and so forth can be understood.
Next, the commentary is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation; second, the summary and inclusion, beginning with "If one considers... and so on.
The initial section consists of six parts; within each part, the general is distinguished to bring out the specific.

Furthermore, each part contains three elements: first, an explanation of the characteristics of the original and the trace; second, a clarification that the characteristics of the original and the trace manifest the harmonious fusion of principle; and third, the citation of textual evidence.

Regarding the statement in the "Principle and Phenomena" (Lishi) section, “From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established”: ignorance serves as the root for all dharmas; ignorance is itself the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and ignorance in turn takes the dharma-nature as its root. One should know that all dharmas likewise take the dharma-nature as their root. The dharma-nature is ignorance, and the dharma-nature in turn takes ignorance as its root; the dharma-nature is ignorance, and the dharma-nature has no place of abiding. Ignorance is the dharma-nature, and ignorance has no place of abiding. Although both ignorance and the dharma-nature are equally without abiding, they serve as the root for all dharmas; therefore, it is said, “From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.”
Since the foundation of non-abiding is thus penetrated, the Absolute Truth (paramārtha-satya) points to principle;
all phenomena (dharmas) are matters, which refers to the three thousand realms as their manifold array.

Regarding the phrase "descending from the origin to manifest traces," this refers to the fundamental and manifested aspects of the principle-nature; it is through these that the external applications of fundamental and manifested aspects come to exist. Therefore, [this progression] begins with the principle and phenomena and extends to the present.

Regarding the six levels of the fundamental and the phenomenal (*honjaku*): the first five levels pertain to both the past and the present, as well as both the fundamental and the phenomenal. Fearing that this might be confused with the phenomenal alone, each level is clearly explained as "the true reality (*shinjitsu-sō*) at the time of the fundamental," up to "the true reality actually attained at the very beginning."

Furthermore, since the sixth stage is already a single layer, it is determined that the preceding five stages possess both the fundamental (ben) and the derivative (ji). By this verification, one knows that the preceding five all belong to the fundamental.

Moreover, in the final section of each of the six stages—where the manifestation of phenomena is evident and the principle is harmonious—it is stated: "Though the fundamental and the derivative differ, they are inconceivably one. This borrows the words of Master Sengzhao to praise the principle of the fundamental and the derivative.
Although Master Zhao spoke of "the fundamental" and "the phenomenal," both the fundamental and the phenomenal belong to the realm of the phenomenal.

Now, regarding what is called the "inconceivable": in terms of phenomena, the fundamental belongs to the past and the phenomenal to the present; in terms of principle, however, there is no longer past or present. Thus, we know that the essence of principle is entirely inconceivable.

If one explains this according to the principles of the fivefold stages of origin (*hon*) and trace (*saku*) as they exist today: in terms of phenomena (*ji*), there are the phenomena and principle (*ri*) within the origin, and the phenomena and principle within the trace; yet in terms of principle, there is no longer any distinction between the phenomena and principle of origin and trace. Therefore, it is said in all cases that they are "inconceivable and one."
The same applies to the other four [categories] as well.
Regarding the sixth, "the past" (*ji*) refers to the "traces" (*ji*), which indicates the Trace Gate (*jimen*) and all teachings of the traces;

"the present" (*jin*) refers to the "source" (*ben*), which indicates the Source Gate (*benmen*). Everything prior to the Source Gate is termed "the past," while everything from the emergence [of the Bodhisattvas] onward is termed "the present. Therefore, it is said that the exposition of phenomena and principles, up to and including the provisional and the real, is designated as the "trace."

Now, it is taught that phenomena and principle, up to and including the provisional and the real, are all designated as the "root. Therefore, we know that if there were no phenomena and principle within the traces, up to and including the provisional and the real, how could they manifest the root of long duration?
Furthermore, although the terms "already" (*yǐ*) and "present" (*jīn*) differ from the preceding five, they likewise provisionally refer to the lifespan and are thus termed the "present original.
If one looks back toward the "initial original," one must further distinguish between "already" and "present" as being different.

The various sutras prior to the Lotus Sutra all still belong to the provisional manifestation (*jaku*). What is elucidated in this present sutra is the true revelation of the primordial origin from long ago; that is to say, what was previously taught and what is currently being taught as the manifestation is now revealed as the origin—only then is it the true teaching.
Regarding the reason why, among the texts cited as evidence across the six sections, the first three cite the *traces* (*ji*) and the latter three cite the *root* (*ben*):

it is because the first three also pertain to both the root and the traces, encompassing both phenomena and principle, as well as teaching and practice, essence and function, and so forth—each containing its own internal distinctions. Since it is stated that the "function of the root" and the "expedient means of the root" cannot be revealed by the texts of the traces, and especially since the Root Chapter is intended for the present context, it is evident that the texts of the traces cannot be cited. For this reason, three citations refer to the traces and three refer to the root.

Furthermore, as for the first three passages, since they pertain to the causal stage (*hetu*), and because the original cause is subtle, they merely invert the traces to reveal the origin; thus, they only cite the *jiamen* (trace-gate).

Next, within the summary and integration, the section from "If one discusses the origin and the trace in terms of the past and the present" up to "inconceivable" serves to clarify the fivefold origin and trace discussed previously, showing that the ten wonders possess both an origin and a trace. It is only when specifically referring to the ten coarse and ten wondrous aspects elucidated in the Origin Gate (*benmen*) of the present sutra that they are designated as the "origin" and the "wondrous origin."

Furthermore, when comparing the sixfold profundity (*ṣaḍ-guṇa*) with the tenfold wondrousness (*daśa-miāo*), there are cases where they are complete or incomplete, and where they are many or few; therefore, it is elucidated once more.
This section consists of three parts:

first, the formal explanation of their mutual inclusion; second, the detailed demonstration beginning with "The first..."; and third, the general explanation of how the phenomena manifest and the principle is harmonized, beginning with "If there were no..."

In the initial text, taking advantage of the context, one proceeds by recognizing the six pairs in reverse order from the end; once the last has been recognized, the remaining five are immediately known, which is why they are explained in reverse sequence.

The reason why the six gates clarify different modes of inclusion is that, among the six gates, three causes and two fruits have already been established; furthermore, these are the two gates of the present sutra. Therefore, they are included differently according to their respective meanings.

Next, regarding the passage in the "Distinguishing and Indicating" section that states, "The original at the very beginning is merely the source (hon) and not the trace (jaku)," etc.: since the original realization was not yet manifested as a trace, it belongs exclusively to the source.
In relation to one another within the intermediate stage, they mutually function as the fundamental and the manifested.

Furthermore, that which is accomplished in the intermediate stage is called "also a manifestation" when it descends to manifest traces, and is called "also the fundamental" when it reveals the original source.

The "already explained" refers to what has been taught today, namely the Trace Gate (jimen); since the Fundamental [Gate] (ben) has not yet been revealed, it belongs exclusively to the Trace. If there were no "already explained," one would simply cite today's Trace Gate; now, when the "presently explained" Fundamental [Gate] is mentioned, it refers to today's Fundamental Gate itself.
Next, in the section explicitly clarifying the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku), there are two parts:
first, the enumeration; second, the explanation.
Within the explanation, there are ten successive layers that clarify these ten kinds of wondrousness.
The initial brief explanation is itself divided into ten sections; the first section is somewhat more extensive, while the remaining nine are concise.
The first section has three parts:

first, the presentation of the fundamental; second, from "If sixteen... onwards, the presentation of the traces used for comparative determination; third, from "If one leaves behind... onwards, the clearing away of the traces to reveal the fundamental.

Regarding the passage in the *Jiwen* (Text on Traces) from "The Sahā world as ink" to "how could it ever be exhausted," this quotes the text from the "City of Transformation" chapter (*Hua Cheng Pin*) of the Trace Gate (*Jimen*). It is inappropriate to cite the words of Maitreya and others here, for Maitreya did not know that the text belongs to the Original Gate (*Benmen*). Alternatively, these words may have been borrowed from the Original Gate and brought here as a metaphor. Even the wisdom-power of a Buddha-elect (*jizhu*), which perceives the three thousandfold world-system with its dust-motes, cannot know [the extent of the ink]. If one were to strictly use the text of the Trace Gate, then the meaning would be consistent only if the twenty-five characters beginning with "Maitreya" were removed; the Master said, "I suspect there is another intention."

Although this quotation from Maitreya’s words is slightly different in its phrasing, the text of the Original Gate (Honmon) merely states: "We abide in the stage of *avaivartika*, yet we do not comprehend these matters. In the present passage, it is stated that one does not know even the number of worlds through the wisdom of provisional emergence (*shutsuga*), let alone their atomic particles (*reṇu*).
If one were to grasp at the objects of cognition, one would merely have to employ the wisdom that issues forth for the sake of provisional truth (*prajñapti*).
Therefore, one should apply what was explained in the preceding passage.

Regarding the phrase "sweeping away traces to reveal the fundamental," it simply refers to those who attained Buddhahood prior to the current number of kalpas; thus, the intervening period up to this day is spontaneously swept away, and the primordial foundation from long ago is spontaneously revealed.
The nine "Sublime" (Miao) sections that follow below are all like this.

From here downward, there are two "Sublime" sections concerning the Original Fruit and the Original Land; these consist only of two passages: one establishing the Sublime and another sweeping away the traces to reveal the Original. The seven subsequent "Sublime" sections directly point to the Original; since they will be explained more extensively below, they are not discussed here—the texts for all of them can be seen [in the source].
Next, regarding the "arising," there are three parts:
first, the statement of the purpose for its introduction; second, the actual arising; third, the summary of the meaning, beginning with the words "The meaning is...
Next, regarding "sameness and difference," there are two parts:
First, the preliminary establishment; next, the explanation beginning with "performing this.
Within the explanation, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the intent of the opening and closing; second, the formal explanation of the opening and closing, beginning with "within the traces."
Within this, there are four parts:

first, clarifying how, within the traces (*traces*), the cause is opened while the fruit is closed; second, clarifying that in the resonance and response (*ganying*) and so forth, there is neither opening nor closing; third, from "The original is opened" (*ben kai*) onwards, clarifying how, within the fundamental (*ben*), the cause is closed while the fruit is opened; fourth, the benefit of the one is likewise identical in intent to the resonance and response and so forth.

In the first section on the traces [of the teaching], the causes are divided into four; in the section on the fruition, the lifespan and nirvana are combined as one set of three dharmas, which are then joined with the lifespan and nirvana of this Fundamental Chapter.

Next, regarding the "Responsive Manifestation" (ganying) and so forth, both the Fundamental (ben) and the Traced (ji) have two locations with identical names; these are identical as functions upon the fruit.

Third, in the Fundamental, the causal union is as previously explained, but here it clarifies the opening of the fruit; whereas in the Traced there is no name for the fruit, which results in separating the three dharmas to constitute the triad of "fruit" and so forth. Since the Fundamental contains the name for the fruit, it speaks only of "separating two."
This section is divided into three parts.

First, the intent of the opening is explained: since the Buddha of the present *Lotus Sūtra* has not yet entered extinction, nirvāṇa is not yet discussed; whereas the Buddhas of the past, having already proclaimed their extinction in the *Lotus Sūtra*, were all [addressing] those with pure capacities.
Next, from "Furthermore, regarding past events" onwards, the text definitively clarifies the opening [of the teaching] based on the fact that the matter has already been settled.
Third, from "Within the traces" onwards, it again explains the reason why [the Buddha] does not employ [certain methods] within the traces.

The final two "Excellences" share the same names, yet their temporal contexts differ between the past and the present. Since there are distinctions regarding the ten aspects of the fundamental and the manifested, as well as their opening and closing, how could one understand the six meanings—such as the equality of these principles—and the ultimate purport of the ten excellences, such as the cause, without first comprehending the ten gates within the manifested aspect?
Next, the citation of supporting texts has three parts:

first, the introductory explanation of the meaning; second, the actual citation; third, the conclusion. The first part [the introductory explanation] has three sections: [The text continues as per the original structure.]

First, the locations of the cited passages are briefly indicated; second, from "However, the former Buddhas... onwards, the general purport of the main text is clarified; third, from "Now, regarding... onwards, it is shown that although the text is concise, its meaning is comprehensive.
The fifth section is the extensive explanation of the ten phrases; these ten phrases are each treated individually, and within them there are two parts:
first, a general clarification of the fundamental wondrous intent, and second, the formal explanation.
The first part, in turn, has three sections: [End of provided text]

First, the general intent of the coming [of the teaching] is briefly clarified; second, from "But the fundamental limit" (*tāvad eva mūlam*) onwards, it is clarified that the fundamental is remote and difficult to know; third, from "Nevertheless" (*yady api*) onwards, it is clarified that it must not remain unknown.
Next, the correct elucidation of the excellence of the cause has two parts:
first, the explanation; second, the critical analysis. The first part further has three sections: [The text continues with the specific sub-sections.]

First, the fundamental [truth] is established; second, from "The Traces Have Many Causes" onwards, the traces are cited to distinguish their differences; third, from "By Means of Three Meanings" onwards, the traces are swept away to reveal the fundamental.
This pattern applies to all subsequent sections of the ninefold wondrous divisions.
The initial passage also has three parts:
first, the citation of the text; second, the explanation; third, from the words "a single phrase" onwards, the conclusion regarding the four meanings of the original cause.
The same applies to all nine subsequent sections.

Regarding the phrase "spreading grass and lighting lamps" and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle four, in explaining the causal conditions from previous lives between the Buddha and Ānanda, states: "In a previous life, Śākya was a potter named Mahāprabha."

At that time, there was a Buddha named Śākyamuni, whose disciples were just like the disciples of the present Buddha. Accompanying the Buddha, they went to the house of a potter to stay the night. The potter provided grass mats and lit lamps, and offered honey syrup to the Buddha and the bhikṣus. He then made a vow to become a Buddha in a future age of the five turbidities, with a name for himself and his disciples no different from those of the present Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "formerly a Māṇava," it is detailed as in the *Śūramgama-samādhi Sūtra* (or *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*).
Because he received the prediction from Dīpaṃkara and attained the stage of non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), it is known that he was a Buddha in all but name.
Regarding the statement, “Formerly he was the Brahmā-śrotriya Ratnasāgara,” it is fully detailed in the second fascicle of the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which says:
“There was a bodhisattva named Śāntamati who asked the Buddha:
‘The worlds of other Buddhas are pure; for what reason does the present World-Honored One dwell amidst these five turbidities to preach the three vehicles?’”
The Buddha said:
"Pure and impure lands all arise from original vows.

In the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, this buddha-world was named Santirana and the kalpa was named Susthita. There was a wheel-turning king named Araṇemin who ruled over the four continents. He had a minister named Ratnasāgara, born of the brahmin caste, who was skilled in divining signs."

At that time, he gave birth to a son endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; the devas constantly came to make offerings to him, and thus they named him Ratnagarbha (Treasure Store).

Later, he left the household life and attained the Way, also named Baozang (Treasure Store). Having turned the wheel of Dharma and delivered sentient beings, he subsequently traveled through various villages.

After preaching the Dharma for the noble king, the king invited him to enter the rains retreat; the king’s seven treasures also spontaneously offered their support, and the king’s thousand sons likewise each provided offerings for three months, as described in detail in the sutras, continuing for a full two hundred and fifty years.

Thereafter, Ratnasāgara came to the Buddha’s presence and received the prediction of his future buddhahood; all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions who had been transformed by the light of Ratnasāgara simultaneously attained the Way.

Next, Ratnasāgara exhorted the Wheel-Turning King to resolve his mind for enlightenment; next, he exhorted the Prince to resolve his mind for enlightenment; next, he caused the gods and the eight classes of beings to resolve their minds for enlightenment, until finally, throughout the entire trichiliocosm, all had resolved their minds for bodhicitta.
Next, within the realms of animals and hells, he manifested the body of a Buddha before each and every sentient being, causing them to be freed from suffering.
During these seven years, among the humans, devas, and the eight classes of beings, all those free from desire offered worship and support.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, he was the teacher of Amitābha": in that *Vyākaraṇa-parivarta* (Chapter on the Prophecy), it is said: "That Buddha first entered samādhi, manifested the pure lands of the ten directions, and assembled all the bodhisattvas. First, he bestowed the prophecy upon Ratnasāgara; next, Ratnasāgara bestowed the prophecy upon Amitābha; and subsequently, he bestowed the prophecy upon the Crown Prince of the Wheel-Turning King."
He said:

"Observe the beings of the human and celestial realms as well as those in the three evil paths; give rise to great compassion, sever all their sufferings and afflictions, and cause them to abide in peace and happiness.
From now on, you shall be named 'Avalokiteśvara' (The One Who Observes the Sounds of the World), and so forth."
"From the crown prince of a Wheel-Turning King down to all gods and people of the world, there are none whose resolve was not inspired by the Brahmin; therefore, he is the teacher of them all."
The third section, "Dispelling Traces," has two parts:
first, the dispelling; second, from "If one attains... onwards, the integration.
The first part has three sections:

First, the method of erasing is presented, wherein one should seek three meanings; second, from "In this life" onwards, the intent behind the method of erasing traces is explained; third, from "If one clings" onwards, the faults of clinging to traces are refuted.

Regarding the first passage: throughout the various teachings of a single lifetime, there are none that do not state that [the Buddha] first attained enlightenment at Gayā; and among the Mahayana scriptures, none surpass the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in its comprehensive integration, yet even the beginning of that sutra states, "He first attained perfect enlightenment at the site of Bodhi. Thus, we know that both the Mahayana and Hinayana accounts of his attainment are proximate [to the truth], and therefore we know this is a provisional manifestation (*jise*).

Regarding the second meaning: if these were the original causes, they should not be manifold; there should only be one perfect cause to elicit one perfect fruit. Since there are four meanings with varying depths, one should know that these are the actual results achieved subsequently, which conform to the capacities of sentient beings. Because the conditions of their capacities differ, the original source descends to manifest these four causal aspects. Thus, we know that these differences certainly belong to the provisional traces.
The third meaning is that it merely reveals the lifespan to point out the original, long-distant foundation, while the intervening period of today naturally falls away of its own accord.
"Wiping away" (fù) means to brush aside or eliminate.

Initially, it was obscured by its traces; now, having brushed away that obscuration, the true reality of the source is revealed. Since this is so for the "Excellence" (Miao), it should be understood that the subsequent categories, such as "Benefit" (Li), follow the same principle.
The following text is self-evident.
Within the threefold refutation of errors, there are three parts:

first, clarifying that clinging to the traces leads to delusion regarding the source; second, using what follows below to understand what precedes above, thereby enabling one to recognize the traces and know the source.

Regarding the four characters "quǎn xià zhī shàng" (using what follows below to know what precedes above), these should likely follow the phrase "the stage of the wondrous analogy of the wheel"; alternatively, they may be a scribal error, in which case each of the two sections would possess both a doctrinal statement and an analogy.
III. "Alas" expresses lamentation and reproach.
Following this, in the section on analysis, the question may be understood.
The answer consists of two parts:
First, there is a general response to the objection that [the Buddha] is not in the first dwelling; next, from "Furthermore, in the interim" onwards, he illustrates the cause by means of the result.
Next, within the marvelousness of the fundamental result, there are also three parts, as before.
The first section has two parts:

first, citing the sūtras to establish the fundamental principle; second, the explanation. Within the subsequent discussion of the differences among the four teachings regarding the traces [of the Buddha’s career], it says: "Or it is said that at the Bodhi tree, upon the grass seat, the thirty-four moments of mind... and so forth. This refers to the three types of bodhisattvas who achieve enlightenment through four stages, as elucidated in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

The origins of the present text are not uniform: some details, such as the Bodhi tree and the celestial robe, correspond exactly to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; others, such as the "Site of the Path of Quiescence" (*śāntimārga-maṇḍala*), correspond exactly to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; and still others, such as the statement that the void serves as the seat at the site of enlightenment, are likewise found in the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna Sūtra*.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 38, states: "The Śrāvaka sūtras speak of spreading a seat of grass; the Mahāyāna sūtras speak of either seeing a seat of grass spread beneath a tree, or seeing celestial cushions spread out—the various heavenly garments of the six heavens differing according to what is evoked by one's merit—or seeing a jeweled throne of immeasurable *yojanas*."
The section beginning with "If it is this" explains the three preceding meanings.
The refutation of errors and so forth follows the text.
Next, within the section on the excellence of the land, the textual divisions are as before; furthermore, within the section on the differences in the traces, there are two parts:
First, this is based on other sutras; second, it is based on the Trace Gate (Jiemen) of the present sutra.
Within the first section, regarding the differences among the four lands, it says: "Some say there is a land in the west named 'Invincible' (Wusheng). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"To the west, beyond thirty-six Ganges-sands of worlds, there is a land named 'Invincible'."
It is further stated:
"In each of the worlds of the ten directions, there is a pure land of Śākyamuni.
Moreover, it is said in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*:
"It is said that Śākyamuni Buddha has a pure land named Ekadīpa-prabhāsa, which is the original home of Śākyamuni.
This, too, is a teaching concerning his manifested traces (*śeṣa*).
Furthermore, regarding the "Land of Eternal Quiescent Light" (*nitya-praśānta-ābhāsa-kṣetra*), there are two aspects:
First the heading, then the explanation.

As in the "Original Gate," the Bodhisattvas who emerge from the earth dwell in the space below; once they have emerged from the earth, they likewise proceed to the sublime seven-jeweled stupa in the void. Both these instances of space represent the *jigguang* (the light of tranquility).

Regarding the passage, "The principle of the Tranquil Light is universally pervasive, like a mirror and like a vessel," and so forth: it is, for example, as when various devas eat from a single precious vessel together, as explained in the third fascicle of the *Zhiguan* commentary.

Regarding the passage from "The three transformations of the land may appear as the Pure Land of Co-residence" up to "the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder": if the purity of these three transformations is based on a similarity to the Land of Co-residence, yet involves moving devas and humans to another land consisting solely of precious trees and precious lion-thrones, inhabited only by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it resembles the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder; hence the use of the word "or. Furthermore, according to the text, it should also resemble the Land of True Reward without Obstruction.

The prose and phrases regarding the "Four Clarifications on Response and Resonance" are largely identical [to the *Fahua wenju*], with the addition after the main text of a detailed analysis (*liaojian*) concerning the coarse and subtle, and the broad and narrow.

Regarding the initial section on the differences in the traces of the four teachings, it states: "The Buddha of the Tripiṭaka illuminates the capacities [of beings] three times a day. Furthermore, in the subsequent section on the Shared Teaching, it says in all cases: "Illuminating the nine dharma-realms," because each respective teaching contains the three vehicles.

Regarding the passage in the *Tripiṭaka* stating, "Furthermore, as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts say, the Buddha entered the city to beg for alms," there are ten causes and conditions: because he was prevented from going out by the parents of a woman; because of those who were ill; because he wished to allow people to see his physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); and because there were those who originally had no intention to give and only gave upon being asked to beg. These ten causes and conditions all illustrate the manner in which the contents of the Tripiṭaka observe the capacities of beings to benefit them.

Next, regarding the statement in the *Vibhāṣā* (Fenbie): "Furthermore, there are four propositions concerning the contrast between the fundamental response (*ben gan*) and the manifested response (*ji gan*), and between the coarse and the subtle," this refers back to the original text. At the time of the actual attainment [of Buddhahood], the capacities of those for whom the teachings were intended also comprised the four teachings; therein, the three vehicles are considered coarse, while the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is considered subtle.
The manifestations within the provisional traces that respond to capacities also do not exceed these four categories, and the same applies to the coarse and the subtle.

Therefore, we do not judge the fundamental and the trace based on the coarse and the subtle; rather, we designate that which is from the very beginning as "fundamental. One should know that at the time of the fundamental, both the coarse and the subtle are equally subtle, whereas within the trace, both the coarse and the subtle are equally coarse; thus, their breadth and narrowness can be understood.
The fourfold categorization of "middling" should be understood as coarse or subtle according to the text.

Furthermore, that which covers many worlds is considered "broad," while that which covers few worlds is considered "narrow. Since the initial descent of the response, as well as the intermediate stages and so forth, also possess breadth and narrowness, we now do not judge based on these dimensions alone. Therefore, it is known that what was accomplished long ago is sublime in both its breadth and narrowness, whereas the intermediate and present times are coarse in both their breadth and narrowness.
The textual passages regarding the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are largely the same as above.

As for the phrase "furthermore, the fourfold analysis is as stated above," this refers to the four propositions based on the fundamental [state] encompassing both the coarse and the subtle, and the provisional traces encompassing both the coarse and the subtle; the four propositions concerning the breadth and narrowness of the fundamental and the provisional traces are likewise so.
Furthermore, one does not determine the "original" (hon) and the "traced" (jaku) based on whether they are coarse or subtle, broad or narrow; rather, one takes the very beginning as the original.
Within the sixth section, "The Subtlety of the Dharma," which clarifies the differences among the traced manifestations, there are two parts:
first, a brief illustration using the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding the three flavors produced from the cow; second, the explanation beginning with "What is... and so forth.
The explanation consists of two parts:
first, the explanation itself; second, the interrogation and analysis. Within the first part (the explanation), there are two sections:
First, the analogy is presented; next, from "The Buddha is also like this" onwards, the main point is applied.
The initial section consists of two parts:
first, the analogies are presented both collectively and individually; second, from "If it were an ox" onwards, the three teachings are briefly summarized as a conclusion.
The first section also has two parts:
first, the general; second, the specific, beginning with "If one eats ordinary grass.

Regarding the initial passage, "A fine calf does not [graze] on high plateaus or in low, damp places," this is cited from the second chapter of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, within the refutation of the old physician.

"If this milch cow does not eat dregs, grain-liquor, or wheat-bran; if she is distinguished from common cattle by her calf; if she is well-trained and gentle, neither galloping in vain nor rushing recklessly; if she has pastures where she is neither on high plateaus—representing *nirvāṇa*—nor in low marshes—representing *saṃsāra*; if she drinks clear water and not turbid water, and is not driven to run or allowed to wander; if she is not kept in the same herd as ordinary oxen—this being the unique quality of the Buddha—and if her food and drink are moderate, being neither emaciated by hunger nor vulgarly satiated—milk such as this is called the secret treasury of *amṛta*."
Regarding the phrase "the grass of forbearance" (*kṣānti-tṛṇa*), its meaning encompasses many aspects; therefore, four flavors are separately set forth as in the text.
Next, within the section on synthesis, there are two parts:
first, the general [explanation], and second, the specific [explanation] beginning with "good destinies."
Within the separate [classification], there are two parts:
first, the four teachings for humans and devas; second, the five flavors. Furthermore, there are two [subdivisions]:

First, [the flavors] are categorized according to the divisions and teachings; second, they are briefly contrasted with the four teachings and four Buddhas, which correctly correspond to the five flavors all emerging from the cow.

Regarding the initial statement that "the two capacities strike out the fourth and fifth flavors," this refers to the Separate and Perfect Teachings within the *Avataṃsaka*; this is an establishment of names based on the divisions and teachings, and other cases may be understood by analogy.
Regarding the subsequent text, it further distinguishes the different explanations according to their respective contexts.
From the phrase "Furthermore" (*punar-aparam*) onwards, the text again employs four propositions to differentiate between the "already" (*atīta*) and the "now" (*pratyutpanna*).

Thus, one should know that the initial clarification of the "already" as the trace and the "now" as the origin remains merely a preliminary approach; the "already" as the trace and the "now" as the origin should be understood through the distinctions made previously.

Regarding the phrase "the original and the present traces": "the original" refers to the beginning; "the present traces" refers to the Trace Gate (*jimon*), which was spoken by the Buddha of the present traces.

Regarding "both traces": that which follows the completion of the original and precedes the Trace Gate is called the "original traces"; this is because the present Original Gate (*honmon*) is likewise spoken by the Buddha of the traces.

Regarding the phrase "now already both the original and the manifest": the initial [period] constitutes the "already-original" (yiben), while the Original Gate (honmon) constitutes the "now-original" (jinben).

Regarding the statement "the fourfold propositions of provisional and real, up to phenomena and principle, etc.": each of these is established as four propositions by mutually contrasting the "already" and "now" with respect to the original and the manifest.

As it was real in the past, so it is expedient now; as it was expedient in the past, so it is real now; there are cases where both are expedient and both are real, and this applies even to matters and principles.
However, taking the initial state as "already" and as the basis, one may understand the preceding examples by analogy.

Among the seven marvelous aspects of the retinue, only the primary characteristics are presented; from Mañjuśrī and Avalokiteśvara down to those who are deluded, the distinct characteristics within their manifested traces are briefly set forth. These are arranged according to the various sections (nikāya) as the characteristics of the sages, and may also be considered as four different types of characteristics.
Regarding the first [section], it is as the text states.
Next is the explanation, which is further divided into two parts:
first, the formal explanation; second, the resolution of doubts.
The initial statement, "the tranquil light of the void of dharma-nature," uses the lower direction and the stupa situated here in this space to represent the tranquil light.

These bodhisattvas dwell in the void of the lower direction, and after emerging, they likewise abide in the void; those in this land who hear the revelation of the provisional to manifest the real and attain the patience of non-arising also abide in the tranquil light of the void.

Although both are equally the empty space that manifests the light of quiescence, those who dwell within it differ in the length of their tenure; the Bodhisattvas who have emerged have long since attained patience, and therefore those who have recently entered among the traces do not recognize those who have been there for a long time.

Regarding the passage in the *Xiaozhijue* (迹中) which states, "Mañjuśrī and Avalokiteśvara may act as teacher and disciple," it refers to how Mañjuśrī was formerly the Bodhisattva *Prabhāsa* (*Miaoguang*), who taught the eight princes of King *Dīpaṃkara*. These eight princes received successive predictions of enlightenment, the last of whom was named *Dīpaṃkara*. Since *Dīpaṃkara* was the teacher of Śākyamuni, *Prabhāsa* thus became the ninth-generation patriarch of Śākyamuni.

In the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, it is recorded that Śākyamuni studied the Way under the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa in the past; since Dharmaprabhāsa Tathāgata is none other than Avalokiteśvara himself, we know that both Mañjuśrī and Avalokiteśvara have previously served as teachers.
Devadatta was none other than the seer Asita, as is fully detailed in this present sutra.
Such individuals as these have, in turn, become his disciples.

Regarding the statement, "When comparing the original and the trace, the number of dust motes in a thousand worlds is few, while the increase in the number of those on the Path is great": the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth in the three-thousandfold world system were his retinue during the time of the original [manifestation]; it simply says that the ground of the three-thousandfold world all split open and immeasurable Bodhisattvas simultaneously surged forth. If one compares this to the retinue within the present trace-manifestation—as described in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" regarding the increase in the Path and the reduction of births—six hundred and eighty million *nayuta* *koṭi* of *Ganges-sand* sentient beings attained the realization of the non-arising of dharmas; a thousand times more attained the power of hearing and retaining; as many dust motes as there are in one world-system attained eloquence; as many dust motes as there are in a great trichiliocosm attained non-retrogression; and those in medium and small chiliocosms, up to those in a single four-continent world and even as many as the dust motes in eight worlds, have only now first resolved their minds for enlightenment. Compared to those who surged forth [from the earth], these are very few.

The fourfold analysis should also follow the preceding text; however, one should distinguish between the "original" and the "traced" solely on the basis of temporal proximity and distance, and never by means of the depth of the Dharma-body or the breadth or narrowness of the conditions for transformation.

Regarding the eighth point, "the wondrousness of nirvāṇa": within the clarification that the manifestations (traces) differ, it first clarifies the intent behind these manifestations; although they differ, fundamentally there is no length or shortness.
Next, from the phrase "or taking" (*vā gṛhṇāti*) onwards, it properly clarifies their differences.

Regarding the meaning of the initial passage which states, "Beginning with the disciples and ending with the vipers and scorpions," the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* enumerates the assembly as consisting of eighty billion times one hundred thousand bhikṣus who have accomplished the Mahāyāna and so forth—a single *koṭi* of practitioners; six billion bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom were great arhats; one *koṭi* of bodhisattvas; two *koṭis* of upāsakas; three *koṭis* of upāsikās; four *koṭis* of Licchavis; five *koṭis* of great ministers; six *koṭis* of kings; seven *koṭis* of queens; eight *koṭis* of goddesses; nine *koṭis* of nāga kings; ten *koṭis* of spirits; twenty *koṭis* of garuḍas; and even all the bee-kings within Jambudvīpa.

Furthermore, to the east, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable and boundless Ganges-sands, there is a land where a Buddha resides named Tathāgata Ākāśasama. He addressed his foremost great disciple: "You should go to the Sahā world in the west; in that land there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni who will soon enter parinirvāṇa.
You may take this fragrant food from this world to offer to that Buddha. After the Buddha has eaten, he will enter parinirvāṇa; you should pay him homage and request a resolution of your doubts."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra, having received the Buddha’s instruction, rose from his seat, prostrated himself, and circumambulated him immeasurable times; then, together with the assembly of great bodhisattvas, he set out for the Sahā world.

Furthermore, from King Ajātaśatru and his consort down to those who can kill by looking with a poisonous gaze, including the "dung beetles, vipers, and the sixteen types of those with evil observances"—the dung beetle is also called the *qiāngwáng* (roller beetle).
The *Erya* says: "The black-armored insect feeds on dung and soil.
*Fu* means "poisonous"; the *Erya* says:
"The locusts were those that had not yet grown wings.
It is also said, "They were three inches wide, with bodies as large as an arm. The *Shiji* states:
"If a viper bites the hand, one must cut it off.
The *chài* (scorpion) is a venomous insect; the *Zuozhuan* states:
"The sting of a bee or scorpion remains poisonous for ten years; its tail-tip is coiled like a woman's hair."
The character "fù" (蝮) is pronounced with the *fu* and *mu* finals; it is not the same as the "fú" (福) in "Fúxīn" (福信).
Some say: since the body of the Bodhisattva Anantagātra is infinite in size, how can it be said that he came here from there?
One should counter-argue as follows:
Since it is said that [Avalokiteśvara] has come here, how can he be "boundless"?

To say he is "boundless" means his body is actually finite, yet is designated as "boundless," just as the lifespan of Amitābha is actually limited, yet is designated as "immeasurable. If his lifespan were truly immeasurable, how could there be an Avalokiteśvara as a successor (upapadya)?
Regarding "lying on one's side due to back pain," this is as recorded in the eighth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation).

Furthermore, regarding sleeping with the head to the north and so forth, these are also characteristics of the Buddha according to the Tripiṭaka; they are fully detailed as recorded in the first fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Next, in the section clarifying the differences, there are two parts:
first, explaining the characteristics by means of two sūtras; second, concluding that the intent of the two sūtras is identical.
The first part further has two sections:
First, the differences are clarified to explain this sutra; next, from the section "The Sutra says," it is cited to demonstrate its identity with the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The initial passage is further divided into two parts: first, the *Zàng* (Āgama) and *Tōng* (Shared) teachings, and second, the *Bié* (Distinct) and *Yuán* (Perfect) teachings.
The first section has two parts:
first, a brief indication of the two differences; second, under the heading "birth-body" (*janma-kāya*), a further explanation of the two distinctions.
Regarding the statement in the explanation of the Three Piṭakas that "he eats alms-food," the third fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* states:

When the Buddha arrived at the city of Pāvā, in the Caitika Garden, there was an elder named Cunda who invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. He prepared a *candanakholaka* (sandalwood-ear soup) specifically for the Buddha; because it was a rare delicacy of the world, he offered it to the Buddha alone.
Ānanda said: "The householder’s provision of offerings brings no merit, for it was at his house that the Buddha took his final meal before entering parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha said:
Do not speak thus.
This householder has now attained great benefit, long life, physical vigor, and a good reputation; he has produced abundant wealth and treasures, and upon death, he will be reborn in the heavens.
Next, within the section on the distinct and the perfect, there are two parts:
first the distinct, then the perfect. Within the distinct, there are two further sections:
First, the position of the Dārṣṭāntikas is cited, followed by the formal explanation.

Within the explanation, the passage from "liberation from form up to liberation from consciousness" to "without remainder" states that since it speaks of the cessation of form up to the cessation of consciousness, this refers to the analytical disintegration of form outside the [three] realms (*dhātu*). Therefore, the exhaustion of the cause is termed "with remainder," while the disappearance of the fruit is termed "without remainder."

In principle, the causes and effects of transformation (*pariṇāma*) should not be divided into two; one should know that [the division] is intended to establish the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*).

Next, the scripture says, "Today, within this assembly," and so forth. This is from the *Sūtra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma* (*Xiangfa jueyi jing*), which shares the same text as the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. It is further divided into two parts: first, the enumeration;
second, the conclusion beginning with "This clarifies... and so on.
Next, the "Concordance of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*" (大經) below consists of four parts:

first, a brief indication of their concordance; second, the actual concordance of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* and others; third, the conclusion regarding their concordance based on the roots of the listeners being sharp or dull; and fourth, the concordance that clarifies the commonality of the text concerning permanence.
The first part is as stated in the text.

Regarding the subsequent passage which says, "Kāśyapa first asked about long life," this refers to the thirty-six questions posed at the beginning of the third sutra, the first of which asks: "How does one obtain a long life and an indestructible vajra-body?"

In the response provided in the following text, the analogy of entrusting gold as found in the "Chapter on Longevity" is employed; however, it is stated that the gold is entrusted only to the young man and not to the old man.
Since it says, "having gone out and returned," when the elder returns and seeks the gold but finds nothing, we know from this that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding and does not perish.
The following "Chapter on the Vajra Body" extensively explains that by protecting the Dharma and upholding the precept against killing, one attains a vajra body.
Furthermore, throughout the subsequent sections of the sutra, it is clarified that [the Buddha] will eternally abide in the future.
The third point is "visible.

Regarding the fourth point, it says in the *Huayan jing changzhu zhong*: "Twenty thousand Lamp-Light Buddhas and others are equal to the light of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding permanence," and so forth. The details of these twenty thousand Lamp-Light Buddhas are as explained in the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* extensively elucidates the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and this One Vehicle is precisely the eternally abiding (*nitya*).

In the ninth section, "Clarifying the Subtlety of Life Span," there are two parts: first, the initial establishment; second, the citation of scriptures, which first cites the original text and then provides an explanation, specifically citing the intermediate [teaching] to correspond with the fundamental [teaching]. Within the clarification that the traces differ, there are two further divisions:
first, the *zàng* (Treasury) and *tōng* (Common); second, the *bié* (Distinct) and *yuán* (Perfect).
The first section has two parts:
first, a brief explanation; second, the judgment that there is no basis for the Dharmakāya [in the Separate Teaching], starting from the words "These two.
Within the Separate and Perfect Teachings, there are also two parts:
First, there is a brief explanation; next, from the words "these [etc. onwards, there is the concluding corroboration by way of illustration.
Regarding the tenfold explanation of the excellence of the benefit: first, the benefit is briefly established; the upper clause establishes it, while the lower clause explains it.

Next, regarding the section beginning with "If the traces," which clarifies that the traces are not identical: these are now listed briefly; in their full detail, they should correspond to the seven benefits and ten benefits as described in the preceding text.

Regarding the phrase "up to the increase of the Path" and so forth: although this refers to the *honmon* (the Original Gate) according to the sutra, since it is designated as the *honmon* within the context of the present world’s *shakumon* (the Trace Gate), we know that today’s teaching properly constitutes the benefit within the Trace. Even that which is called "intermediate"—from the time after the original accomplishment until now—is termed intermediate; if those who manifest the Original and thereby obtain benefit still achieve the benefit of the Trace, how much more so for today?

The section beginning with "By means of the traces" again raises the characteristics of the fundamental benefit; since the original text is narrow, one must understand the fundamental by way of the traces. Therefore, in the section on the "fundamental of the fundamental," it clarifies that the characteristics are manifest, harmonious, and identical. Although there are many traces, they all take the fundamental as their basis; hence, it is called the "fundamental of the fundamental."
The fundamental reality has long since passed; if one does not rely on its traces, how can one recognize that fundamental reality?
This is the meaning of the analogy: "like pointing at the sky by waving away its shadow.
Regarding the sixth section, the "Analysis of the Three Times," there is first a brief establishment of the position, followed by a detailed analysis through questions and answers.
The first section has three parts:

first, citing the sutra to show the characteristics; second, the explanation beginning with "If past... and so forth; third, the conclusion beginning with "The three periods of time... and so forth. Within the conclusion, there are two parts:
First the Dharma, then the analogy.
Within the subsequent questions and answers, the first follows the text as it stands.

Regarding the second question: if one says that all Buddhas possess emanated bodies, and since Many Treasures is also included among the number of Buddhas, he too should have emanated bodies; why then is it said that his entire body remains undispersed?
This constitutes a further objection:
if [the Buddha] remains in his entire body, why does it say elsewhere that he "listens to the sutras in various places"?

In the response, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is first cited to explain the first of the eight recollections (*aṣṭānusmṛti*), the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), which states: "Since it is called a 'transformation body' (*nirmāṇakāya'), it is precisely a 'divided body' (*vibhakta-kāya')."

The Master said: "I shall cite the explanation by Shenhui of Nanyue. Relying on the scriptural text, it says that at the time of his passing, he addressed the fourfold assembly, saying: 'Those who wish to make offerings to my entire body should erect a great stupa. When the scripture was produced as proof, his entire body was found within the stupa; through the power of his vows, he heard the scriptures everywhere."
According to the Southern Huayan school, after the Parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni, the entire body remained undivided; "undivided" means it was not like the fragmented *śarīra* relics.
This does not preclude the fact that other Buddhas may also possess divided bodies.
From "As he entered" onwards, it clarifies that the *Lotus Sūtra* is both perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) and eternal (*nitya*).
From "He sang aloud" onwards, it clarifies that he possesses the four virtues (*catur-guṇa*) as proof of his eternity.

Regarding the phrase "the Great Dharma of True Purity": "True" refers to the virtue of permanence (*nitya*), and "Purity" refers to the virtue of purity (*śubha*). Since both permanence and purity are present, how could there not be self (*ātman*) and bliss (*sukha*)?
Therefore, it is said that "the two virtues may be known."
Since the entire body of Prabhūtaratna still pervades the ten directions, we know that all Buddhas likewise possess emanated bodies.

As for the statement, "The dull-witted do not even perceive it while reading the text," this refers to those who fail to realize that this sutra is fully endowed with the four virtues, and who erroneously judge the *Lotus Sutra* to be unclear regarding eternal abiding; on this basis, it is said that both ancient and modern [interpreters] are all dull-witted.
In the subsequent question-and-answer section, the questions regarding the Buddhas revealing their fundamental nature are as stated in the text.

Regarding the answer, the phrase "the initial wondrous enlightenment points to the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) as the fundamental" means that because it is attained for the first time; even if one at the level of the first stage is empowered to become a Buddha of Wondrous Enlightenment, the first stage is still pointed to as the actual fundamental. According to the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*, this should be analyzed using four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): namely, the fundamental is low while the trace is high, and both the fundamental and the trace are low. Of these, the first stage only admits of these two propositions.

Now, in discussing the traces (*traces*), one relies on the teaching of the fundamental basis (*mūla*). The basis is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), while the traces are the eight phases [of a Buddha’s life]. Prior to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), there is no fundamental basis of the Dharma-body; therefore, one cannot argue that the basis is superior and the traces are inferior, for this would still entail a fault. Furthermore, one cannot argue that both the basis and the traces are equally superior.

If both the origin (*hon*) and the trace (*seki*) are sublime, or if the origin is sublime while the trace is inferior, these two phrases apply exclusively to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*myōkaku*). Since the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment is the ultimate position beyond which there is nothing higher, there can be no cases where the origin is inferior while the trace is sublime, nor where both the origin and the trace are inferior.

From the second dwelling upward, through to the stage of supreme enlightenment, all possess four permutations. When the second dwelling manifests as the first dwelling, the first dwelling is the trace while the original is high and the trace is low. When the second dwelling manifests as the third dwelling, the third dwelling is the trace while the original is low and the trace is high. When the second dwelling manifests as the second dwelling, it is both original and trace high when compared to the first dwelling, yet both original and trace low when compared to the third dwelling.

The current text precisely establishes that the fundamental is low while its traces are high. If one were to say that prior to the first stage there is nothing vertically indicated, taking the essence as the fundamental and the function as the trace, then both this fundamental and these traces would be low.
If one follows this intent, all Buddhas fully manifest their original nature.

Furthermore, because they have made vows, it is said that their lifespan is long and far-reaching within the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*); the actual lifespan of the first stage is likewise immeasurable. Thus, when it is said that they "make vows and speak of their lifespan," it means that by attaining the Dharma-body, one necessarily attains long life; when conditions arise and sentient beings' capacities ripen, they then fulfill their former vows, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, another interpretation of the 'original Buddha'": this refers to the body of wondrous enlightenment (miaojue), wherein its own essence and function are taken as the original and the trace. This is a statement in which both the original and the trace are exalted, lacking only the single phrase concerning the trace being low while the original is high.

Regarding the question, "What is the meaning of the 'Chapter on the Five Buddhas'? it is as explained in the extensive revelation of the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means), where it is stated regarding each of the five buddhas that they likewise, through immeasurable means, ultimately lead all beings to the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*). If this is so, then there is not a single buddha who does not reveal and manifest [this truth].

The meaning of the answer is that the Buddha likewise should not universally open up the provisional; the scripture’s statement that "all" refers only to those cases where the provisional is opened and revealed in order to emerge from the defiled land.

Furthermore, regarding the question, "If that is so, then by using the wondrous to refute the wondrous, the example would also have to be wondrous," since the preceding text used the fundamental wondrous to refute the phenomenal wondrous, the phenomenal wondrous becomes coarse.

From the phrase "it should also" onwards, the argument proceeds by challenging the subtle nature of that which has been refuted; since the refutation itself has become coarse, the ten coarse objects being refuted should likewise become subtle.

From the phrase "the object being refuted" onwards, he again uses the four abidings (*catur-vihāra*) as a further analogy to challenge: if that which is coarse—the object being refuted—can become subtle, then the afflictions of the four abidings, which are also objects being refuted, should likewise become subtle.

In the subsequent response, the difficulty regarding the four abidings is again cited to illustrate the initial difficulty; if one were to rely on the meaning of suddenness (*tun*), then the four abidings would themselves be wondrous, and it should be as you have asked.

"The phrase 'how much more so the wisdom of the four abidings' uses an analogy to resolve the initial objection: if even the coarse delusions of the four abidings can still be considered wondrous, how much more so the wisdom of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing—would these not be wondrous?"

The meaning of the subsequent question is as follows: after the original manifestation was accomplished, during the intervening period of descending traces, both the partial and the perfect, the provisional and the real, are equally termed "provisional. Because these are merely traces, they are all provisional.
Is "expedient means" (*upāya*) itself partial, such that it may all be termed "partial"? Next, the answer regarding the distinct meaning is that they are not comparable:

since phenomena (*dharma*) are fixed as being either in the fundamental or in the vestigial, they are fixed as either partial or perfect; the teaching (*śāsana*), however, is not so. When in the fundamental, both expedient and real are fundamental; because they are fundamental, they are real. When in the vestigial, both expedient and real are vestigial; because they are vestigial, they are termed expedient. This applies to the partial and the perfect, and even to essence and function (*tattva* and *vṛtti*).

The principle having been established: when referring to the fundamental essence (*tattva*), one speaks of essence and function; when referring to the manifested traces (*vyañjana*), both essence and function are employed. If the teaching refers to the fundamental essence, then both essence and function are real; if it refers to the manifested traces, then both essence and function are provisional. One should know that essence and function alike constitute this Dharma. By analogy, the same applies to phenomena and principle, principle and teaching, and teaching and practice. These may be understood accordingly.

Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The phenomena and principle within the fundamental [teaching] are first attained and thus considered subtle; the phenomena and principle within the provisional traces are only now attained and thus considered coarse. Other teachings, practices, and so forth may be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the four phrases: the "distinct" [teaching] involves the coarse stages prior to the grounds while realizing the Path as subtle; the "perfect" [teaching] is as the text describes.
As for "involving the subtle within the coarse," this is because it simultaneously encompasses the intermediate [teaching].
Furthermore, regarding the explanation: that which "carries both the coarse and the subtle" comes from the Shared [Teaching].
That which "both carries and does not carry" carries the stages prior to the [Bodhisattva] grounds but does not carry the Tripiṭaka.

That which "neither carries nor does not carry" neither carries the Tripiṭaka or the Shared [Teaching], nor does it not carry the Distinct [Teaching]; the same applies to the connection between the two teachings, as it neither carries the Three Piṭakas nor does it not carry the Shared [Teaching].

Regarding the third phrase among the five flavors: in the Vaipulya (fangdeng), the first three [periods] are "accompanied" while the last one is "unaccompanied"; the Prajñāpāramitā may be understood by analogy.
Regarding the fourth phrase: it is neither "accompanied" by the Zang and Tong, nor is it "unaccompanied" by the Bie.
Regarding the phrase "The question states that since the two types of coarseness are not the same," this asks about the *zàng* (Treasury) and *tōng* (Shared) vehicles.
In the response, the statement "Matters have degrees of depth and shallowness, etc. indicates that while the *tōng* [vehicle] is immediate (*jik*), the *zàng* [vehicle] is not immediate.
Regarding the phrase "Questioning whether the Separate [Vehicle] carries the Real [Teaching]," this asks about the distinction between the Separate and Perfect Teachings.
Both manifest the Middle Way, yet the Separate Vehicle carries it while the Perfect does not.

Next, regarding the question "Carrying both or one," etc., this also asks about the distinction between the Separate and Perfect Vehicles, taking the stages prior to the [Bodhisattva] grounds as "carrying both."

Next, regarding the section following "General Discussion" (*tōron*), although it does not directly answer the questions, it provides an extensive analysis; every single phrase therein is actually an answer, though the questions have been abbreviated.

As for the passage beginning with "Question: Regarding the *Honji*," there are six layers of *honji* and *suijaku* at the beginning of the fascicle; to which of these six layers does the present "Ten Subtleties" (*jūmyō*) belong?
Regarding the response that says "it is indeed," etc., this was already distinguished at the beginning of the fascicle; here it is asked again.

Why? At the outset, it was stated that the five layers of the *honji* (original ground) constitute the fundamental, while the intermediate [teachings] of today constitute the *shaku* (traces). Since the five pairs of the *honji* belong to the fundamental, one does not know how these five pairs correspond to the fundamental.
Therefore, he asks again.

The current answer is still somewhat ambiguous, merely stating that "the ten subtleties are discussed together. If this were the case, then phenomena and principle, principle and teaching, teaching and practice would be nothing other than the cause; and the provisional and the real, as well as essence and function, would be nothing other than the functions of the fruit, for the fruit must necessarily have an essence.

When applied, it immediately evokes supernatural powers and the preaching of the Dharma; those who are reached by this preaching of the Dharma become members of the retinue and receive benefit. Longevity and nirvana are likewise merely dharmas belonging to the fruit.
Therefore, they are not described separately, but are simply referred to as "discussed together.
In the seventh section, which judges the coarse and the subtle, there are two parts; first, they are judged by comparing the fundamental (ben) with the manifested traces (ji).
Next, the section beginning with "Furthermore, within the traces" uses the preceding six gates to provide a judgment. Regarding the initial passage:

if the provisional traces were not first revealed and clarified, and one merely judged them as coarse or subtle while asserting they are no different from what was realized in the fundamental [reality], how could one know that the subtlety within the traces does not equal the coarseness of the fundamental? This is because the judgment is not made based on the revelation of the provisional versus the ultimate or the relative versus the absolute; rather, it is discussed solely in terms of the long-distant actualization. Therefore, whether coarse or subtle, neither the intermediate nor the present [teachings] were previously attained. Consequently, the coarseness previously attained is also called "subtle," and the subtlety of the intermediate and present [teachings] likewise becomes "coarse."

Next, regarding the judgment based on six layers: having already completed the sequential synthesis of the preceding analysis—which merely opened up and revealed the distinctions between the long and short periods and so forth—one should further conduct a detailed judgment within that very opening and revealing of the long and short periods, etc., concerning the six gates of the provisional traces as coarse and the fundamental reality as subtle.
Within this, there are three parts:

first, the explanation; second, the illustration by analogy; and third, from "If one generates... onwards, it further clarifies the characteristics of the mutual manifestation and mutual fusion of the six gates of the original and the trace, as well as the inconceivable equality and so forth.
Within this, there are two parts: first, a brief explanation based on the pair of phenomena and principle; second, understanding the remaining five pairs by analogy.

Furthermore, regarding the terms "past" (*yi*) and "present" (*jin*): these refer to what was already attained in the past as the "root" (*ben*) and what is currently being practiced today as the "trace" (*ji*). Since each successive stage of the intermediate period contains the teachings of the five flavors, the four flavors and the Trace Gate are designated as the "past," while the revelation of the long-lasting life-span is designated as the "present. Thus, the distinction between "past" and "present" also involves the discussion of the coarse and the subtle across different eras.
Next, the clarification of the provisional and the real consists of three parts.

First, the provisional and the real are distinguished through the correspondence between the original and the manifested; herein, the provisional and real within the manifested stage are judged to be provisional, while both the provisional and real of the original ground are sublime because they have been accomplished for a long time.

Next, from "Furthermore" onwards, the three aspects of self-practice and so forth are again discussed by comparing the original (hon) and the manifested (jaku). Thus, the original is itself the other of the manifested, and the mutual relationship between the original and the manifested constitutes a single instance of self and other.

Third: From "Furthermore" onwards, the text again clarifies the identity of principle by assigning three meanings each to both the original (hon) and the trace (jaku). Regarding phenomena, one understands that within the original, the manifestation of the coarse is also subtle; whereas within the trace, the opening [of the provisional] and the abolition [of the real] remain coarse. In principle, however, there is neither coarseness nor subtlety.
The meaning of the initial passage is fully contained within the "Judgment on the Coarse and the Subtle"; therein, there are two parts:
first, the direct elucidation; second, from "The traces are provisional while the source is real" onwards, the elucidation of their mutual integration.
Second, because the principle is inconceivable, it is said that "the dharma-nature is neither ancient nor modern," and so forth.

Next, the passage beginning with "self" (*sva*) concerns the transformation of others within the fundamental [nature]; this too is called "wondrous. There should likewise be an inconceivable interpenetration (*yūnyō*), but its absence from the text is due to abbreviation. It should rather state: "The principle of dharma-nature is neither self nor other; though self and other differ, they are one in inconceivability."
The third section also has two parts:
first, the explanation; second, the integration and conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are again two parts:

Regarding the opening statement, "Furthermore, within the traces, the provisional is established based on the real," and so forth: although the intent behind establishing the provisional based on the real is to lead back to the real, many people take the provisional that was provisionally established to be the ultimate; thus, they fail to understand both.

If one discards the provisional to reveal the real, the intent lies in that which is discarded—the provisional. Because one initially wishes to discard it, this provisional is refuted as not being ultimate. Since the provisional consists of phenomenal dharmas that are easily understood by people, throughout the Buddha’s teachings prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, his intention was always directed toward the real; yet the followers of the two vehicles did not understand this from beginning to end, even as they failed to attain non-retrogression. When the time came to discard the provisional, he said, "You all, come and go; the place of treasure is near. Although everyone knew that the place of treasure was not there, this was like having already set out on a long journey from the very first moment of reaching the shore of treasure. Moreover, since they had already traveled three hundred *yojanas*, pointing to my fruition is itself pointing to that wondrous cause; therefore, it is said to be "easily fathomed."

Regarding the statement, “The *Avataṃsaka* clarifies non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) by primarily elucidating phenomena and numerical categories,” this is an illustration cited to explain the previous point concerning the ease with which provisional [teachings] may be fathomed.

All phenomena and dharmas are nothing other than provisional dispensations; for throughout the long eons, the Tathāgata has established skillful means for the sake of all sentient beings. Thus, once the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have been bestowed, they are all subsequently set aside. Since these provisional dispensations pertain to the realm of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is for the sake of those who are non-retrogressive that these phenomena are predominantly taught; this enables them to realize the principle of non-retrogression within those very phenomena.
