Furthermore, the stages of the non-retrogressive position differ in their levels of height. If one is in the non-retrogressive position prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), by merely hearing the enumeration of phenomena, one knows that phenomena are themselves principle; thus, by opening up the provisional to reveal the real, one enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) and attains the non-retrogression of mindfulness. Being able to realize that this very provisional is the true aspect (*dharmatā*), how could one seek the true aspect apart from this?
In order to counteract those who have regressed, it is said: "The integration of the first stage is as previously described.
Question:
What is the difference between the provisional and the ultimate in this eighth section compared to the judgment made in the seventh section?

Answer: Previously, the "Root" (ben) and "Trace" (ji) were used to distinguish between the coarse and the subtle, as well as through six gates; now, by means of the provisional and the real, as well as the self-practice and so forth, the provisional and the real are explained—namely, that the Root is the Real and the Trace is the Provisional, and that the self is the Root while the other is the Trace.

Furthermore, by interpreting "opening" (*kai*) and "revealing" (*ken*) as the provisional and the real, the provisional and real that consist in opening the traces to reveal the source are alone designated as the provisional and real within the source; therefore, the intent here is to clarify once more that the single principle is without difference.
Question:

In the ten wonders of the迹门 (Ji-men), within each individual wonder, every section first provides a provisional judgment (*pan*) and then an opening (*kai*). Why is it that in the present 本门 (Ben-men), there are only these categories of the coarse and the subtle, as well as the provisional and the real, which all seem to carry the intent of a judgment, yet lack a separate establishment of an "opening"?
Answer: This differs slightly in its intent from the Trace Gate (Ji-men). In the Trace Gate, once the definitive meaning has been established, it must necessarily be opened up. Why is this so?

As stated in the *Jian* (Judgment): "Whether in terms of teaching or flavor, the former is coarse and the latter is subtle. If [the three vehicles] were not opened up, people would claim that apart from the third and fourth [vehicles], there exist separately the Perfect [Vehicle] and the *amṛta* (clarified butter). Therefore, the opening of the three is itself the Perfect, and the fourth is itself the *amṛta*."

Now, the ten sections of the Present Teaching (Honmon) are not like this; whereas in the previous extensive explanation of the ten [sections of the Trace Teaching], each was explained through three meanings as the Trace, which—though recently established as having a different meaning—is considered "coarse. To sweep away the Trace and point toward the Origin (Honzon), their meaning is identical to the "wondrous" (Myō). Based on this, it already constitutes a judgment of the Opening (Kai) in terms of phenomena (ji); furthermore, each is said to be "inconceivable one" (fushigi-ichi), which again opens up all things in terms of principle (ri). Fearing that people might not understand, two further gates are separately established here to judge the preceding coarse and wondrous; this judgment is itself the opening. How much more so, since these two texts further open them up in terms of principle?
Question:
For what reason is there no opening of the principle in the Section on the Trace? Answer:
The initial opening based on the object (*viṣaya*) already concerns principle (*tattva*).
Furthermore, in the Trace Gate (*jia-men*), there are teachings that expound this principle; thus, if the teaching is opened, it signifies that the principle is opened.

Now, in this Fundamental Gate (*ben-men*), which concerns the person and phenomena, although the person and phenomena are opened, one must still open the principle. Because the realization of the fundamental and the trace differs, they are both described as the inconceivable one.

It should be understood that this concludes the general explanation from its beginning down to this point. If one sweeps away the traces to point to the fundamental source, this is an opening of the discussion based on phenomena (*dharma*). If, however, one employs inconceivable interpenetration, then phenomena open up to enter into principle (*li*). If one does not comprehend the purport of these ten gates, by what single principle could one crown them all?

Although the single principle is the same, the ten gates of phenomena are distinct; the one inconceivable reality and the ten wondrous aspects are eternally differentiated. That they are different yet not different—this is precisely what is meant by this.
The ninth section, explaining the benefits, has two parts:
first, the actual explanation of the benefits; second, the benefits of the propagation [of the teaching].
The initial text further has two parts:
First, the dual presentation; second, the dual explanation.
Within the explanation, there are two parts: first, the explanation itself; second, the comparative evaluation beginning with "If one discusses the true path.
The first part also has two sub-sections.
First is the explanation, followed by the conclusion beginning with "That is to say. The former [explanation] is further divided into two parts:
first, the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), and second, the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
The physical body [of the teaching] also has two parts:
first, hearing the Trace Gate; second, hearing the Origin Gate.
Within the initial hearing of the Trace Gate, there are further four sections:

First, the benefit within the ten profundities is clarified; second, the benefit within the six stages of identity is clarified; third, starting from "like Śāriputra," their types are briefly indicated; fourth, starting from "that is," it is concluded.
Regarding the first passage: it refers merely to the benefit derived from the retinue of the stage of practice through wisdom.
However, one must exercise careful discernment: since wisdom arises from explanation, it is obtained in its entirety;
yet, as for the wisdom that destroys delusions, it must be distinguished according to the fruit, and the same principle applies to the stages, which encompass both the profound and the shallow.

The retinue may attain [this state] at most for a single lifetime; practicing the meaning of not yet transcending the realms is not through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). As for the remaining [defilements], such as the failure to shatter ignorance (*avidyā*) along with the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃjñā-kleśa*), they are categorized according to their secondary delusions (*upakleśa*). Thus, the interpretation of their benefits is collectively considered a single, true benefit.

The meaning of the three dharmas belonging to the fruit can be extended to the cause; thus, according to the Śrāvaka vehicle, all would enter the first stage (*ādikṣānti*). Now, because we follow the ultimate fruit, it does not extend to the cause.
Next, regarding the primary section (*mūlaparivarta*), there are three parts:

first, clarifying the benefit of the ten wonders (*daśa-prakṛti-vaipulya*); second, the benefit of the six identities (*ṣaḍ-yukti*); third, clarifying the increase of the path and the decrease of birth.
Next, within the section on the benefits of the Dharma-body, there are three parts:

first, the clarification of the characteristics of the benefit; second, from "Why is this so? onwards, the clarification of the reason for the benefit; and third, from "Therefore, it is distinguished" onwards, the citation of scriptural evidence.
Next, regarding the section on "comparative evaluation" following the phrase "If one discusses," there are four parts:

first, a brief differentiation of similarities and differences; second, borrowing the Lesser Vehicle as an analogy starting from "It is like..."; third, differentiating the quantity and depth starting from "The preceding Trace Gate..."; and fourth, indicating the textual judgment of stages starting from "One should discern..."

The initial passage states: "If one discusses the true path, the two instances are not different; yet the functional application of provisional wisdom cannot be compared [to it]. This means that regarding the benefit obtained at both the Dharma-body stage of the Original Gate and the birth-body stage of the Trace Gate, the perfected principle realized is without depth or shallowness; therefore, it is said they are "not different."

How could one equate the stage of the first abode’s patience with the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) with the bodhisattvas of a single lifetime who possess the Dharma-body in the Root Chapter?
The second, third, and fourth [abodes] are as stated in the text.
Next, the benefits of the propagation are explained in two parts:
First is the formal explanation, followed by the resolution of doubts.

Within the formal explanation, the intent is to distinguish between the different modes of benefiting—latent and manifest—at two locations. First, regarding the statement that "the trace gate provides latent benefit," this refers only to bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) and not to entering a specific stage; therefore, it is termed "latent. This is as in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit" (*Punyaparikīrtana-parivarta*), which is the manifest mode.
Furthermore, the emergence from the earth to propagate the sutra also manifests further benefits.

Whether it be the various bodhisattvas who have reached this stage and received further benefit within the Trace Gate (*jimen*), those who newly receive benefit in the Essential Gate (*honmon*), or even those not included among these categories of beneficiaries, they all receive secret benefit; therefore, it is said that they "simultaneously obtain the benefits of the Trace Gate."
Next, in the section explaining the resolution of doubts, there are two parts: first, the doubt; second, the explanation.

Within the explanation, the phrase "awaiting the time" (*daiji*) refers to how, in the *Avataṃsaka*, one does not awaken until reaching the third stage of samādhi, and even within each of those stages, there is an awaiting of the time. For example, while at the side of the Buddha, no benefit was gained until one awaited [the presence of] Mañjuśrī and entered the room of Vimalakīrti; likewise, even after [reaching] nirvāṇa, one does not awaken until waiting for the time when a future Buddha appears in the world.

"Waiting for companions" refers, for example, to waiting for the five bhikṣus at the Deer Park; after delivering these five, he benefited beings through his teachings everywhere, as seen in the four great bodhisattvas in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, or Śāriputra, Maitreya, and others in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, or Mañjuśrī entering the sea to lead countless multitudes to the Buddha's presence, or Kāśyapa, King of Virtue, Siṃhanāda, and others in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Furthermore, it is as when the Buddha retained Jñānakūṭa to wait for Mañjuśrī, or when his emanations did not answer to wait for a future Buddha; it is also like the five hundred śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and bhikṣuṇīs mentioned in the "Chapter on Upholding," all of whom were waiting for their companions.

Furthermore, "waiting for the opportune time" refers, for example, to waiting until Mañjuśrī has finished answering questions, waiting until Maitreya has finished expressing his doubts, waiting until Mañjuśrī emerges from the Dragon Palace, or waiting until Gadgadasvara arrives from the east; all such instances constitute "waiting for the opportune time."

Thus we know that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas pervades all places; yet, when manifesting through the collective transformation of various bodhisattvas, it takes those bodhisattvas as its companions.

Following the two passages cited as evidence for the two gates of the Trace and the Origin, the one who propagates this Dharma is precisely the one who makes a vow to propagate this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* through both the gates of the Trace and the Origin.
Next, the contemplation of the mind has three parts:
first, the explanation; second, the citation of scriptural evidence; third, the conclusion on the benefits, beginning with the words "This is precisely...
The initial section further contains two parts:
First the object, then the contemplation.
Regarding the object, there are two parts:
first, that which cannot be contemplated; second, the clarification of that which can be contemplated.
There are two further points to be observed:
first, the establishment [of the position], and second, the explanation beginning with "What is it?
In the explanation, it says: "What is it?"
Regarding the passage from "The Buddha’s suchness is like the suchness of sentient beings" up to "the aspect of benefit," it is as stated in the sub-commentary below:
"May I swiftly attain a suchness equal to the Buddha’s suchness; may the lifespan of this teaching of suchness likewise be immeasurable."

To contemplate suchness in this manner—wherein suchness is itself the principle—is to give rise to contemplation upon hearing its name; this constitutes the practice of contemplation. Continuing until one ultimately achieves the Unsurpassed Way, it thus encompasses the six stages of "identity."
The contemplations are again threefold:
first, that which is not to be contemplated; second, from "My likeness" (*ātman-tathatā*) downward, that which is to be contemplated; third, from "I also vow" downward, the great vow.
Next, regarding the initial question in the section on critical analysis, it asks: what is the nature of their similarities and differences?

Regarding the answer concerning the three pairs and six phrases: the first two phrases are established in terms of the perfect principle (*yuanli*), where "name" and "meaning" stand in mutual relation because they are non-different.
The next two phrases concern the present title’s designation of "wondrous" (*miao*), which refutes the "greatness" (*da*) of the Hinayana;
and the *Dapin* (Large Sutra) title’s designation of "great," which refutes the "wondrous" of the Hinayana. These should also be understood in correspondence with the teachings (*jiao*) and so forth.

The third pair of phrases also corresponds to the "Small Exposition" (Kṣudraka-vibhaṅga), and they should likewise correspond to the "Teachings" (Śāsana) and so forth; this can be seen by reflecting upon it.
Next, the question regarding "the Great, the Sublime, and the Equal" is posed with reference to the first two of the preceding six phrases.

Regarding the section from "Next, the Question" to "Briefly Refuting It": the first part is the question, while the portion beginning with "Briefly" is the answer. Briefly speaking, both [the conditioned and the unconditioned] may be termed "permanent"; however, if one refutes them, there is only impermanence and nothing that can be called permanent. Even in the Hīnayāna, there are three types of unconditioned phenomena that are permanent; yet, from the perspective of the Mahāyāna—such as in the *Ratnagotravibhāga* (Treatise on the Jewel Nature)—the two vehicles still involve inversions such as regarding the impermanent as permanent. Although the names are the same, the underlying principles differ, and thus they are refuted. As for the statement "neither is this wondrous," since it was briefly termed "wondrous," the refutation reveals it to be impermanent; therefore, it is said of both: "Since it is impermanent, it is also not wondrous."
In the subsequent response, the answer is given merely as a provisional concession rather than a refutation.

From the phrase "Even granting this" (*zòngzhī*) onwards, the previous refutation is conceded; since there already exists the permanence of the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), yet it is further stated that their permanence is distinct, this constitutes a withdrawal of the concession, which is why it is called "distinct" (*yì*).

Next, regarding the phrase "furthermore, both": this means that both the Great and Small Vehicles are equally termed "constant," and the Small Vehicle should ultimately converge with the One Vehicle; this constitutes an objection based on the *Lotus Sūtra*.
In the response, there is likewise first agreement and subsequently a distinction.
Next, regarding the word "both": is it not the case that the coarse impermanence of the Mahāyāna does not accord [with the Hīnayāna]?
The meaning of the answer below under "example" is the same as before; the former is the same while the latter is different.
The section beginning with "how so? provides the explanation, which explains only the side of agreement, while the sense of the difference is as previously stated.
△ Next, the lotus is explained. First, the topical outline is presented; second, the explanation follows.
The explanation of the first section has three parts:
first, clarifying the analogy; second, clarifying the underlying principle; third, harmonizing the two explanations.

Regarding the initial statement that "the text of the seven similes is extensive," this is because many words and meanings are employed to fully manifest the provisional and the real; this differs from the lotus flower, which manifests the complete principle through only twelve characters.
Next, within the section on the Principle of the Dharma, there are three parts: the Dharma, the Parable, and the Application.
In the Parable, it says: "The spider draws out its silk and imitates this by weaving a web. The *Bowuzhi* states:

"Fuxi created the Eight Trigrams; Shennong created the Five Grains. Huodi, a subject of the Yellow Emperor, created the boat; Weifu, a subject of the Yellow Emperor, created the mortar and pestle; Chiyou, a subject during the time of the Emperor, created weapons and fire; the Yellow Emperor created the ceremonial caps and crowns; Rongcheng, a subject of the Yellow Emperor, created the calendar; Qibo, a subject of the Yellow Emperor, created medicine; Zhengshou, a subject of the Yellow Emperor, created mathematics. Gaoyao, a subject during the time of Shun, created the penal system; Jizhong created the chariot; Boyi created the well; Mengtian created the brush; Cai Lun created paper. As for the creator of the net, none has been seen. By this analogy, one can understand that all things created by the ancients were established according to principle."
Within the section on the "Convergence of the Three," there are two parts:
first, a brief clarification of the intent of the convergence; second, the actual convergence.
Within the latter, there are again two parts:
First the question is raised, followed by the answer.
Within the answer, there are three parts:

first, the explicit explanation of the application of the analogy; second, from "those of sharp faculties" onwards, the explanation of the reason for the analogy; third, from "in this way" onwards, the conclusion.
Next, the explanation of the ancient interpretations is divided into two parts:
first, the accounts of various masters; second, the account of Guangzhai.
The first section has two sub-divisions:
First, the three masters are discussed individually; next, all the masters are discussed collectively.
Regarding the first three masters, there is no refutation.
Within the subsequent group of masters, there are two parts:
First, the items are listed; next, the section beginning with "These ten and the six" provides a brief refutation.

Regarding the statement in the initial listing that "these ten are a partial expression of the meaning of the 'Excellence of Practice'": according to our school’s *Xingmiao* (Excellence of Practice), this practice fully encompasses unconditional compassion as well as precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Within wisdom, it includes the aspects of birth-and-death, non-arising, the immeasurable, and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*). This is not to mention the sequential and non-sequential modes, the increasing enumerations, and so forth, up to the revelation of the single mind wherein the five practices subsume all phenomena.

The initial statement that "Buddha-nature arises from conditions" does not include the unconditioned (anabhisamskāra), but refers only to the principle-nature (li-xing) manifesting through conditions.

Since the second passage also says it "arises from conditions," it comprehensively includes the adornment of merit and so forth; however, this merely implies the sense of eventually giving rise to the fruit of Buddhahood.

The third intention is that one merely knows that the nature of the mind does not transcend birth and death; as one has not yet engaged in cultivation, this is simply the beginning of the holy practice of precepts.

The fourth intention is that upon seeing [the truth], one enters the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and attains Buddhahood through the eight aspects; however, this wisdom of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-prajñā*) is still not ultimate.
The fifth meaning refers to the principle of progressing from the subtle to the manifest; thus, it is also included within the holy practice of precepts.

The sixth meaning clarifies that the non-duality of skillful means and reality is the fundamental essence of principle, which is precisely the fundamental essence of principle preceding the holy practice of precepts.
The seventh meaning is that the cause necessarily contains the fruit; since the fruit has not yet manifested, it still resides within the immeasurable practices prior to the ground.
The eighth meaning is that bodhisattvas of dull faculties as well as those of the two vehicles are still encompassed by the merit of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

As for the ninth meaning: the place of rebirth is still general and inclusive of expedient means; because one has merely entered the lotus pedestal through cultivation and has not yet reached ultimate perfection, this is why the unconditioned holy practice has not yet been completed.
If a single meaning is missing from the text, it may be understood by analogy with what precedes it.
Even the practice of the Sage himself was not yet exhaustive, let alone the practices of those such as the sick children of the Brahma-heaven;
thus we know that these ten are merely a small portion of the excellence of practice.
Regarding the statement, "These six parables are merely a fragment of the meaning within our school’s teaching on the 'Excellence of the Dharma,'" the first sense is as follows:
among the three [vehicles], the provisional still covers the real; it is merely the Dharma of the Hīnayāna.
The second intention refers merely to the opening of the provisional through the extensive Dharma.
The third intention refers merely to the manifest and the secret.
The fourth intention refers merely to the single intention of abolishing the provisional and establishing the real.
The fifth sense refers merely to that which is explained.

The sixth sense refers simply to the combined use of the provisional and the real; however, as it is manifest yet indeterminate, it encompasses only the four periods [of the Buddha’s teaching]. Since the eight teachings are not fully covered within these four periods, it is called the "partial sense."
Next, the refutation of the Guangzhai [School] consists of two parts:
first, the citation [of their position], and second, the refutation. Within the refutation, there are two sections:

First, the correct view is refuted; next, from the words "Furthermore, [I] assist," below, one borrows the opponent's own terminology to assist in revealing the correct view—this is to discuss the true nature (*dharmatā*) in terms of cause and effect.
Third, scriptures and treatises are cited, based on the original sūtras, the treatises, and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.
The initial citation of the treatise has three parts:

first, the listing of the seventeen names; second, the citation of the treatise’s explanation beginning with "the remaining names"; and third, the present explanation of the treatise’s intent beginning with "now, the explanation."
The initial listing of names is as in the text.

Next, in the *Vyākhyā*, it says: "The remaining names are not explained; if one now wishes to briefly understand the meaning among the seventeen names in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*, since the sixteenth is named 'Saddharmapuṇḍarīka,' one should know that all these names are simply different appellations for the 'Dharma-puṇḍarīka.'"

Furthermore, while other names consist merely of dharmas without metaphors, only this sublime Dharma presents both dharma and metaphor together; therefore, one should know that the sixteen names may likewise be applied by means of the lotus metaphor.

Regarding the term "wondrous Dharma" (Saddharma), there are three aspects each for its original and manifested dimensions (*honji* and *suijaku*), such that nothing else can serve as a metaphor; therefore, it is likened to the lotus flower.

The remaining sixteen names also encompass the original and manifested dimensions, each possessing three meanings. Because the various sutras of the manifested dimension do not fully express the Buddha’s intent, they are said to be "limited."
Now, in this sutra, there are three aspects—provisional, fundamental, and the opening and setting aside of teachings; since the Buddha’s intent is inexhaustible, it is called "immeasurable.
Moreover, after his attainment of enlightenment, he opened and set aside [teachings] in various places, which is why it is called the "Immeasurable Meaning" (Ananta-artha).
The term "most excellent" (parama) means "superior," which is synonymous with "wondrous"; it is also an expression of praise for both the provisional trace and the fundamental reality.
The term "vaipulya" (fangdeng) is also called "broad and level": it is named "broad" because the trace and the fundamental reality encompass all things;
it is named "level" because the single reality is non-dual.

Regarding the phrase "teaching the Dharma for Bodhisattvas": in the Trace Gate (Jikimon), the assembly is transformed entirely into bodhisattvas; in the Origin Gate (Honmon), they further advance and become exclusively bodhisattvas. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "If one hears this sutra, this is the practice of the bodhisattva path."

Regarding the phrase "protected by the Buddha's mindfulness": it means protecting the Real (the ultimate truth) by employing the Provisional; revealing the Real by opening up the Provisional; and protecting the Principle by abolishing the Provisional to reveal the Real. It is called "mindfulness" because of this protection, and "protection" because of this mindfulness; the relationship between the original and the trace is explained accordingly.

From the time he first attained enlightenment, he contemplated the use of the Real; because sentient beings lacked the capacity [to understand it], he sought expedient means and contemplated the use of the Provisional.
Once his expedients were sufficient, he contemplated the manifestation of the Real; when the One Reality was manifested, the provisional was set aside and the real remained.

The Buddha has long since attained perfection, yet sentient beings continue to wander in saṃsāra; therefore, he contemplates manifesting his traces to rescue these deluded followers. Although beings receive the Way, they remain confused by its immediate manifestations; thus, he intends to reveal the distant origin and set aside those immediate traces.

Regarding the "Buddha’s Secret Treasury": only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom it; it is called "secret" because it is not bestowed at improper times, and it is called a "treasury" because it contains all dharmas, and so forth.
Regarding "the treasury of all Buddhas": because there is no Buddha who does not enter the secret treasury of the three virtues, and because they exist equally therein, it is called "all."

Regarding "the secret syllables of all Buddhas": the provisional and the real are mutually identical, and the same applies to the fundamental and the manifested; because no one knows this, it is called "secret."
It is called "Esoteric" (Mi) because it takes "esoteric" as its name.

Regarding the phrase "giving birth to all Buddhas": opening the provisional to reveal the real allows one to recognize the source from which the Buddhas of the traces arise; opening the traces to reveal the fundamental allows one to recognize the source from which the Buddhas of the fundamental arise.
Regarding the phrase "the Buddha’s place of enlightenment," the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is precisely the site where both the provisional and fundamental Buddhas attain the Way.

Regarding the phrase "the Dharma wheel turned by the Buddha," the Dharma wheels turned by all Buddhas throughout the three periods of time do not transcend the two gates of the provisional and the real, or the fundamental and the provisional.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha’s solid śarīra," this sutra is itself the dharma-body as a complete, solid śarīra; it is not like the fragmentary śarīra of the physical body. Because it is truly and fundamentally immovable, it is called "solid."

Regarding the phrase "great skillful means" (*mahopāyakauśalya*): since "skillful means" is already a synonym for the lotus flower, why did the ancients judge that the "Skillful Means" chapter (*Upāya-paryāya*) was named after its ancient title? Scriptures such as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Kṣāranidhāna* (or *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa*) also contain chapters titled "Skillful Means. How could one conflate their meanings simply because the names are identical?

The intent of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and other such texts is that, in a hidden sense, they incorporate the three vehicles within their own essence; thus, they are termed "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Now, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the internal expedient means of the sole Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*) within its own essence; therefore, it is called "expedient means."
"Abiding in the primary meaning" refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as the very basis of abiding.
"Comprehending immeasurable names" means that in other sutras, even the provisional and the ultimate have not yet been mutually integrated, let alone the fundamental and the manifested.
Now, these two gates encompass everything without exception; as explained above, I have briefly delineated their general outlines.

Were one to discuss this exhaustively, each of the two meanings should be analyzed in contrast with [the other], and each of the six meanings should likewise be contrasted with them, while citing scriptural passages to verify each point individually. Only when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is translated and interpreted through these sixteen alternative names can it truly be said to accord with the intent of the text.
Regarding the second part, "Explaining the Meaning of the Three Liberations," there are two sections:
first, the formal explanation; second, the re-explanation beginning with "What is...
Entering [the path] is due to practice, while abiding and entering are designated as stages; this has already been briefly explained in the third fascicle within the "Excellence of the Object."
*Fahua Xuanyi Shiqian*, Fascicle Fifteen and Fascicle Sixteen,
composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhǎnrán.
Next, regarding the citation from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, it merely uses the lotus flower as a metaphorical dharma-gate;
thus, it is not yet sufficient to reveal its subtlety.
In the present text, we shall likewise provide an explanation based upon its aspect of cause and effect.

A latent doubt may arise as follows:

"In both instances, the *udumbara* can serve as a metaphor for this provisional and ultimate [teaching]. Furthermore, the word 'all' in the sutra universally encompasses all capacities, and the phrase 'appears but once in an age' is sufficient to signify the finality [of the teaching]. Why, then, is this not used as the metaphor, but instead the lotus?"

However, regarding the two instances in the sūtra where the udumbara flower is mentioned—first, "The udumbara flower appears but once in a long time," and second, "For example, all cherish and delight in the udumbara flower"—the present text mentions only that it "appears but once in a long time."
Furthermore, regarding the concluding phrase of one particular passage, ancient and modern commentators have explained:
"This resembles a lotus flower; therefore, it is used as a metaphor.
For this reason, it is precisely appropriate to employ the lotus flower, as it contains a complete analogy within its nature.
Regarding the use of metaphors for the Three Clarities (*trividyā*), there are two parts:

first, an exposition of the eight metaphors for *nirvāṇa* as discussed in general treatises; second, an explanation that the partial metaphors found in various sūtras and śāstras do not represent the ultimate truth.

As for the "eight metaphors of *nirvāṇa*," various sūtras and śāstras employ different metaphors, some of which are partial and others of which are universal. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states, there are eight kinds of metaphors: the concordant metaphor (*anuloma-upamā*), the discordant metaphor (*pratiloma-upamā*), the manifest metaphor (*sākṣāt-upamā*), the non-metaphor (*na-upamā*), the prior metaphor (*pūrva-upamā*), the subsequent metaphor (*paścāt-upamā*), the metaphor of both prior and subsequent (*pūrvapaścāt-upamā*), and the universal metaphor (*sarvatraga-upamā*).

The metaphorical comparison is exactly as explained in the sutra; thus, the fifth [chapter] states: "His countenance is as upright and beautiful as the full moon, and his white elephant is as fresh and pure as the Snowy Mountains. The full moon cannot be identical to the face, nor can the Snowy Mountains be identical to the white elephant. One cannot use a metaphor to represent true liberation, yet such metaphors are employed for the sake of sentient beings.
Now, in this case as well, it is impossible to illustrate the Sublime Dharma through metaphors; yet, for the sake of sentient beings, it is illustrated by means of the lotus flower.
In the subsequent section beginning with "Now, as for the flower," there are two parts within the formal explanation:

The first section also has two parts:
first, indicating the meaning of the preceding text; second, clarifying the intended meaning of the present analogy.
The full meaning of the first part is as presented in the text of the first fascicle.

Next, the section beginning with "Beginning and End" provides the conclusion: in the Trace Gate, giving is the beginning and opening is the end; in the Origin Gate, descending is the beginning and sweeping away is the end. Following this is the "majority analogy," which is actually a "complete analogy.

Now, although we do not say "complete" but rather "majority," this flower, while serving as an analogy for the ten meanings of both the fundamental and the provisional, cannot by any means serve as an adequate metaphor for such matters as cause and effect, self and other, long and short periods, and the timely [teachings], up to the wondrous essence of the true reality (dharmatā), the wondrous doctrine that grasps that essence, the functions of that essence, and the characteristics of the analytical distinctions among these three—essence, doctrine, and function. How could this flower possibly be used to illustrate them?
Since the principle is complete while the phenomena are incomplete, it is said to be "for the most part.
Within this, there are two further parts:

The initial passage briefly describes the characteristics of the two pervasive metaphors: the "Lion Dharma-gate" universally illustrates the great functions of the Tathāgata’s fruition, while the subsequent "Pārijāta Tree Dharma-gate" universally illustrates the practitioner’s progression from cause to fruition.

Now, the lotus alone can metaphorically represent the two preceding meanings: in terms of the Root Gate (Honmon), it signifies that the great function of the person of fruition is boundless, continuing incessantly from stage to stage and never ceasing; in terms of the Trace Gate (Jakumon), it is likened to the practitioner who, from cause to fruit, is ripened at every stage and enters the Perfect [Teaching] at every position.
Within this section, there are two parts:
first, two analogies are cited; second, from "Now likewise" onwards, the meaning is concluded to demonstrate their identity.
The intended meaning is as previously explained and can be understood through reflection.

Regarding the statement, "For example, the Dharma-gate of the Lion’s Roar," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 23, first enumerates the various species of lions, their physical characteristics, and the sounds of their roars; it then concludes by stating, "The Tathāgata-siṃha is likewise."
Born from the pure seeds of the six *pāramitās* and the four noble truths, dwelling in the great mountain valleys of *śamatha*,
with the head of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), cheeks gathered with all virtues, the wide eyes of untainted right view,
the gait of lustrous concentration and wisdom, high and broad eyebrows, and the white fangs of the four fearlessnesses.
The Benefit [of the Dharma] is his chin, firm and full through the Four Right Efforts; the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment are his even and closely set teeth;

the practice of the contemplation on impurity is his protruding red tongue; the cultivation of mindfulness and wisdom is his high-set ears; the eighteen unique qualities are the luster of his body hair; the three gates of liberation are the firm flesh of his body;
the three modes of manifestation are his straight spine; and the perfection of knowledge and conduct is his belly.

He does not manifest [the physical form]; his waist is slender through patience; he is far removed from the long tail [of ignorance]; he is established in the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*);
he knows the yawns of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); his mouth is the unimpeded liberation (*pratisaṃvid-vimukti*); he subdues all those of external paths and wrong views with his majesty;
and he awakens all sentient beings from the sleep of the Four Noble Truths (*catuḥsatya*), and so forth.

Regarding "the great sūtra on the Pārijātaka tree": among the twenty-seven sūtras of the *Vyūha* (Universal Simile) section, it uses the stages from the yellowing of the leaves to the full blossoming of the flower as a comprehensive metaphor for the Buddha’s disciples, from their initial renunciation of the world until their attainment of the fruits of the path.
The Sūtra says:

"In the Heaven of the Thirty-three there is a pārijātaka tree; its roots penetrate the earth to a depth of five yojanas, and its branches and leaves spread fifty yojanas in all directions. When the leaves ripen, they turn yellow."
When the devas see this, joy arises in their hearts, thinking: "These leaves will surely fall before long.
When the leaves have fallen, they again feel joy, thinking: "This branch will surely change color before long."
When the branches have changed color, he again feels joy, thinking: "This color will not last long; it will surely produce blisters.
Having seen this, he rejoices again, thinking: "These blisters will not last long; they will surely produce buds."
Having seen this, they rejoice again, thinking: "This bud will surely open before long.
When it opens, its fragrance will pervade fifty yojanas and its radiance will shine afar for eighty yojanas; at that time, the devas will spend the three months of summer enjoying themselves below."
My disciples are also like this. The yellowing of the leaves is a metaphor for the thought of renouncing the home;

the falling of the leaves is a metaphor for shaving the hair; the change in color is a metaphor for the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of fourfold motion); the appearance of blisters is a metaphor for the arousal of the bodhicitta; the beak is a metaphor for the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes who have seen their nature; the blossoming is a metaphor for attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; the fragrance is a metaphor for the innumerable sentient beings of the ten directions upholding the prohibitive precepts; and the light is a metaphor for the renown of the Tathāgata’s name pervading everywhere.
"The three months of summer are a metaphor for the three samādhis; the gods receiving pleasure is a metaphor for the Buddhas abiding in Great Nirvāṇa, which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure.

The first analogy illustrates the vastness of the objective realm, while the remaining nine are somewhat abbreviated. The preceding objective realms consist of six, which, when combined with the realm of non-truth, make seven;

here, too, all are fully illustrated by analogies. the exposition and the conclusion.

Within the first part: the external appearance, the internal nature, the substance as the essence, the power to generate desire, the activity of the various implements, the opening of the flower as the cause, the spreading of the filaments as the condition, the lotus seed as the fruit, the formation of the receptacle as the retribution, and the fact that the beginning and end do not differ, which constitutes the ultimate equality.
From the beginning to the end of the "Lotus," it concerns only the marks (lakṣaṇa) up to the retribution-body (vipākakāya).

Next, in the detailed explanation following the phrase "For example" (*tadyathā*), there are ten sections; each begins with a simile, followed by an application (*yoga*) to the teaching, and then an authoritative citation (*sūtra-pramāṇa*), and so forth.
In the initial explanation of the analogies, it is said that sentient beings possess all dharmas from beginningless time, just like a stone lotus.

The phrase "If black... and following explains the characteristics of the stone lotus; the phrase "At the beginning of the kalpa... and following explains the non-arising and non-ceasing within the aforementioned six lines. Since the principle and characteristics are spontaneous, it is called "without seed."
Flowing on until now, it neither increases nor decreases, and thus is not extinguished.
The section beginning with "All" below serves as the application of the analogy;

the text is abbreviated. "Not stained by adventitious dust" applies to the first phrase; "the layering of birth and death" below applies to the second phrase. Following the momentum of the phrasing, one then applies [the concepts of] being neither square nor round: because it is square, it abides; because it is round, it moves.

Now, that which accords with the intended meaning does not abide because it is not square, and does not move because it is not round; thus, it neither abides in birth-and-death nor moves within birth-and-death. Because it does not abide, it is not extinguished; because it does not move, it is not born.
Next, regarding the explanation of "nature" (*dhātu*), the first part follows the text as it stands.

Next, it says "the wisdom-vow is not lost," and subsequently mentions "afflictions. These two meanings—namely, the non-loss of the wisdom-vow mentioned previously and the presence of afflictions—appear somewhat contradictory, yet together they constitute this very nature.

Wisdom and vows are the seeds planted in the past, while afflictions are the inherent nature (*liju*). Thus, although one is said to abide amidst delusion, the essence of those delusions is entirely [wisdom].
The passage beginning with "Furthermore, all... further clarifies that which is attained through cultivation; because there exists the nature of what is yet to be realized, *prajñā* can arise.

Next, in explaining the four virtues within the essence, these are treated as the four subtle elements (*tanmātra*); they are unmoved by birth and death, yet their rational nature remains indestructible. This interpretation of the intent of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* follows the first commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
Next, in explaining the powers (*bala*), four propositions are combined. The section beginning with "Like a lion" provides a further analogy for his exceedingly great courage and valor.

Next, regarding the citation of the sutra: "moving through boundless birth-and-death" is like the vital breath that grows and develops; "shattering the wheel of existence from time immemorial" is like the function of a drill boring through skin. Here, "existence" refers to the cause and effect of the twenty-five states of existence, which revolve like a wheel.
The section on "Jambudvīpa" below provides scriptural evidence for the ability to generate the bodhicitta.

In explaining the process of its formation: "black skin" is like ignorance (*avidyā*); "multitude of virtues" is like internal endowment; "generating the mind" is like the desire to arise; "freedom from delusion" is like certainty; "compassion" clarifies the characteristics of generating the mind; and "accomplishment" is like the final step. From the root and stem to the final step, and from the initial generation of the mind to the ultimate fruit—it is thus.
Next, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* is cited to verify the beginning and the end.
Next, the "Thus" (*evam*) is explained; the application of the metaphors within the causal section, where each element is paired with its respective simile, is complete in the text.
Finally, the citation from the sūtra serves merely to verify that the aforementioned true cause is like a flower abiding in space.
Next, this should also be explained generally within the context of the twelve links of dependent origination; therefore, it is said, "it is explained generally as above.
Now, to briefly explain the general in relation to the specific, the aforementioned eight characters refer directly to ignorance (*avidyā*).
From the "Parable of the Four Truths" onward, although the phrasing is general and pervasive, it can be seen through careful examination.
Next, regarding the nine parables below, although the text is general and pervasive, the essential meaning is fully contained therein.

Regarding the fact that while the initial statement speaks of "wondrous wisdom," the middle section mentions only "three wisdoms": this is simply because the three wisdoms are used to subsume the twenty wisdoms, and thus the intended meaning is already largely exhausted; moreover, a single mind is further established to correspond with the preceding [categories] as a sequential progression.

Next, regarding the mention of the stages from the desire realm concentration up to the fourth dhyāna within the section on the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), this is explained by way of illustration based on the stage of subduing delusions; it does not mean that those in the five grades must necessarily cultivate mundane dhyāna.
Regarding the phrase "opening and blooming according to the sun": both white lotuses and blue lotuses open due to the sun.

Some say that white lotuses open because of the sun and blue lotuses because of the moon; thus, among the devas, the opening and closing of flowers is used to represent day and night, while the sleeping and rising of dragons represents spring and autumn.

Regarding the phrase "like drifting silk threads and thin mists": when one looks at a lotus pond from downwind toward another person's pond, the lotuses, grasses, and other vegetation atop the water appear as if they were made of drifting silk threads.
Furthermore, that which resembles thin mist is this very lotus transferred into another person’s pond.

This account has been passed down through ancient customs and is universally acknowledged; even the various subtle meanings within the original text can be understood thereby. Were it not for the Great Master’s wondrous realization, how could he have used these pervasive metaphors to illustrate both the fundamental and the manifested?
△ The preceding section has concluded the explanation of the individual names.

These individual names constitute a title that combines both the Dharma and a metaphor; however, when ancient scholars explained the titles of various sutras, some followed only the person, such as the *Ugra-paripṛcchā* (The Questions of the Householder Ugra), while others followed only the Dharma, such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
Some [interpretations] proceed from the perspective of person and dharma, such as the *Renwang banruo*;
yet how could merely making such a statement reveal the profound significance underlying the name?

Consider, for instance, how our own school explains the two characters "Sublime Dharma" (*miaofa*): they occupy over two hundred sheets of paper, encompassing far more than just person and dharma, or dharma and analogy.
Even with such an exegesis, I fear it may not fully exhaust the profound purport of the sutra.

Furthermore, other sutras have little bearing on the specific needs of this audience; thus, in interpreting this particular sutra, one must not proceed with superficiality. For this reason, the Master has been earnest and insistent time and again; these elaborations are certainly not superfluous flourishes, but rather arise from a sense of necessity.
This section has two parts:
first, a brief re-examination of the specific names; second, the formal explanation.

Regarding the first part, the term "Hu-yin" (Hu-sounds) was used because, since ancient times, before scholarly debates had arisen, anything coming from the West was referred to as "Hu. It should actually be called "Fan-yin" (Sanskrit sounds), for it originated from the lineage of Brahmā and thus constitutes both the Sanskrit language and the Sanskrit script.
The account of Brahmā’s initial descent is fully detailed in the commentaries (*shu*) and the seventh fascicle of the *Zhi guan chao*.

The art of writing in this land originally had no beginning; it was merely established by those of great authority (*daquan*) according to the customs of their respective regions. Thus, when Cangjie first observed bird tracks, the *Gantong zhuan* states: "Cangjie built the Writing Terrace, also known as the Gao-si Terrace.
There was a man surnamed Gao who, along with his three brothers—four brothers in total—built this terrace, hence it was named Gao-si Terrace; it was there that Cangjie created the script."
Some say this was the Dharma hall where Kāśyapa Buddha preached the Dharma; thus we know that Kāśyapa Buddha secretly transformed beings in this land.
Next, in the formal explanation, one first lists how those sounds differ in their lightness and heaviness, and whether they have translations or not, which is not fixed in this region.
Regarding the terms "Chu" and "Xia": Jing-hua (the capital) is called Xia, while Huai-nan is called Chu; though their pronunciations and terminology differ, what they signify is no different.
It is the same with those lands: although they share the same Sanskrit sounds, there are slight differences in the weight [of vowels and consonants] across various countries.
Next, within the opening of the chapter, there is the listing of the sections and their explanation.
Regarding the initial statement that "there is no equivalent translation," this is further divided into two parts:
first, the listing of those for which there is no translation; second, the exposition of the five meanings.
The initial section has two parts:
first, establishing that there is no equivalent translation; second, recounting the interpretations of others.
Since those interpretations are not entirely correct, it is necessary to open this up into five sections; all five sections follow the intent of the *Abhidharma* and the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.
Within this, there are again three parts:
the heading, the enumeration, and the explanation.
In the enumeration, first the [other] schools are listed, followed by the present school; its meaning is expanded into three sections to explain five points.

The explanation consists of two parts: first, the formal explanation of the five meanings; second, the explanation of the etymological definitions. The first part further consists of two sections: 1. The formal explanation of the five meanings. 2. The explanation of the etymological definitions. Regarding the first section, there are again two parts: [the explanation of the five meanings and the explanation of the etymological definitions]. As for the first of these:
First the explanation, then the conclusion.
The initial section consists of five parts; regarding the first, the explanation of "the Dharma-fundamentally possesses three meanings," there are further two sub-sections:
first, an itemized explanation, and second, a synthesis into a dharma-gate.
The initial section also has two parts: first, a general explanation; second, a specific explanation.
Regarding what is called "general," the sutra is the foundation of all dharmas.
Following the section on "worlds" below, the specific explanation also has two parts:
First, a brief response; second, an extensive explanation.
Within the extensive explanation, there are three parts:
first, clarifying that the Buddha’s words take the Buddha’s own words as their basis.
Next, from "If later" onwards, it clarifies that the Buddha’s sūtras are the foundation of the treatise;

third, from "Various non-Buddhists" onwards, it clarifies the refutation of non-Buddhists who lack the foundation of the Buddha’s sūtras, and therefore their fundamental doctrine cannot be established.

The initial statement regarding "whether general or specific" refers to the general and specific aspects of a single sutra, the general and specific aspects of various sutras, and the general and specific aspects of various teachings.
The phrase "Therefore, the sutra... and following cites scriptural evidence as the basis for the teaching.
Regarding the statement, "Each individual sūtra has immeasurable sūtras as its retinue," the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Avataṃsaka*, the "Inconceivable" (*Acintya*), says:

"According to the faculties, natures, and conducts [of beings], it extensively expounds unspeakably many billions of nayutas of sūtras; each and every sūtra is good in the beginning, middle, and end, giving birth to all bodies of phrases and bodies of flavor."

Furthermore, the thirty-sixth [chapter] states: "All Buddhas, within a single body, manifest as many heads as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. Each head manifests as many tongues as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. Each tongue produces as many sounds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. Each sound produces as many sūtras as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. Each sūtra explains as many dharmas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers. Each dharma explains as many sentence-bodies (*padakāya*), flavor-bodies (*rasakāya*), and dharmas of sentences and flavors as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers; these sentences and flavors are called their retinue."
"The retinue [of the Buddha] merely follows the categories of the Dharma as found in those sūtras.

Next, regarding the statement in the *Yìběn* (Original Meaning) that "one seeks one phrase to express one meaning," etc., it is as stated in the thirty-first fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*: "In response to Kāśyapa’s question regarding whether the roots of goodness of icchantikas are indeterminate—being sometimes severed and sometimes not severed—Kāśyapa further asked:
'For what reason, World-Honored One, do you speak of them as being indeterminate?'"
The Buddha said:
"It is like medical prescriptions, all of which are for the purpose of curing illness.

Sometimes, under a single name, one may explain immeasurable names; for example, the Great Nirvāṇa is also called non-arising, non-emergence, non-action, refuge, dwelling-place, liberation, lamp-light, the other shore, fearlessness, and so forth."
There are cases where a single meaning is expressed by immeasurable names, such as the Lord Śakra, who is named Kauśika, Vāsava, Maghavan, Indra, Sahasranetra, Śacīpati, Vajraśikhara, and so forth.
There are also cases where immeasurable meanings are expressed by immeasurable names, such as the various synonyms for the Buddha or the Tathāgata.

Within the initial explanation, the first citation from the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* establishes that the very foundation of the First Vehicle constitutes the essence of the vehicle.

Next, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* explains the meaning of the vehicle (*yāna*) through a sequential interdependence: True Suchness (*tathatā*) occupies the first position as the very basis of the vehicle;

this "basis" is its essence (*svabhāva*). Next, within the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are three different points: first, regarding the cause of the vehicle, it takes the "basis" as its cause; "cause" here refers to True Suchness, which is the essence of the vehicle.

Next, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* states that "concealment and manifestation" refers to the fact that the equal *dharmakāya* is called "concealed" because it remains hidden within the *saṃkleśas*, whereas *nirvāṇa* is "manifested" because it has already been fully perfected.
Although there are manifestations that appear and disappear, none of them fail to constitute the essence of the Sūtra.
Next is the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* (Twelve Gates Treatise); the fundamental basis of the First Vehicle is precisely this essence.

Regarding the term "master of the vehicle" (*yāna-svāmin*): it is because of the white ox that one is enabled to reach the destination, and thus it is called the "master"; therefore, the function of the master is not taken as the essence of the vehicle itself.
Next, regarding the discussion on the essence and intention, there are four parts:

first, the initial inquiry; second, from "The Commentary" onwards, citing the treatise to clarify the essence and intention; third, from "For what reason" onwards, resolving doubts; and fourth, from "This small and great" onwards, the conclusion.
Regarding the subsequent passage from "If there is impermanence" up to "the three seals of the Dharma," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 20, states:
"All phenomena are impermanent; all phenomena are without self; nirvāṇa is quiescent extinction."
Question: Why is it that within the state of quiescent extinction (*śānti*) one speaks of only "one" and not "many"? Answer:
The first seal explains the five aggregates; the second seal explains that all things are without self; the third seal is called "nirvāṇa" because it is the fruit.
If one speaks of impermanence, it destroys the "mine-ness" of external five desires.
If one speaks of non-self, it destroys the internal self.
Because the notions of "self" and "mine" are destroyed, this is the quiescence of nirvana.

When a practitioner contemplates impermanence, they give rise to weary detachment; yet, once they have become weary of suffering, they may still harbor attachment to the subject who contemplates. Therefore, there is a second contemplation of non-self.

When one investigates that which is capable of observation until it can no longer be apprehended, all phenomena are found to have no basis of support; they simply return to quiescence. For this reason, it is called the Seal of Quiescence.
Question:

In the Mahāyāna, all phenomena are non-arising, characterized by a single mark which is the markless. How is it that within this [teaching], it is said that all phenomena are selfless and impermanent, termed the "Seals of the Dharma"? How can these two modes of teaching not be mutually contradictory?

Answer: Contemplating impermanence is precisely the contemplation of the causes and conditions of emptiness. It is just as when one contemplates that form is impermanent from moment to moment, one thereby knows it to be empty: because past form has disintegrated, it cannot be seen and thus lacks the characteristic of form;
because future form has not yet arisen, being without action or function, it cannot be seen and thus lacks the characteristic of form.
Because the present does not abide, it cannot be seen and cannot be conceptualized; therefore, it has no form or characteristics (*nimitta*).

Because it lacks form and characteristics, it is empty and devoid of arising and ceasing. Non-arising and ceasing and arising and ceasing are in fact one and the same; there is only the difference between an extensive and an abbreviated explanation.
Question:
Since the Mahāyāna speaks of a single true reality (ekasatyalakṣaṇa), the Śrāvaka teachings should likewise speak of the dharma of the single true reality.
Answer:
Within the Śrāvaka teachings, there are three seals of the Dharma; these are explained extensively as four and briefly as one.

Impermanence constitutes the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of the Origin; selflessness constitutes the Truth of the Path; and the quiescent extinction of Nirvāṇa constitutes the Truth of Cessation. Therefore, in the Mahāyāna, it is taught that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, possessing a single characteristic which is the absence of characteristics. This absence of characteristics is precisely the quiescent extinction of Nirvāṇa.

The treatise states: "Regarding the phrase 'clarifying the Dharma-seals within the Mahāyāna,' these were taught in the common sections prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; since the number of Dharma-seals in the Hīnayāna is likewise different, they must be carefully distinguished."
If this sutra alone clarifies the true nature (*dharmatā*) as the single Dharma-seal, it is therefore necessary to investigate and distinguish [its meaning].
Regarding the third section, which correctly reveals the essence, there are three parts:
first, an exposition based on the dharmas; second, an illustration by means of analogies; and third, an exposition based on various triads of dharmas.
The first section has three parts:
first, indicating the essence; second, distinguishing it by means of the three tracks (*triyāna*); third, distinguishing it through a comprehensive examination of all wondrous aspects.
Within this, there are further two parts:
First, there was an extensive discussion regarding the objects (*viṣaya*); next, there was a brief indication of the remaining nine excellences.
Question:

In the previous section on the excellence of wisdom and practice, all instances were distinguished by the statement, "The object is the essence, which is the Dharmakāya; wisdom and practice are the thesis, which is the function. Why, then, is each of these objects distinguished once again here?
Answer:

In general discourse, when revealing the provisional to manifest the real, all dharmas are of the same essence as that which follows; however, in this instance, we are selecting the provisional and the real in contrast to demonstrate their essential characteristics, and for this reason, they are distinguished.
Next, the section on analogies consists of two parts:
the analogy and the conclusion.
Within the analogy, there are two further parts:
The analogy and its application are presented in three parts within the initial section on the pillars and beams:

first, the direct analogy for the substance; second, the analogy for the function of that substance, beginning with "If the house..."; and third, the citation of the *Śāstra*, beginning with "The *Śāstra*..."
The first analogy consists of two parts: first the analogy, followed by the application.

Regarding the initial passage from "not the beam" to "the emptiness within the house": emptiness is used as an analogy for the essence (*tattva*), while the house is an analogy for the thesis (*pakṣa*). Emptiness is that which is apprehended (*grāhya*), and the house is that which apprehends (*grāhaka*). While the apprehending subject may be manifold, emptiness cannot be manifold; the apprehended object is the essence, and the essence cannot be manifold; the apprehending subject is the thesis, and the thesis consists of cause and effect, and is therefore not one.
Next, regarding the analogy of “the sun and moon being the warp of heaven” and so forth, this is a further citation of analogies for clarification.

Heaven takes the sun and moon as its warp; the earth takes the four seas as its weft. The sun and moon revolve completely throughout the heavens; while there may be two suns and moons, there cannot be two heavens.

Regarding the phrase "the public minister assists the sovereign": "public" refers to the beginning of the five ranks; within these five ranks, all ministers together assist the sovereign. While the five ranks may be numerous, the sovereign cannot be many.
Regarding the term "the five ranks," it refers to the Gong, Hou, Bo, Zi, and Nan.
The Gong signifies "correctness"; he should serve as the correct exemplar for the King in practicing the Way of Heaven.
The Hou signifies "waiting"; he should serve as the King's sentinel for extraordinary events.
The "Bai" (elder) means one who leads; he should lead the people by governing them for the sake of the King.
The "Zi" (son) means one who is compassionate; he should love the people as a son of the King.
The "Nan" (male) means one who takes responsibility; he should fulfill his duties and manage affairs for the King.
The combined text is very concise; it may be understood by referring to what precedes.
Section Four, "Citing Scriptural Evidence," has two parts:
first, the actual citation of evidence; second, from "Therefore we know" onwards, the summary of the meaning.
Next, the extensive refutation of the false is divided into two parts:
first, the statement of the purpose; second, the extensive refutation itself.
This section consists of six sub-parts:
The chapter is divided into sections for exposition.
Within the exposition, there are first two parts concerning ordinary beings:
first, a general enumeration; second, an explanation.
The first section has two parts:
first, the enumeration; second, the conclusion.

Regarding the meaning of the first part: why is it that while the text primarily distinguishes [the practitioner] from ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), it also simultaneously distinguishes them from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and followers of the Hīnayāna?
Answer: This is said by way of comparison.
If even those outside [the Buddhist path] and the followers of the Lesser Vehicle do not possess reality, how much less so the ordinary persons with dull faculties?
The subsequent explanation has two parts:
first, clarifying the worldly and evil; second, from "If [it were] Zhou and Kong" onwards, clarifying the worldly and pure-and-recteous.
The first section has two parts:
First the explanation, then the conclusion.
Within the explanation there are three parts:
first, a brief judgment; second, the "or" section on the characteristics; third, the "internally" section clarifying the faults.

The first part is as stated in the text. The subsequent passage concerns practice; regarding the summary that says, "Or [one] uses a skull filled with excrement before a multitude of people," and so forth—these are all things that dull-witted ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) with heavy fetters (*dauṣṭhulya*) are fully capable of doing. However, those with sharp-witted externalists (*tīrthika*) each add their own objects of veneration, sectarian tenets, and so on, up to supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and the *Veda*. As for these ordinary beings, the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"There are two kinds of madness: the first is that which everyone knows to be mad; the second is the evil and perverse self-nudity, which others do not recognize as madness."
For example, there was once a Dharma Master in South India who sat upon a high seat to preach the Five Precepts to a king. Many non-Buddhists were present in the assembly listening to the Dharma.
At that time, the king posed this challenge:
"If you say that giving alcohol or drinking it oneself leads to madness and folly, why is it that nowadays those who are mad and foolish are so few, while those with right view are so many?"
The various non-Buddhists said:
"Excellent, excellent!
This challenge is most profound; this shaven-headed one on his high seat will certainly be unable to answer it."
For the sake of the king's benefit, the Dharma Master pointed toward the various non-Buddhist practitioners with his finger and spoke of other matters.
The non-Buddhists said to the king:
"This question was extremely profound, yet he could not answer it; out of shame for his own ignorance, he spoke of other matters instead."
The King said to the non-Buddhists:
"When the one on the high seat finished his reply, he did not speak further out of consideration for you.

Previously, when he pointed at you and said you were no less than madmen, it was true: you smear your bodies with ashes, go about naked without shame, eat excrement from human skulls, pluck out your hair and lie upon thorns, hang yourselves upside down to smoke your noses, enter the water in winter, and roast yourselves by fire in summer—all of these are the signs of madness."
Furthermore, you say that selling meat or selling salt constitutes a violation of the Dharma;

yet, when one receives a cow as a gift at a sacrifice to the gods and sells it immediately, you say this accords with the Dharma. Since the cow is indeed meat, you are a person who is deluded and confused.
"The Dharma Master protects you and does not speak of it.
Furthermore, regarding the practice, this is the same as for those of dull faculties.
As for "the afternoon meal" (*pū-si*), the dictionary states it is the "meal of the *shen* hour."
Furthermore, the *Chuci* says, "He fed on its dregs and husks," which refers to taking food.
"Gué" (譎) means expedient deception.
Duke Huan of Qi was upright and not gué; "gué-gui" (譎詭) refers to strange and extraordinary transformations.
Next, within the mundane True Dharma, there are again three parts:
first, a general explanation; second, citations from the sutras; and third, a concluding refutation.
Taken as a whole, these do not transcend the realms of humans and devas.

Regarding the phrase "the scriptures of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius": the Duke of Zhou established the rites, and Confucius edited the Odes; "scriptures" refers to the Five Classics, the Seven Classics, the Nine Classics, and so forth.
"Ji" (archives) refers to the "fun ji" (burial archives), which are the "Three Funs.
The Three Funs are the books of the Three Sovereigns.
"Dian" (canons) refers to the "Five Dian," which are the books of the Five Emperors.
In ancient times, characters such as "book" (書), "simplification" (簡), "ancient records" (故籍), and "chapter" (篇) all contained the radical for bamboo.
"Methods of governance" refers to the principles for governing the family and the state, which consist of loyalty and filial piety.

"Ritual laws" include works such as the Three Rites (*Sanli*); "military arts" include works such as the Six Strategies (*Liutao*); "medical arts" include works such as those of Shen Nong; and "astronomy" refers to Confucius’s *Threefold Preparedness for Divination*, through which he knew the celestial phenomena above, human affairs in between, and the geography below.

Regarding the "Eight Trigrams" (Bagua): East is Zhen, West is Dui, South is Li, North is Kan, Northwest is Qian, Southwest is Kun, Southeast is Xun, and Northeast is Gen. Each trigram gives rise to seven others; seven times eight makes fifty-six, which, when combined with the eight pure trigrams, total sixty-four trigrams.
The various hexagrams, their images, and their judgments cannot be fully exhausted here; those skilled in divination can know all things through them.
"The Five Elements" are as recorded in the sixth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
"Relatives" refers to the six types of kin—namely, parents, siblings, wife, and children—each having their own respective kin.
"She" (the local altar) refers to Hou Tu (the Lord of the Earth), and "Ji" (the grain deity) refers to Hou Ji; this is roughly as explained in the sixth and tenth records of the *Zhi Guan*.

Without parents, one cannot be born; without teachers and elders, one cannot achieve completion; without a sovereign, one cannot attain honor. In the life of a person, these three matters are of equal importance. When the state is secure, the family is secure; when the family is secure, one can practice filial piety. Therefore, one must first ensure the security of the state.

Regarding the phrase "birds have no leisure to perch" and so forth: if one follows the Confucian tradition, nets and traps are not set until the otters have performed their sacrifice, and hunting is not undertaken until the jackals have performed theirs; the otters sacrifice in the second month and the jackals in the eighth. Thus, one eliminates extravagance and excess, just as King Tang removed the nets from three sides of his hunting grounds.
In ancient times, nets were spread across the four directions; thus, the incantator said:
"The four quarters are boundless, yet all shall enter my net. Therefore, it is said that "the birds have no leisure to perch."
Tang removed the nets from three sides, yet the one who offered prayers said:
"May those who violate the mandate fall into my net.
As for the phrase "oxen and horses turn inward," it means that if one follows the laws of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, oxen and horses will naturally return [to their proper place].
If even worldly phenomena can produce such responses, how much more so those that transcend the world?
Zhang Ling was swallowed by a giant python, and Ji Kang was slandered by Zhong Hui; thus, the accounts in the records and biographies claiming they attained immortality are erroneous.
Thus we know that in this land there can be no immortal arts; how could one achieve flight and ascension by consuming numinous fungi or swallowing jade-essence?

Therefore, the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of the Western Land do not manifest apart from meditation (*dhyāna*); hence, both [the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya* and its commentary] conclude by stating: "Discourse on craving belongs to the dull defilements."
"Discourse" (lun) refers to that which is composed by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Next, regarding the external [discourses], they are categorized into two parts:
first, a general account of their unreality; second, from "If this... onwards, a specific presentation of their characteristics.
The first part is as stated in the text.
The second part is divided into two sections: first, this land; second, the Western land.
The first section also has two parts: first, clarifying the characteristics of the views; second, from "It is simply... onwards, the conclusion and refutation.

Within the refutation, the statement "it does not go beyond the four simple propositions" means that those who calculate [the self] as being "true of itself" still belong to the category of existence, while those who calculate it as being "spontaneous" still belong to the category of non-existence.
Regarding the term "even granting" (*zhòng*), if one speaks from the perspective of concession, it is truly impossible for [the fault] to arise.
Furthermore, within the section on the Western Region, there are also two parts:
first, clarifying the perceived signs; second, the refutation.
Regarding the initial statement, "The power of the non-Buddhist treatises caused Li Chang to accept the challenge," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 18, states:
"The brahmins of Vaiśālī and others offered a great reward for their jewels, commissioning them to debate with the Buddha."
Having been hired, he composed the *Pañcaśata-praśna* that very night; together with Li Chang, he went to the Buddha’s dwelling and asked the Buddha:
"Is there one ultimate path, or are there many ultimate paths?"
The Buddha said:
"There is but one ultimate path; there are no many.
The Brahmin said:
The various teachings each claim to possess the ultimate path.
The Buddha said:
"Though they are many, none of them is ultimate."
Why is this? Because all [other views] are based on false attachments, they are not ultimate.
The Buddha said:
"Has the brahmin Mṛgaśiras attained the Way?
He replied,
"Among all paths, he is the foremost."
At that time, the bhikṣu Mṛgaśīrṣa was fanning the Buddha from behind. The Buddha asked the brahmins, "Do you recognize him?
The brahmins replied:
Śrīvidyutprabha felt shame and bowed his head.
The Buddha spoke a verse, saying:
Each person claims their own view to be ultimate; yet if they harbor self-attachment, each will deem the other wrong. All such positions are not ultimate.
When such people enter into debate and clarify the principles of meaning, they each find fault with one another, harboring sorrow over defeat and joy over victory.
The victor falls into the pit of arrogance; the vanquished plunges into the prison of sorrow. Therefore, the wise do not fall into these two states.
Know this through the power of reasoning: among the teachings of my disciples, there is neither falsehood nor absolute truth. What dharma do you seek?
"You wish to refute my doctrine, but such a thing can never be; the All-Knowing One is invincible, and you will only bring about your own destruction.

Regarding the account of Dīrghanakha, as recorded in the fifth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it is fully contained within the categories of the view of non-existence (*nāstika-dṛṣṭi*), the view of both existence and non-existence (*ubhayatobhāva-dṛṣṭi*), the view of neither existence nor non-existence (*anubhayatobhāva-dṛṣṭi*), and the view that transcends words (*avyapadeśya-dṛṣṭi*); because the views held by those non-Buddhist outsiders are so skillfully formulated, they are subsumed under many such categories.
Next, the refutation of the middle [position] has three parts: first, a general refutation; second, a sequential refutation of each clause beginning with "Or at times"; and third, citing evidence.
Thus, these restatements are merely a repetition of the fourfold set of propositions.

Regarding the statement, "At times, one may take the presence or absence of folds as being existent, and so forth," this was merely listed by name in the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation). Here, I provide a brief explanation of the coarse aspects, using compound phrases to illustrate their characteristics.

The first phrase is abbreviated; it should be stated as "there is existence, there is non-existence, and the unconditioned exists," which refers to the existence and non-existence belonging to the category of existence (*bhava*).
Although there is a distinction between existence and non-existence, they both equally belong to existence; therefore, they are subsumed within existence.
The three propositions regarding "non-existence" (asat) may be understood by analogy with this.
If one considers them in terms of the complete four propositions, there is the case where all four belong to existence (sat), which is subsumed within existence.
The three phrases concerning "the peerless" can be understood by analogy with this.
